contested: The 1930 boundary marks the transition in migration, not the expiry of every contract. The guide’s regular contract-number series ends in 1929 and labels 1930 arrivals free immigrants. Hoefte places the turn to free colonists around 1930, says penal sanctions remained in force in Suriname until 1932, and dates the wind-down of contract labor to 1935. These sources do not identify the exact last contracted departure. Later free-immigrant and farmer-colonist projects, and the separate British-Indian and Chinese streams, remain outside this case.
note: The consulted overview does not measure how many recruits were misled or how many former workers took up the land offer. An uncultivated plot does not establish that the land was unoccupied; these passages do not demonstrate a shared displacement outcome for Indigenous communities. Arrival and return totals extending to 1939 or 1954 are not counts for this event. The route follows the archival guide: Hoefte’s p. 147 sentence appears to name Java, rather than Suriname, as the destination after Amsterdam. Her literary scenes from Deli and Suriname are not used as documentary evidence for this account.
geometryExplanation: The guide names departure ports, Paramaribo and plantations, but the consulted sources do not locate the workers’ receiving plots or establish a defensible event footprint. No port coordinate, plantation boundary or uniform voyage line is inferred from those names.

name: Japanese wartime deportation of Nauruans to Chuuk
displaced: Nauruans deported from their island to the Truk group; survivors returned in 1946
settlers: Japanese occupation authorities directing the deportations and forced work
evidence: Nancy Viviani’s historical account, drawing on deportees’ reports and wartime and postwar records
story:
Japanese occupation authorities deported Nauruans to the Truk group in two transfers in 1943. The first left on 30 June and the second on 16 August. Viviani places the first deportation amid worsening food shortages on Nauru; the families selected were told they would be taken to an island with plentiful food.

On the receiving islands, the deportees faced inadequate food and lacked housing and medical care. Japanese authorities forced Nauruan men into airstrip construction. The deportees built huts for shelter and canoes for fishing. Viviani reports hundreds of Nauruan deaths on Truk during 1944 and 1945.

The surviving deportees returned to Nauru on 31 January 1946. Viviani describes their reunion with people at home alongside news of relatives’ deaths and the destruction of their homes.
contested: Viviani questions the suspicion that landowners were deported to make disposal of their property easier. She states that Japanese documentation was unavailable to her. The reason given to families about food does not establish the full purpose of the deportations.
note: This case follows the Nauruan deportees. Banabans moved to Nauru, Chinese deportees and accompanying priests remain distinct groups in Viviani’s account.
placeGloss: Viviani uses Truk for the island group called Chuuk in the event record. No exact landing place or voyage route is reconstructed.
geometryExplanation: The wartime passages identify the Truk group without naming the receiving islands. The book’s map of Nauru depicts 1965 district geography, not wartime deportation sites or routes.

name: Kaptai Dam: reservoir flooding and displacement
displaced: Chakma and other Indigenous Jumma communities whose homes and cultivated land were flooded
settlers: Pakistan government and the Kaptai hydropower project
evidence: Source-attributed accounts by Mangal Kumar Chakma on the PCJSS website and Nalori Chakma for International Rivers
story: The Pakistan government’s Kaptai hydropower project flooded homes and cultivated valley land in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, then in East Pakistan. Nalori Chakma’s International Rivers account dates the start of construction to 1957 and completion to the early 1960s. Mangal Kumar Chakma, writing on the PCJSS party website, describes the loss of paddy fields and vegetable gardens, the flooding of much of Rangamati town, and inadequate compensation and rehabilitation. He reports that some displaced Chakma and other Jumma people went to India or Myanmar. He also describes displaced plough cultivators who remained in the Hill Tracts and were compelled to take up shifting cultivation after losing valley fields.
contested: These are critical advocacy accounts, and International Rivers draws on PCJSS as well as other publications. They are not two independent displacement censuses. Their area figures and chronology are inconsistent or insufficiently explained; no affected-area total, removed population share or compensation rate is calculated here. Claims of deliberate destruction of the Jumma economy, universal cultural loss or uniform treatment of displaced households are not established by this bounded reading.
note: The modeled 1957–1964 interval does not establish a final displacement date or completed rehabilitation in 1964. Later settlement programs and armed conflict are separate event histories. The inherited Imported unfree labor value of zero does not mean the reservoir displacement was voluntary. The full Parveen and Faisal article cited by International Rivers was not available for direct reading.
placeGloss: The Karnaphuli River and Rangamati identify the reservoir setting. India and Myanmar are broad reported destinations; no individual household journey, receiving site or affected-land boundary is reconstructed.
geometryExplanation: The accounts identify the reservoir setting, named river valleys and broad migration destinations. Their illustrations and area figures do not establish a dated affected-land boundary or a cohort-specific journey. The named river and town are narrated; no authenticated coordinate or footprint is supplied by this assessment.

name: Nepet colonial transition
dates: 383 BCE commission; alternative foundation tradition 373 BCE

periods.yearLabel: 383 BCE commission; alternative foundation tradition 373 BCE

displaced: Prior residents and landholders in Nepet’s attributed colonial territory; founding-time effects on residents remain unmeasured
settlers: Roman colonial authorities and intended settlers; the founders’ number and composition are unresolved
evidence: Livy’s commission notice, Velleius’s alternative foundation sequence, and Monica Chiabà’s reconstruction of colonial land use
story:
Livy records the appointment of three commissioners to establish a colony at Nepet. Monica Chiabà places this commission in 383 BCE. Livy assigns a separate group of five commissioners to divide the Pomptine territory.

Chiabà describes Nepet’s colony, like neighboring Sutrium, as established on territory confiscated from Falerii, chiefly to defend Roman citizens’ new settlements in former Veientine and Capenate territory. This territorial connection is her reconstruction; it does not date a new confiscation in 383 or identify a founding-time removal cohort.
contested: Velleius’s sequence places the foundation of Nepe ten years after Sutrium, conventionally 373 BCE. Chiabà favors a joint foundation in 383. The commission is not proof that settlement was completed then, and the competing dates do not establish a ten-year implementation delay or two colonial waves. Livy’s earlier account of Nepet’s recovery, killings and restoration of property concerns a separate episode; its victims and restored residents cannot be counted as the colony’s founding cohort.
note: All eight profile traits retain insufficient-evidence status. The inherited values for government direction (25), legal and property machinery (50), and lethal coercion (0) are not supported point estimates. Imported unfree labor remains unknown because its applicability gate is unknown.
placeGloss: Nepet is modern Nepi on the western Faliscan frontier; Livy’s English text uses Nepete and Velleius’s uses Nepe.
geometryExplanation: Chiabà locates the town on a tufa promontory between two valleys and describes its frontier position. These passages do not delimit the colony’s land or a settlers’ route. No assessed coordinate or historical footprint is supplied here.

name: Deportation of South Sea Islanders from Australia
displaced: South Sea Islander residents deported from Australia; Islanders who remained are outside this removal cohort
settlers: Australian federal government implementing removal under the Pacific Island Labourers Act of 1901
evidence: National Museum of Australia institutional history; deportation dates and approximate totals, not individual removal files
story: Australia’s federal government required most South Sea Island labourers to leave under the Pacific Island Labourers Act of 1901, part of the White Australia policy. The National Museum of Australia dates the deportations from late 1906 through 1908. It reports that more than 7,500 Islanders were sent to their countries of origin, including people who had arrived in Australia too young to remember those countries. About 2,500 Pacific Islanders remained. Islanders had campaigned against the law, sending protests to the Prime Minister, Governor-General and King; the museum records no major change to the Act. This outward removal of residents is separate from earlier recruitment into Queensland.
contested: The museum gives an aggregate account, not individual destinations or exemption decisions. Its earlier recruitment total does not count this deportation cohort. The read article does not establish household losses, resettlement conditions or a uniform experience after removal.
note: Imported unfree labor remains unknown in the inherited profile: the applicability gate is unknown, and an unfree-incomer share cannot establish imported labor by itself. This is not a zero or a finding that departure was voluntary. Legal and property machinery, elimination over incorporation, lethal coercion, durability and separation from homeland also retain limited-evidence displays.
placeGloss: Australia is the departure setting. Islands named in the museum’s earlier recruitment history do not identify each deportee’s destination.
geometryExplanation: The read museum article supplies no assessed departure port, receiving-island coordinate or individual route for this deportation event.

name: Bukhara: surrender, forced dispersal and military levy
displaced: Bukhara residents expelled from the city and compelled into Mongol military service
settlers: Mongol forces under Chinggis Khan
evidence: Peter Jackson’s scholarly synthesis of accounts by Ibn al-Athir and Juwayni
story: Bukhara surrendered to Chinggis Khan’s forces in 1220, while its citadel continued to resist. In Peter Jackson’s account, the residents negotiated terms after the defending troops had fled, but their property was forfeited and they were compelled to help attack the citadel. Once it fell, residents were driven out, divided into groups and deported. Jackson also recounts plunder, sexual violence against women and the killing of people found inside the city. Deportees were incorporated into the Mongol forces and taken toward Samarqand, where they were used to intimidate the city. His account also identifies forced levies from Bukhara among those employed against Khujand.
contested: Jackson distinguishes the treatment of cities that surrendered, resisted or rebelled and cautions against sweeping claims in the medieval narratives. This account follows his Bukhara reconstruction; it is not an independent reading of Ibn al-Athir or Juwayni. No population total, death toll, artisan count or removed share is established here, and the treatment of neighboring cities is not transferred to Bukhara.
note: February–March 1220 is the inherited modeled date window, not an exact capture date verified here. The 17 March date in Jackson’s campaign narrative belongs to Samarqand. Later return and rebuilding are outside this stop. The inherited Imported unfree labor value of zero does not mean that Bukhara’s residents were free from forced labor or deportation; the complete profile and its evidence limits are retained.
placeGloss: Bukhara is the city of expulsion. Samarqand and Khujand are named military destinations in the account, not verified final homes for all deportees or a reconstructed itinerary.
geometryExplanation: The read account identifies the cities and distinguishes Bukhara’s urban population from its resisting citadel. It provides no authenticated coordinates, dated city footprint, expulsion assembly area or cohort-specific route. Named destinations are narrated; no modern city boundary or straight-line journey is substituted.

name: Akosombo Dam flooding and Volta Basin resettlement
displaced: Volta Basin residents displaced by reservoir flooding; New Ajena residents provide the article’s local housing example
settlers: Government of Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah and authorities carrying out the resettlement program
evidence: Iain Jackson’s 2019 housing account, republished by CCE Online News; New Ajena recollections and the separate Akosombo worker town
story: In Ghana’s Volta River project, reservoir flooding displaced residents from homes and farmland upstream of the Akosombo Dam. Iain Jackson’s 2019 housing account describes New Ajena as a resettlement village replacing the former Ajena, which the lake submerged. Its small core houses provided a single room and raised veranda, intended for residents to enlarge later. Jackson reports interviews with residents who had lived there since the early 1960s: they recalled some larger families being forced to move from multi-room homes into one room, with overcrowded and unsanitary conditions. Akosombo’s town for hydro-power workers was a different development. Jackson contrasts its planned services with New Ajena’s more limited provision. In the wider resettlement program, he reports food distributed in exchange for labour and residents compelled to clear land.
contested: The New Ajena interviews do not establish the experience of every resettled community. Jackson’s descriptions of later services and resident additions belong to his 2019 account; they are not conditions verified today. Aggregate village, acreage and housing-production figures are not used to quantify this case.
note: The atlas retains the inherited 1961–1966 interval; the read housing article does not independently establish both endpoints or show that displacement and rehabilitation were complete in 1966. Imported unfree labor retains its inherited value of zero. That measure does not establish that relocation or the site-clearance work was voluntary.
placeGloss: New Ajena is the resettlement example; the former Ajena was submerged. Akosombo’s dam-worker town is a separate place and housing program.
geometryExplanation: The read article names the dam, former Ajena and New Ajena but supplies no assessed coordinate, reservoir boundary, affected-village footprint or individual relocation route.

name: Culebra: resident relocation for a naval range
displaced: Culebra residents required to move outside the Navy bombardment zone; the cited report does not give the number moved
settlers: United States federal government and Navy; Congress and federal land agencies in range closure and land disposition
evidence: Congressional Research Service report, 7 July 2005: required resident relocation, naval use through 1975, land disposition and later cleanup limits
story: In 1901, the United States government placed Culebra under Navy control for training and required residents to move outside the bombardment zone. David Bearden’s Congressional Research Service report describes this relocation within the island; it does not give a count of those moved. The Navy conducted training on Culebra and in surrounding waters through 1975. Responding to public safety concerns about live-fire training, Congress directed the Navy to cease operations and relocate them elsewhere under the Reserve Forces Facilities Authorization Act of 1974. In 1975, the Navy transferred land to the General Services Administration for conveyance to nonfederal entities for conservation and public recreation. The federal government retained a portion, which the report described in 2005 as a National Wildlife Refuge managed by the Department of the Interior. Closure left a further cleanup problem. The report records limited surface removal of munitions from publicly accessible areas since 1995, including beaches and campgrounds, while comprehensive cleanup remained unbegun in 2005.
contested: The report’s figure of 1,700 describes the civilian population living in the relocation areas in 2005, not the number removed in 1901. Its account does not identify household destinations, compensation or parcel boundaries. The 1975 closure does not establish complete restoration of residents’ land or unrestricted access. Cleanup observations describe 2005, not present conditions. Culebra’s relocation and closure are distinct from the report’s Vieques history.
note: The analytical profile is inherited from the frozen scientific release. Government direction has a supported value; legal and property machinery retains a partial-evidence range. The other six traits remain insufficiently evidenced for solid point displays. Imported unfree labor is unknown, not zero: the applicability gate is unresolved. These limits do not negate the documented requirement that residents relocate.
placeGloss: Culebra, off Puerto Rico. The reported movement was from the bombardment zone to other areas of the island; exact relocation points are not established here.
geometryExplanation: The consulted report identifies Culebra and relocation outside the bombardment zone but does not locate the removed households, receiving sites or historical tract boundaries. No route or tract is inferred from the Navy’s headquarters or from Vieques.

name: Qin: amnesty relocations to Yan and Deng
displaced: Amnestied persons under Qin penal authority relocated to Yan and Deng; their number and household origins are not supplied by the annual entry
settlers: Qin authorities and the army led by Bai Qi; amnestied persons placed in the captured territory
evidence: Shiji, Basic Annals of Qin, year 28; scholarly discussion of penal relocation by Anthony J. Barbieri-Low and military logistics by Kiyoshi Miyake
story: In 279 BCE, the twenty-eighth year of King Zhaoxiang, Bai Qi attacked Chu and captured Yan and Deng. The Shiji records the pardoning of guilty persons and their relocation there in the same annual entry. The two towns belong to this joined account of capture and placement. Anthony J. Barbieri-Low explains that qiān, the verb used for the relocation, carries a punitive sense in penal and deportation contexts, even when a person’s sentence had been commuted. In discussing Qin amnesty relocations, he leaves open whether convicts could volunteer or were selected by officials. Kiyoshi Miyake interprets the settlement of criminals along the Han River campaign as support for military logistics. That is his reconstruction of their role; the annal itself records relocation without specifying their duties.
contested: The annal supplies an annual date, not the duration of residence or a relocation timetable. It gives no count of the people moved or account of the captured towns’ residents sufficient to measure their removal or replacement. Rang and Nanyang occur in separate preceding annual entries; Ying’s capture follows in year 29. Miyake’s English prose misaligns the preceding Rang and Nanyang years with the Chinese annal quoted in his footnote, although both place Yan and Deng in year 28. No continuing cohort across these places is established here.
note: The inherited profile shows government direction as a partial-evidence range; the other seven traits lack sufficient evidence for solid point displays. Imported unfree labor remains unknown because its applicability gate is unresolved, despite the recorded penal status of the incomers. This is not a finding that the relocation was voluntary or that no compelled labor occurred.
placeGloss: Yan and Deng in the Qin–Chu frontier campaign. The joined annal does not locate the movers’ households or provide their routes.
geometryExplanation: The consulted event passages do not establish relocation origins, exact receiving sites or historical tract boundaries. No coordinates are borrowed from the separate Rang or Nanyang cases, and the two towns are not collapsed into an invented central point.

name: Umayyad conquest of Iberia and early consolidation
displaced: Communities under Visigothic rule, including people killed, captured or driven to flight; residents who remained under new rulers
settlers: Arab and Berber troops under Umayyad commanders Tariq ibn Ziyad, Musa ibn Nusayr and Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa; local rulers negotiating submission
evidence: The Chronicle of 754 in modern translation, and Daniel G. König’s study and translation of the transmitted Treaty of Tudmir; UNESCO supplies a modern Toledo reference coordinate
story: Tariq’s forces crossed from North Africa into Iberia in 711. Musa followed in 712, and his son Abd al-Aziz governed from about 714 until his assassination around 716. The Chronicle of 754 describes the defeat of King Roderic and violent submissions during the advance. It describes Musa’s advance to Toledo, the killing of nobles, captivity and people fleeing to the mountains. In the southeast, a treaty attributed to Abd al-Aziz and the local ruler Tudmir, also called Theodemir, is dated April 713. Its transmitted terms promise protection from killing, captivity and separation of families, and protection for churches and religious practice, conditional on submission and tribute. These are promises made in a regional agreement, rather than a record of how every community was treated. König describes a conquest in which negotiated relationships existed alongside resistance broken by force.
contested: The treaty survives in accounts written centuries later, with differences in city lists and obligations. König discusses doubts about the transmitted wording while treating an early submission agreement as plausible. He also identifies the Chronicle’s Theodemir passages as interpolations, so those passages cannot simply be counted as independent contemporary confirmation. The Chronicle’s account of devastation is rhetorical and supplies no measured peninsula-wide death or displacement total. The approximate endpoint around 716 marks this early conquest and consolidation episode; it does not establish that every district was subdued by then.
note: The profile retains the existing judgments for Government direction and Legal and property machinery. The other six traits have insufficient evidence for solid point displays, including Imported unfree labor, whose applicability remains unknown. Uncertainty about the extent of violence or population change does not negate the recorded killings, captivity and flight.
placeGloss: The point is UNESCO’s modern heritage reference for Toledo, one city named in the conquest account. The wider event includes other Iberian conquest and submission zones, including Tudmir’s southeastern territory.
geometryExplanation: A city reference point provides orientation. It does not locate an execution, trace an army’s journey or define the conquered territory. No modern national border, treaty-city polygon or flight route is used.

name: São Tomé and Príncipe: plantation settlement and enslaved labor
displaced: Enslaved Africans transported from mainland societies to the islands, including people from Benin, Kongo and Angola; early settlement also included transported convicts and Jewish children forcibly separated from their families
settlers: Portuguese crown and colonial officials, settlers, merchants and plantation owners; the islands’ landowning and slaveholding elite also included people of mixed descent and free Africans
evidence: Gerhard Seibert’s historical studies; Cruz, Thomas and Ceita’s study of early sugar plantations; Benjamin Moran’s 1876 diplomatic report of emancipation legislation
story: The Portuguese colonized São Tomé and Príncipe when the islands were uninhabited. Effective settlement of São Tomé began under Álvaro de Caminha in 1493; settlement of Príncipe began shortly after 1500. The settlers included convicts and Jewish children forcibly separated from their parents, alongside some volunteers. Africans brought from Benin and later Kongo and Angola were enslaved in households, food production and sugar plantations. Crown land grants helped establish the estates. Sugarcane fields are documented in 1506, and two mills were operating by 1517. Enslaved people escaped into São Tomé’s forested south, where communities developed beyond colonial control. The islands’ society also included free Africans and people of mixed descent who owned land and enslaved people. The early sugar economy declined, and sugar production disappeared during the seventeenth century. Domestic slavery and the slave trade continued while much agriculture shifted to subsistence and provisioning ships. Coffee and cocoa brought a renewed plantation economy in the nineteenth century, initially using enslaved labor. Emancipation followed several legal and local steps. Seibert describes plantation workers demanding immediate freedom after the 1875 emancipation law and Governor Gregório Ribeiro yielding to that demand. In March 1876, the American diplomat Benjamin Moran reported a new law, proclaimed by the king on 3 February, that released people still classed as freedmen and apprentices from their remaining service obligations. Plantation owners subsequently relied on contract workers; Seibert describes contracts extended without consent and coercive conditions continuing beyond the emancipation transition.
contested: The dates encompass different phases of island colonization and coerced labor, not continuous sugar production or an unchanged labor regime. The 1493 start belongs to São Tomé, not both islands simultaneously. Seibert’s account of local emancipation following the 1875 law and Moran’s report of accelerated legal emancipation in 1876 describe different actions; their exact relationship is not established here. The 1876 law took effect upon publication in the province, whose date is not supplied in Moran’s dispatch. Its royal proclamation date does not establish the provincial publication date. The endpoint does not mean all forced labor ended in 1876. No total for people removed across the entire period is asserted.
note: All eight traits retain their supported-point displays from the frozen scientific release. These are inherited analytical judgments, not population percentages. The inherited Settler replacement family label does not establish that an indigenous island population was replaced: the documented forced movement brought people from elsewhere to previously uninhabited islands.
placeGloss: São Tomé and Príncipe in the Gulf of Guinea. The sources name mainland regions from which enslaved people were brought, but this case does not reconstruct individual capture sites or sea routes.
geometryExplanation: No route, capture-site point or plantation boundary is drawn. The named islands and source regions identify the setting; the broad event spans changing places and populations, and the Praia Melão site cannot stand in for all of them.

name: Circeii under Volscian control (source-qualified)
dates: early fifth century BCE (precise capture year unresolved)

periods.yearLabel: Early fifth century BCE; precise year unresolved
periods.orderingAnchorExplanation: The numeric−500 is a playback ordering coordinate only, not an asserted capture date. Frozen start and end remain null.

displaced: Roman colonists and other residents of Circeii; the accounts disagree over expulsion and continued residence
settlers: Volscian forces; the tradition assigns their command to the Roman exile Coriolanus, whose role is unresolved
evidence: Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch give different accounts of Circeii’s surrender or capture; Monica Chiabà assesses the literary tradition
story:
In Monica Chiabà’s reconstruction, the Coriolanus tradition may preserve a Volscian takeover of Circeii in the early fifth century BCE. What happened to the town’s residents differs sharply between the accounts. Livy reports that the Roman colonists were expelled and the town handed to the Volscians.

Dionysius describes Roman colonists living alongside native residents. In his account, the townspeople opened the gates as the Volscian army approached. Nobody was killed or expelled; the commander took clothing, a month’s provisions and money, then left a small garrison to guard the town and prevent rebellion. Plutarch describes Circeii’s voluntary surrender without harm.
contested: These are competing accounts of the same takeover, not evidence of an expulsion followed by peaceful resettlement. Chiabà considers it probable that Plutarch drew much of his Life of Coriolanus from Dionysius, and discusses contradictions and anachronistic invention in the early Roman tradition. The exact capture year, Coriolanus’s role and the population outcome remain unresolved. The killings and enslavement described at other towns in the surrounding narratives cannot be assigned to Circeii.
note: All eight profile traits retain insufficient-evidence status. Imported unfree labor remains unknown because its applicability gate is unknown. The inherited profile does not resolve the conflicting accounts of the residents’ fate.
placeGloss: Circeii is the coastal Latium town discussed by Chiabà in connection with the Circeo promontory and San Felice Circeo. Livy’s displayed English text spells it Cerceii.
geometryExplanation: The readings identify the town but supply no assessed coordinate for this takeover, garrison, displaced people or territory. An attempted scholarly gazetteer lookup did not yield usable location data. No route or historical footprint is reconstructed.

name: Kitakami campaigns and fortified administration
displaced: Emishi communities in the Mutsu and Kitakami frontier; resident farmers driven from Taga during the 780 rebellion
settlers: Japanese imperial court, expeditionary forces and provincial officials; local Emishi leaders incorporated into court administration
evidence: Karl F. Friday’s study of the court campaigns and the Morioka City museum’s English exhibition guide; court chronicles are read through these modern accounts
story:
In 774 the Japanese imperial court ordered a military campaign against Emishi resistance in the northeast. Successive expeditions met defeats as well as victories. Friday describes an imperial assault on the Emishi village of Toyama that drove people out of their strongholds and off the surrounding cliffs. In 780, Iji no Azumaro led a rebellion, killed provincial officials and attacked Taga, routing its garrison and forcing resident farmers to flee. The army sent against the rebels broke up in 781 without a decisive result.

The court also extended its presence through fortified administrative centers and local leaders. The Morioka museum dates Isawa’s fortress to 802 and Shiwa’s to 803, describing them as combined military and administrative facilities. Its account says recent excavations suggest that Shiwa’s Emishi accepted the construction while retaining their own power. Friday argues that continued fortification and the incorporation of Emishi leaders through ranks, titles and local office accounted for more of the court’s territorial gains than its large expeditions.

In 805 the court reconsidered the burden of the wars and construction of the new capital and ordered them halted. It nevertheless commissioned a final campaign in 811 and then declared the Emishi pacified. Friday treats this as a change in official policy and outlook rather than completed control: Emishi communities retained a distinct identity, and local Emishi leadership remained part of the administration.
contested: The museum describes the 801 campaign as a conquest of the Kitakami basin north of Isawa. Friday emphasizes the scarcity of details for the later campaigns and argues that much of the northeast was no more firmly controlled after the wars than before. The court’s declaration is therefore not treated here as uniform conquest, population replacement or the disappearance of Emishi identity. The museum describes Emishi as a political category and records differing local relationships with the state. Its Ooshima evidence chiefly concerns the middle ninth to early tenth centuries, after this episode; it cannot be backdated to 774–811. Neither the consulted campaign account nor the local archaeological guide supplies a complete displaced-population count or replacement share.
note: Government direction retains a supported point in the inherited profile. The other seven traits have insufficient evidence for solid point displays, including Imported unfree labor, whose applicability remains unknown. The campaign period is a connected sequence with reversals, not a claim of continuous fighting or one 37-year migration. The earlier Mutsu reorganization and 725 transfer remain separate events.
placeGloss: The account concerns the Mutsu and Kitakami frontier, including Taga, Isawa and Shiwa. Named places do not define a conquered territory or a measured population movement.
geometryExplanation: The consulted sources name forts and localities, but this packet has not verified coordinates for a source-qualified marker, a conquest boundary or a relocation route. The museum’s location figures are orientation aids, not a measured campaign or displacement map. No marker or route is drawn.

name: Scottish Highland and Island Clearances
displaced: Highland and Island tenants, crofters and cottars affected by eviction, relocation and pressure on access to land
settlers: Estate landlords and managers; commercial sheep farmers took larger holdings
evidence: Scottish History Society overview and National Records of Scotland’s guide to the Napier Commission records
story:
From around 1750, estate reorganization for higher rents consolidated small holdings into larger farms, many let for sheep. Evicted tenants often received smaller, poorer crofts. In the first wave, beginning in the 1780s, some owners moved tenants to coastal plots for fishing and kelp work. Others expelled them from their estates.

For the Sutherland estates in 1809–1821, the Scottish History Society reports nearly 15,000 people relocated, with interior land turned over to sheep and crofts established along the coast. It describes violent evictions and resistance, and cautions that Sutherland was atypical.

After 1825, falling prices and the decline of kelp employment deepened hardship. The potato failures of 1836–1837 and 1846–1848 added subsistence crises. Some landlords evicted poor tenants and sometimes financed emigration.

Land protest in the early 1880s brought crofters’ grievances before the Napier Commission, appointed in 1883. The Crofters’ Holdings (Scotland) Act followed in 1886, providing tenure protection and machinery for determining crofters’ rents.
contested: The case follows a regional transformation through differing local phases, not a single removal operation. Sutherland’s figure is not a total for the Highlands and Islands, and emigration cannot all be classified as forced removal. The 1886 endpoint marks legislation, not the restoration of all lost land. Much Napier testimony was retrospective; the surviving estate returns cover only part of the region.
note: The eight-trait profile retains the accepted release’s judgments, including its zero for imported unfree labor. These are ordinal analytical values, not population percentages. The two sources used for this narrative do not recertify the entire profile.
placeGloss: The Highlands and Islands of Scotland; Sutherland is one estate example, while the 1880s protests included Skye, Lewis, Tiree and western Sutherland.
geometryExplanation: The readings describe dispersed estates, townships and coastal relocations without an assessed coordinate set or a single clearance boundary. No regional center, removal route or overseas destination is inferred from those place names.

name: Anti-Tutsi violence, exile and blocked return in Rwanda
displaced: Tutsi people killed or forced to flee Rwanda in successive outbreaks of violence
settlers: Participants in anti-Tutsi violence; Rwandan authorities restricting return; Tutsi refugees seeking refuge in neighboring countries
evidence: UNHCR’s historical account of the 1959–1963 exile and Human Rights Watch’s retrospective account of the 1959–1966 and 1973 waves
story:
Outbreaks of violence forced Tutsi people to flee Rwanda between 1959 and 1966 and again in 1973. Human Rights Watch’s World Report 1992 describes tens of thousands massacred and several hundred thousand forced into exile across those outbreaks. It identifies the refugees’ main countries of residence as Zaire, Burundi, Uganda and Tanzania.

Exile continued long after the attacks. UNHCR describes the refugees from the 1959–1963 crisis as denied repatriation for the next three decades. Human Rights Watch records that President Juvénal Habyarimana’s government initially opposed return on the grounds of limited national resources. By the report’s 1991 context, he had said refugees were welcome to return, but no significant number had done so. A declared welcome had not yet produced substantial repatriation.
contested: These dates bound successive outbreaks, not one continuous expulsion or a claim that exile ended in 1973. Human Rights Watch’s estimate of 400,000–700,000 Tutsi exiles concerns the population living in exile in its 1991 account; it is not a count newly removed in a single outbreak or a measured 1959–1973 total. Its broad estimates of killings and forced exile are not a complete household or property-loss record. The later return-policy statement qualifies an absolute claim that return was always forbidden, without establishing that return was safe or widely achieved. This case does not include the 1990–1994 wartime cohorts, the 1994 genocide or the later Hutu refugee exodus. Responsibility for attacks and official exclusion is not assigned collectively to every member of an ethnic group, and refugee status does not establish participation in the RPF.
note: The inherited family is Expulsion or flight without replacement. All eight traits retain their existing supported-point displays, including the zero for Imported unfree labor. These are the frozen release’s profile values, not new estimates derived from the refugee totals. No population replacement share is inferred from those totals.
placeGloss: Rwanda is the place of removal. Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), Burundi, Uganda and Tanzania are the neighboring countries of refuge named in the account; they are not a claim about particular camps, routes or a successor-settlement project.
geometryExplanation: The sources identify Rwanda and neighboring countries of refuge, but the consulted evidence does not establish verified departure points, camps or routes for these early waves. No country centroid is substituted for a refugee location, and no marker or route is drawn.

name: Scandinavian conquest and settlement in the Danelaw
displaced: English landholders and communities in Northumbria, East Anglia and parts of Mercia, where conquest and settlement changed rule and control of land
settlers: Scandinavian raiding groups and their leaders; settlers, families, artisans and merchants associated with the armies and later migration
evidence: Chronicle accounts of conquest and land division, assessed alongside Ben Raffield’s historical and archaeological study and Yumi Yokota’s analysis of place names
story:
Scandinavian armies conquered much of Northumbria, East Anglia and Mercia during campaigns beginning in 865. The Great Army brought together allied raiding groups rather than the forces of one Scandinavian state. Its members included families, artisans and merchants as well as combatants. Settlement took place in an already inhabited landscape.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Halfdan (Healfden in the Ingram translation) dividing Northumbrian land in 876, after which the newcomers cultivated it. Its entry for 877 describes the army sharing out part of Mercia and leaving part to Ceolwulf; the 880 entry records settlement and land division in East Anglia. These accounts identify changes in possession and use of land without counting the settlers or the residents who lost holdings.

Political control and settlement varied by locality. Raffield argues that the evidence supports fragmented centers of power, with relationships between urban leaders and rural communities often unclear. Scandinavian newcomers and English residents also developed mixed cultural practices. In the tenth century, West Saxon and Mercian rulers extended their control over the areas of Scandinavian settlement. The Chronicle’s 954 entry records the Northumbrians expelling Eric and King Edred taking rule.
contested: The name Danelaw is used here for areas of Scandinavian settlement and influence, not a single state with fixed borders. Raffield questions the later territorial model and treats his interpretation as preliminary. Place names reveal contact and influence, but Yokota shows why they cannot directly identify the ancestry or number of a ninth-century population: names could be adopted by English speakers and created long after the first settlements. The chronology also depends on the edition. Raffield dates the Great Army’s arrival to 865; the Ingram/Giles compilation places its arrival in East Anglia under 866. The land-division dates above follow that compilation, while Raffield places some movements a year earlier.
note: The interval follows the conquest and settlement sequence through the political change of 954. That endpoint does not date the end of Scandinavian migration or the disappearance of settlers and their descendants. The land-division accounts do not establish a region-wide expulsion or a replacement share.
placeGloss: Northumbria, East Anglia and Mercia were inhabited English kingdoms. The case concerns changing areas of Scandinavian settlement within them, including York and settlements farther south.
geometryExplanation: The sources describe changing regional areas and debate the dating and interpretation of individual sites. They do not supply one verified settlement boundary or relocation route for this episode. No representative coordinate has been verified for the case, so no marker or route is drawn.

name: Safavid campaigns and Georgian deportations to Iran
displaced: Georgian civilians in Kartli and Kakheti, including women and boys taken captive and deported to Iran
settlers: Shah Abbas I and Safavid forces and officials; Georgian rulers, nobles and resistance forces
evidence: Hitchins’s account of the Georgian campaigns, Perry’s account of deportation and resettlement, and Matthee’s reading of contemporary accounts
story:
Shah Abbas I sent a campaign against Kartli and Kakheti in 1614. When nobles in Kakheti revolted in 1615, his troops ravaged the country. The campaigns brought killings and forced removal to Iran. Rudi Matthee identifies the punitive Georgian campaign of 1616 as an episode of mass killing, capture and enslavement, including women and boys.

Deportation also redirected people toward places the shah wanted to develop. John R. Perry records a transfer to Farahabad on the Caspian in 1615. That group mixed peasants from Karabakh and Shirvan who had fled to Georgia with people from Georgia and Ganja described as rebels. It cannot supply a Georgian-only total.

In his discussion of the wider campaign and its aftermath, Keith Hitchins describes an apparent plan to remove or kill the Kakhetians and settle Qizilbash and other Turkmen tribes in their country. This is evidence of a replacement plan, not a record of its full completion. His wider account of Georgians in Iran distinguishes agricultural settlement from military and royal-household service, and notes that some nobles entered service voluntarily. Those broader histories do not identify every destination or fate of the people removed in 1614–1616.
contested: The scale of killing and deportation is uncertain. Matthee attributes large totals to a chronicler; they are reported estimates, not a census of the people removed in this event. The retained Hitchins text contains a malformed deportation number, which is not used. Perry’s mixed Farahabad group and his estimate for deportations across the Safavid period cannot be counted as this case’s Georgian population. A missionary report from Gori in 1629, discussed by Matthee, looks back over a wider period of devastation; it does not extend this event to 1629. The Armenian deportation and New Julfa program of 1604–1605 are a separate case. Later fighting and the broader incorporation of Georgians into Safavid society do not demonstrate completed population replacement, universal assimilation or an end to Georgian resistance.
note: The family and all eight traits are inherited unchanged. Government direction and Imported unfree labor retain supported-point status; the other six traits remain insufficient-evidence displays. The inherited zero for Imported unfree labor is not a new conclusion that these campaigns involved no captivity, enslavement or compelled movement.
placeGloss: Kartli and Kakheti are the Georgian source territories. Farahabad is the Caspian destination named for Perry’s mixed 1615 transfer. Hitchins places a Georgian agricultural community in Faridan in Isfahan province within a wider settlement history, without assigning it a measured share of this event’s deportees. Abbas is rendered ʿAbbās in the sources; Qizilbash appears as qezelbāš.
geometryExplanation: The consulted accounts name source territories and several kinds of destination, but do not provide verified coordinates, routes, event-specific destination shares or a completed replacement footprint. No centroid or schematic arrow is substituted for a deportee location; no marker or route is proposed.

name: Nubian displacement by the Aswan dams
displaced: Egyptian and Sudanese Nubian communities whose homes and land were flooded or made uninhabitable
settlers: Dam-building and resettlement authorities in Egypt and Sudan
evidence: AUC Social Research Center project history, Robert A. Fernea’s ethnographic account, and Negm-el-Din Mohammed Sherif’s account of Sudanese Nubia
story:
The first Aswan Dam, built in 1902, and its later heightenings flooded homes and farmland in Egyptian Nubia. Robert A. Fernea describes unequal effects: northern communities rebuilt on higher, rocky ground, while southern communities retained more agricultural land. Loss of productive land also pushed people toward work in cities. These earlier adjustments were distinct from the compulsory resettlement brought by the High Dam.

In Egypt, the 1964 relocation took Nubians to the Kom Ombo area north of Aswan. The American University in Cairo’s Social Research Center describes New Nubia resettlement as compulsory and reports considerable stress despite plans to preserve self-sufficiency and identity. The government provided housing, utilities and irrigated land for sugar cane. Those provisions do not establish that displaced households recovered all they had lost.

The reservoir also submerged homeland in Sudanese Nubia. Sherif, a Sudan Antiquities Service official involved in the salvage campaign, describes this loss alongside the rescue of monuments. AUC’s project history records Sudanese Nubian resettlement on land irrigated by the Khashm el-Girba dam; it describes a researcher’s later visit there in 1969. This is a different receiving area from Egyptian Kom Ombo.

Nubian life continued after relocation. AUC researchers documented surviving culture as well as social change, and Fernea described the longstanding importance of kinship, marriage and language. Writing in 1980, he also reported Egyptian Nubians’ efforts to explore settlement along the new lake. This was a hope for return, not a report of completed restitution.
contested: This case includes both Egyptian and Sudanese Nubians across 1902–1964, but the consulted sources provide more detail about Egyptian households and resettlement. The Sudanese receiving-area statement is AUC’s retrospective account; no exact Sudanese removal date or count is established here. Fernea’s 50,000 refers to people actually living in Egyptian Nubia, distinguished from a larger population with homes and family ties there. It is not a combined displaced total for Egypt and Sudan. Earlier voluntary moves near Kom Ombo, labor migration and rebuilding after the old dam must not all be counted as compulsory 1964 relocation. Sherif’s generalized claim of willing acceptance does not demonstrate consent by every household. Cultural continuity and rescued monuments do not establish full restitution, and homeland loss does not mean Nubian culture disappeared. Later research and hopes of return do not extend the plotted event beyond 1964.
note: The family and all eight traits are inherited unchanged as supported points. These values are not newly estimated displacement totals, compensation rates or measures of cultural survival. The inherited zeros for Settler implantation and Imported unfree labor do not deny the forced removal of Nubian communities.
placeGloss: Kom Ombo is the Egyptian resettlement area north of Aswan. Khashm el-Girba names the Sudanese dam and irrigated receiving area in AUC’s account, which uses several spellings of the name. Old Nubia is a homeland term in these sources, not a verified reservoir boundary.
geometryExplanation: The sources identify affected river communities and receiving areas, but this authoring pass has not verified household departure points, resettlement coordinates or routes. A heritage-rescue map cannot substitute for displacement geometry, and Kom Ombo cannot stand for Sudanese destinations. No marker, route or inundation polygon is proposed.

name: Mongol capture of Samarkand and removal of artisans and young men
displaced: Samarkand residents selected as craftspeople and young male levies; other residents killed, driven out, ransomed or subjected to further levies
settlers: Chinggis Khan, Mongol forces, his sons and kinsmen, and the officials appointed to administer Samarkand
evidence: Juvaini’s account in John Andrew Boyle’s translation, Peter Jackson’s historical synthesis, and Ulrike Halbertsma-Herold’s study of imperial workshops
story:
Mongol forces under Chinggis Khan captured Samarkand in 1220. Juvaini describes a surrender followed by the dismantling of defenses, the forced assembly of residents outside the town, plunder and killing. Some people received protection; others were killed after hiding or during the remaining resistance. The account does not describe the destruction of every inhabitant.

Juvaini reports that 30,000 survivors were selected for their craft skills and distributed among Chinggis Khan’s sons and kinsmen. He gives a similar number for a levy of young men. Some of the levies went with Chinggis Khan to Khorasan and others with his sons to Khwarazm. Remaining survivors were allowed back into the town under a ransom demand. Juvaini also records repeated later levies, without dating each one. These movements took people from the city for the conquerors’ use; the levy destinations do not establish where every artisan was sent.

The city’s losses continued beyond the initial assault. Jackson relays Changchun’s December 1221 report that the city’s population stood at about a quarter of its former level. That comparison cannot separate deaths from captivity, departure or other causes of depopulation. Later evidence also traces some artisans eastward. Jackson describes about 3,000 artisan households, many from Samarkand, transported to Xunmalin in northern China and mentioned by Rashid al-Din some seventy years later. This mixed household population is not the same measure as Juvaini’s reported number of craftspeople.
contested: The figures are transmitted source reports, not audited counts. Jackson questions the reliability of large conquest-era totals and distinguishes killing from later population losses. Halbertsma-Herold’s workshop discussion also includes people from Samarkand and Bukhara; it uses workers where Jackson uses households. Those units cannot be interchanged. Her broader discussion of hereditary service does not establish the fate of every Samarkand captive or descendant. The sources do not provide a complete destination register, a mortality rate, or a share of the original population permanently removed.
note: The retained interval is 1220–c. 1223 CE. The capture belongs to 1220, although Boyle’s note corrects the chronicle’s year and questions its precise dating. Later levies are undated in the passage. The approximate endpoint does not date a final Samarkand shipment: Jackson’s note giving an arrival in 1223 concerns artisans from Khwarazm. The later workshop evidence is follow-up context, not another event inside this interval. The family and all eight traits remain inherited; the zero for Imported unfree labor does not mean these removals were voluntary or involved no captive labor.
placeGloss: Samarkand (Samarqand in the sources) is the source city. Khorasan and Khwarazm (Khorazm in Boyle’s translation) are the destinations named for levies. Xunmalin is a later eastern workshop location for a mixed population. These are distinct places and evidential contexts, not a single documented route. Chinggis Khan appears as Chingiz-Khan in Boyle’s translation.
geometryExplanation: The sources name the city, levy destinations and a later mixed workshop population, but do not verify coordinates or a single route for this event. No point or line is substituted for an unknown captive location or destination share.

name: Expulsion of Jews from Castile and Aragon
displaced: Jewish residents of Castile and Aragon who left under the 1492 expulsion order
settlers: The crowns of Castile and Aragon under Isabella and Ferdinand
evidence: The Alhambra Decree in an English translation hosted by Florida Atlantic University, and Ariel Hessayon’s review of François Soyer’s history of persecution in Portugal
story:
On 31 March 1492, Isabella and Ferdinand issued the Alhambra Decree, ordering Jewish residents to leave their realms by the end of July. The order covered children and adults, including people born elsewhere. It threatened death and confiscation for those who remained or returned in defiance of the decree. Its stated rationale blamed Jewish contact with Christians for departures from Catholic practice. These were the rulers’ allegations and justification for collective expulsion.

Before the deadline, the decree promised royal protection and permitted residents to sell or otherwise dispose of movable possessions and real estate. Goods could be taken out by land or sea, subject to restrictions that prohibited exporting gold, silver, coin and other banned items. These provisions describe the legal order. They do not show that everyone received protection or a fair price.

Conversion offered a way to remain. Portugal became a refuge for exiles who left: Hessayon reports that many Castilian Jews sold property at discounted prices before paying a substantial entry tax. He also describes restrictions on permanent settlement in Portugal. The number entering Portugal is disputed, and it is not a count of everyone expelled from Castile and Aragon.

Some exiles converted to Christianity and returned to Castile. The later Portuguese expulsions and forced conversions belong to separate events.
contested: The decree is evidence of royal commands and penalties, not a record of every local enforcement action. Its sale provisions and confiscation penalties do not establish blanket confiscation of all departing residents’ private property. Hessayon’s account is a scholarly review of Soyer’s book; the book itself was not consulted. The review contrasts very different estimates of arrivals in Portugal and describes some converted return, but it does not establish a comprehensive 1492 expulsion or return total. Its wider diaspora list covers several expulsions and roughly a century and a half. Earlier conversos fleeing the Inquisition, Portuguese actions in 1496–1497 and the removal of Jewish children to São Tomé are not added to this case’s 1492 cohort.
note: The family and all eight traits are inherited unchanged. They are ordinal summaries, not percentages of people expelled, property confiscated or return prevented. The Separation from homeland value does not mean that no exile ever returned; the narrative preserves the reported return of some people after conversion.
placeGloss: Castile and Aragon are the realms named in the 1492 case. Portugal is a documented destination for part of the expelled population, not a substitute for every exile’s destination. The decree’s place of issue, Granada, is not the departure point for all those displaced.
geometryExplanation: The sources name the affected realms and describe arrivals in Portugal, but they do not establish a single departure point, a complete route or a bounded expulsion footprint. Granada identifies where the decree was issued, not a common origin of the exiles. The review’s border camps and later ports concern different stages and subsets of movement. No verified event-specific coordinates or historical territorial geometry are supplied here, so no marker, route, polygon or reference registration is proposed.

name: Northern-iwi invasions of Ngāi Tahu communities and territory
displaced: Ngāi Tahu people attacked at Kaikōura, Kaiapohia and Akaroa/Ōnawe, including Tama-i-haranui and his wife and daughter, who were captured
settlers: Ngāti Toa under Te Rauparaha and Te Pēhi Kupe, and northern allies; Captain John Stewart and the brig Elizabeth; Ngāti Tama chief Te Pūoho and his war party; Ngāi Tahu defenders led at Tuturau by Tūhawaiki
evidence: Basil Keane’s Te Ara account of the South Island battles and Te Pūoho’s final campaign, read with its neighboring sections to distinguish other peoples and earlier movements
story:
War parties from Ngāti Toa and northern allies attacked Ngāi Tahu communities in a succession of South Island campaigns. Basil Keane’s Te Ara account links Te Rauparaha’s southern ambitions to control of pounamu trade. It places the attack and killing of Ngāi Tahu at Kaikōura after the opening southern campaigns around 1827. A party then went to Kaiapohia pā, where Te Pēhi Kupe was killed while trading for pounamu.

In 1830, Ngāti Toa persuaded Captain John Stewart to carry them to Akaroa aboard the brig Elizabeth. Tama-i-haranui, also called Te Maiharanui, and his wife and daughter were captured. The account states that he was subsequently tortured and killed; it does not describe every captive’s fate. This attack involved a European captain and ship as well as the invading war party.

Ngāti Toa successfully attacked Kaiapohia and then Ōnawe pā at Akaroa in 1831. In its wider southern account, Te Ara describes conquest across much of the South Island, but also records that Ngāi Tahu had acquired muskets and became harder to fight. The campaign sequence included resistance and reversal.

The final northern war party in this account was led by Ngāti Tama chief Te Pūoho. It traveled from Golden Bay along the West Coast, crossed the Southern Alps and reached Tuturau in Southland in late 1836 or early 1837. Ngāi Tahu leader Tūhawaiki assembled a force and surprised the party. Te Pūoho was killed and the others were taken prisoner.
contested: This short account establishes attacks, killing, capture and pā conquest, but does not measure displacement, settlement or a lasting population change across the island. Its statement about the extent of conquest does not establish permanent whole-island replacement or a formal land-title regime. It supplies neither complete casualty and captive totals nor the civilian and combatant composition of those affected. The Elizabeth passage identifies transport of the invading party to Akaroa; it does not provide a complete route for the captives.
note: The 1827–1837 interval is an approximate outer window: Te Ara begins the southern sequence around 1827 and places the Tuturau encounter in late 1836 or early 1837. This case concerns its Ngāi Tahu sequence. The earlier attacks on Rangitāne and Ngāti Kuia, the 1822–1824 Kāpiti migration and consolidation, and the 1835 invasion of the Moriori homeland are distinct events. The family and all eight traits remain inherited. The insufficient-evidence displays and Imported unfree labor’s not-applicable status do not negate the documented violence or capture.
placeGloss: Kaikōura, Kaiapohia, Akaroa/Ōnawe and Tuturau are the named locations in the Ngāi Tahu sequence. Golden Bay, the West Coast and the Southern Alps describe Te Pūoho’s approach. These places do not define one continuously occupied territory or a complete captive route. The source spelling Kaiapohia is retained.
geometryExplanation: The consulted account names several attacks and a broad approach, but supplies no verified coordinates, common settlement footprint or complete captive route. No point or schematic line is substituted for those unknowns.

name: Maasai conservation evictions from Serengeti, Ngorongoro and Loliondo
displaced: Maasai pastoralists losing homes, grazing land and access to cultural sites in northern Tanzania
Existing Msomera residents losing land to the government’s resettlement program
settlers: British colonial authorities in Tanganyika; the Tanzanian government, conservation authorities and security forces
evidence: Human Rights Watch’s July 2024 investigation, a December 2024 dispatch by Oryem Nyeko, and its World Report 2026 account of events in 2025
story:
British colonial authorities declared Serengeti a national park in 1951. Human Rights Watch’s historical account connects the removal of communities from the park with the creation of the Ngorongoro Conservation Area in 1959. Ngorongoro was intended as a permanent homeland where Maasai pastoralists would coexist with wildlife. Over subsequent decades, conservation authorities restricted cultivation and access to grazing, water and cultural sites. Earlier resettlement attempts also met with return or onward movement.

The recent operations were distinct. In Loliondo, north of the conservation area, the government moved in June 2022 to turn village land into a game reserve. Human Rights Watch reported security forces using tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters and bystanders, followed by further violence and destruction of homes. In the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, a separate government program began moving residents to Msomera village in June 2022.

Authorities described the Ngorongoro relocation as voluntary. Human Rights Watch’s investigation found that cuts to education and health services, limits on movement and grazing, and abuses by conservation rangers pressured residents to leave. Interviewees described inadequate consultation, and some women were excluded when a male household head registered the family. These findings concern the reported conditions and decision process; registration alone did not demonstrate agreement by every household member.

At Msomera, the government provided houses, land, cash assistance and infrastructure. Relocated residents nevertheless described housing that did not fit their families, compensation that did not cover their resettlement costs, and difficulties obtaining water. Msomera already had pastoralist residents, including Maasai families. They reported that authorities allocated land they occupied or used to the incoming households, without adequate consultation, and threatened people who questioned the process. Government officials, surveyors and contractors directed the land allocation and construction.

Later reports qualify the 2024 account. In December 2024, Nyeko reported an announcement of two investigation committees, an earlier pledge to restore services, school-dormitory funding and removal of a vehicle fee for residents. Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2026, describing events in 2025, reported that the committees launched in February and that some restrictions were lifted pending their investigations. These steps did not establish complete restoration of services or land.
contested: The inherited case covers conservation displacement from 1951 onward; it does not make every removal a 1951 event or combine Loliondo and Ngorongoro-to-Msomera into one operation. Human Rights Watch’s 2024 investigation used interviews conducted in 2022–2023, including affected residents and a government administrator. Its interview sample was not a population census. The report gives a government estimate of 3,010 people in 551 households relocated from Ngorongoro to Msomera as of January 2023. A plan for about 82,000 people to leave by 2027 and a census population estimate of 100,793 measure different things; neither is an already-removed total. Housing and assistance do not establish universal consent or full compensation. Loss of access to cultural sites does not mean Maasai culture has disappeared. The later update describes 2025 as reported in World Report 2026; it does not verify conditions in September 2026 or completion of the planned relocation.
note: The family and all eight traits are inherited unchanged. These ordinal summaries are not percentages of residents relocated, shares consenting or measures of cultural survival. The incoming households at Msomera and the residents already there are described separately; this authoring does not recode the profile from their shared Maasai identity.
placeGloss: Serengeti, the Ngorongoro Conservation Area and Loliondo are distinct parts of the history. Msomera is a receiving village in Handeni district, Tanga region. Its existing residents are part of the relocation’s consequences, not inhabitants of empty land awaiting settlement.
geometryExplanation: The sources identify affected areas and Msomera as a receiving settlement, but this pass has not verified event-specific coordinates, departure points or displacement boundaries. The roughly 600-kilometer distance reported for Ngorongoro-to-Msomera does not identify an actual travel route. Loliondo operations and earlier Serengeti removals cannot be represented by that single movement. No marker, route, polygon or reference registration is proposed.

name: Arab-Muslim conquest of Egypt and establishment of Fusṭāṭ
displaced: Egyptian residents subjected to warfare, exactions and flight; civilians sheltering in Alexandria, distinct from withdrawing Byzantine troops
settlers: Arab-Muslim forces under ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and the new garrison authorities
evidence: John of Nikiu’s translated chronicle, modern historical studies, and a dated supply receipt described by the Austrian National Library
story:
Arab-Muslim forces under ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ entered Egypt in late 639 or early 640. The Byzantine fortress of Babylon surrendered in 641; Alexandria was handed over under an agreement providing for Byzantine withdrawal in 642. A Byzantine expedition briefly recovered Alexandria in 645–646 before the Arab reconquest. These military reversals form the event’s closing phase.

The conquest involved violence, coercion and negotiated submission. John of Nikiu describes bloodshed at Fayum, the binding and dispossession of Roman magistrates, forced supplies, and residents abandoning possessions and fleeing to Alexandria. His sweeping language about flight is not a count of Egypt’s population. His account of the Alexandria agreement allows Byzantine troops to leave by sea with their property, while promising protection for Christian churches and allowing Jews to remain. It also describes angry resistance to the agreement among Alexandrians. Negotiation does not establish unanimous consent or universal fulfillment of its terms.

In that treaty sequence, John reports that Egyptians sheltering in Alexandria asked the patriarch Cyrus to secure permission for them to return to their cities as subjects of the conquerors. Cyrus negotiated according to their request. This is evidence of a request and negotiation, not a measured return rate. The same account describes the retention or appointment of local officials and further demands for supplies and canal labor.

Fusṭāṭ became a garrison and administrative center. Bruning, de Jong and Sijpesteijn describe the reuse and alteration of Byzantine structures around Babylon, and the mobilization of workmen and building materials through local administrators. Sijpesteijn distinguishes this urban establishment from a general redistribution of rural estates: her study reports housing plots allocated to Muslim army leaders around Fusṭāṭ and Alexandria, and Arab soldiers moving into houses vacated by departing Byzantines in Alexandria. In the sources she reviews, conquest-era rural confiscations are not recorded. That qualified finding does not establish that no individual resident lost land.

The new rulers also drew supplies from Egypt. The Austrian National Library identifies a Greek-Arabic receipt dated 25 April 643 for 65 sheep. This is one documented transaction, not a population measure. Continued administration, urban settlement and military exactions can therefore be described without asserting a countrywide replacement of Egypt’s residents.
contested: The chronicle’s translated, textually mediated account and its confessional language require attribution. Modern studies also depend partly on overlapping narrative sources. Christides argues that Copts and Melkites were not uniformly opposed political camps; neither group can be assigned one response to the conquest. Sijpesteijn’s note on reports of massacre and exodus after Alexandria’s reconquest raises the possibility of later fiscal-legal fabrication. No casualty total or mass exodus count for that episode is asserted here. The read sources do not establish a national removal, settlement or return rate.
note: The frozen interval remains late 639/early 640–646 CE. The refugee request belongs to John’s account of the first Alexandria settlement, not to the 645–646 reconquest; the passage does not separately date the refugees’ return. Later seventh- and eighth-century rural settlement and church changes are outside this case. The inherited family and full eight-trait profile remain unchanged; this narrative does not recertify their scalar values.
placeGloss: Babylon here is the Byzantine fortress around which Fusṭāṭ developed in Egypt, not Babylon in Mesopotamia. Alexandria and the Fayum are distinct settings in the account. Fusṭāṭ also appears as Fustat; John of Nikiu is also styled John of Nikiou.
geometryExplanation: The read sources identify several cities and a broad conquest area but provide no verified coordinates, shared displacement route or dated occupation polygon. Named places alone do not locate all displaced residents; the consolidated stop therefore has unknown geometry.

name: Russian occupation and flight from Åland during the Great Wrath
displaced: Åland residents who fled to Sweden; communities affected by occupation elsewhere in Finland remain a distinct regional context
settlers: Russian imperial forces and occupation authorities
evidence: Visit Åland’s historical chronology, with regional context from Rokua Geopark’s account of the Great Wrath
story:
The Great Wrath was the Russian occupation of Finland during the Great Northern War. Rokua Geopark’s historical account dates the occupation to 1713–1721, when Finland had been part of Sweden. Within this broader episode, Visit Åland’s chronology records devastation by Russian forces in Åland in 1714 and the flight of a majority of the population to Sweden.

The same Åland chronology places the inhabitants’ return in 1721–1723. Flight and subsequent return are both part of this case. The brief entries give neither an exact number of people who left nor a measure of how many returned. They support displacement followed by return, without establishing that every inhabitant fled or that every refugee came back.

The wider occupation affected regions differently. Rokua Geopark describes devastation, killings, forced transport to Russia and internal flight in its account of North Ostrobothnia and the surrounding region. These regional experiences provide context for the occupation; they do not establish an Åland death toll or an Åland deportation total. The available Åland entries likewise do not describe a durable incoming settler community replacing the people who fled.
contested: Both consulted pages are heritage accounts. Visit Åland provides a short chronology; Rokua Geopark names historical works and records that were not independently read here. Its regional figures cannot be applied to Åland or treated as national totals. The Åland entries do not measure household losses, the extent of property destruction, the completeness of return or lasting changes in landholding.
note: The frozen event remains 1713–1723. The broader occupation chronology begins in 1713; the Åland entry dates devastation and flight to 1714, followed by return in 1721–1723. No exact departure day or return rate is inferred. Later occupations are separate events. The original family and every field of the eight-trait profile remain inherited; these brief accounts do not recertify their scalar values.
placeGloss: Åland and Sweden are the places named for flight and return. North Ostrobothnia, Oulu and Kainuu belong to Rokua Geopark’s regional context; they are not alternative names for Åland or locations assigned to its refugees.
geometryExplanation: The sources identify Åland and Sweden but do not verify departure or landing points, refugee routes, or a dated occupation footprint. A line between modern place centers would imply more precision than these entries provide. The single consolidated stop therefore has unknown geometry.

name: Argentine conquest and Indigenous confinement in the Chaco
displaced: Qom (Toba), Wichí, Moqoit (Mocoví), Pilagá and other peoples of the Argentine Chaco losing access to land and subsistence resources; Napalpí residents were principally Qom and Moqoit
settlers: Argentine army and national and territorial authorities; private landholders, agricultural settlers, timber enterprises and sugar companies
evidence: Juan and Valeria Iñigo Carrera’s historical account of land dispossession and labor recruitment, and Carlos Salamanca’s account of Napalpí’s formation and constraints on Indigenous life
story:
Argentine military campaigns and private occupation of land restricted Indigenous access to rivers and hunting grounds in the Chaco. The 1884 campaign reached the southern Chaco and the southern and eastern edges of the central Chaco. Juan and Valeria Iñigo Carrera describe it as a culmination of military expansion, without treating it as the final campaign.

Loss of subsistence land pushed Indigenous people into work for timber enterprises and sugar producers. The sugar industry of Salta and Jujuy recruited people from the central-western Chaco, including Qom, Wichí and Pilagá communities. Labor demand was seasonal and had grown markedly from the 1880s. The account connects recruitment with violent dispossession; it does not reduce the process to an unrestricted choice of employment.

After Rostagno’s 1911 military expedition, the state established the Napalpí reduction in the center-east of what is now Chaco province. A reduction was a settlement administered to concentrate Indigenous residents and discipline their work and movement. Napalpí came under the General Directorate of National Territories and drew people from different parts of the Chaco, principally Qom and Moqoit. Its program promoted wage labor and separation from the forest. Productive establishments surrounded it within a few years as the colonizing frontier advanced.

Confinement did not eliminate movement. Salamanca describes hunting and gathering continuing, residents moving, and spaces in which people could partly escape administrative discipline. He also explains that this openness helped maintain a cheap labor supply for neighboring producers. Continued subsistence practices and mobility coexisted with coercive settlement and exploitation.
contested: This case retains the 1884–1917 event window. The sources do not establish 1917 as the end of dispossession, labor coercion or Indigenous movement. They describe different parts of the Argentine Chaco and do not supply a single affected-population or mortality total. Napalpí’s principally Qom and Moqoit population cannot stand for every community in the wider region. The 1924 Napalpí massacre and the major cotton expansion of the 1920s fall outside this window. Salamanca’s note dates an official ban on travel to western sugar mills to 1924; it is not evidence that all such travel was already prohibited by 1917.
note: The primary family and complete eight-trait profile are inherited unchanged. The ordinal values are not population shares, a mortality estimate or evidence that every resident experienced the same degree of confinement. Continued mobility does not establish restored land access or unrestricted consent.
placeGloss: The Argentine Chaco is the affected region. Napalpí is one state reduction within it; the sugar-producing districts of Salta and Jujuy were labor destinations for people from the central-western Chaco. These are different parts of the process, not one verified route.
geometryExplanation: The sources locate the broad campaign zones, Napalpí and sugar-producing districts. Salamanca’s maps show a regional location and a later cadastral layout, including the site of the 1924 massacre. They do not establish a georeferenced 1884–1917 confinement boundary or a complete labor-removal route. No verified event-specific point, route or historical polygon is supplied; the world map remains background context.

name: Malayan Emergency forced resettlement into New Villages
displaced: Predominantly rural Chinese residents, including people classified by colonial authorities as squatters and other rural dwellers, forcibly moved into controlled settlements
settlers: British colonial authorities and the Federation of Malaya government directing resettlement; estate and mine employers regrouping labour settlements
evidence: Rhoderick dhu Renick Jnr’s published extract and exposed notes, Richard Stubbs’s study of competing historical interpretations, and Tom Rice’s commentary on a government resettlement film in the Imperial War Museums catalogue
story:
During the Malayan Emergency, British colonial authorities and the Federation of Malaya government forcibly moved rural residents into settlements intended to separate them from communist insurgents. The Briggs Plan expanded this policy from 1950. It chiefly affected rural Chinese people, including both those whom officials called squatters and other residents. Their displacement does not establish that they belonged to the Malayan Communist Party or its armed forces.

Resettlement proceeded rapidly, alongside the regrouping of labour settlements on rubber estates and at tin mines. The totals describe different categories and dates. Renick’s published extract reports nearly 650,000 people resettled or regrouped into more than 550 new villages.
