Stubbs contrasts government figures with Kernial Singh Sandhu’s estimate of 385,000 people resettled by the end of 1951, out of a later total of 573,000 in 480 villages. These figures cannot be added together or treated as a single count of forced moves.

The authorities used settlement, policing and food controls to restrict contact with insurgents. Conditions varied, and rapid relocation did not ensure secure housing, suitable farmland or effective protection. Rice’s catalogue commentary describes the breakdown of a long-established Hakka community at Pulai, with one group resettled three times. At Mawai, an insurgent attack in October 1951 killed four informers and abducted 36 young men; the government then closed the settlement, causing further losses of homes and crops. These examples distinguish the actions of armed groups and officials from the civilian population caught between them.

Government publicity presented the new settlements as places of safety and improved services. Rice explains that the 1951 film A New Life – Squatter Resettlement omitted barbed wire and dissatisfaction. Stubbs describes a continuing historical debate: some scholars regard population control under the Briggs Plan as the decisive turning point, while others stress its early failures and the importance of later administration, political change and other factors. Forced relocation is well documented; an account of its success must distinguish policy aims, uneven conditions and disputed explanations of the war’s outcome.
contested: The case retains the 1948–1960 Emergency window. It does not imply that every settlement began in 1948, that all coercive controls ended in 1960, or that later conflict belongs to this same interval. Renick’s exposed note dates the Briggs Plan to June 1951, whereas Stubbs and Rice date its implementation in Johore to 1 June 1950. Stubbs also reports conflicting government counts: 450,000 resettled by September 1951 in one retrospective account, and 401,698 in 343 areas by the end of 1951 in another. These are attributed estimates, not interchangeable censuses. Resettled civilians, regrouped estate and mine labourers, detained people and people deported abroad are distinct categories.
note: This is a case of coercive state resettlement during counterinsurgency. The complete inherited family and eight-trait profile are unchanged. Their ordinal values are not population percentages or evidence that residents were overseas settlers replacing another population. The film itself and the original records and books cited by the three authors were not independently viewed or read.
placeGloss: The case concerns settlements across peninsular Malaya. Johore marks the first phase of the Briggs Plan described here; Mawai and Pulai are separate local examples, not a complete origin-and-destination route.
geometryExplanation: The sources identify a peninsula-wide program and several settlements, but the reviewed material provides no verified coordinates, historical settlement boundaries or complete removal routes for the 1948–1960 event. A modern place point would not establish the geography of the whole program. No case marker, route or polygon is proposed; the map remains background context.

name: Norman conquest of England: aristocratic dispossession and the Harrying of the North
displaced: English landholders who lost lordship or became subordinate tenants; northern English inhabitants affected by famine and flight during the Harrying.
settlers: William I and incoming aristocrats, including Count Alan of Brittany and Ilbert de Lacy, who received lordships in England.
evidence: The National Archives explains Domesday’s record of landholding before and after the conquest. Aleksandra McClain examines northern lordships and surviving native subtenants; C. P. Lewis disputes the usual interpretation of the Harrying and Domesday waste.
story:
William I conquered England in 1066. Landholding was reorganized beneath the king and his tenants-in-chief. In Yorkshire, William gathered estates into compact lordships for leading barons, including Count Alan of Brittany at Richmond and Ilbert de Lacy at Pontefract. The Domesday survey, ordered at Christmas 1085 and carried out in 1086, recorded holdings and resources before and after the conquest. The National Archives gives Odiham in Hampshire as an example: land previously held by Harald was recorded under William.

In the winter of 1069–70, William campaigned against northern rebels and a Danish invasion force. Lewis’s account identifies famine and a refugee crisis in accounts from Evesham and Beverley, while arguing that the famine was probably localized within the region. The scale and interpretation of the Harrying remain disputed.

The new lordships did not remove every English landholder. McClain finds many native subtenants in Yorkshire. Alric retained his manor at Upper Hopton between 1066 and 1086, but now held it under Ilbert de Lacy; Godwine at Huddersfield had a similar change of status. Some native subtenants also acquired land they had not held in 1066. These regional records preserve continued landholding within the new hierarchy.
contested: Lewis rejects the genocide interpretation of the Harrying and questions the later accounts of Symeon of Durham and Orderic Vitalis, neither an eyewitness. His publisher summary retains severe consequences, famine and refugees. Both Lewis and McClain challenge a direct reading of Domesday waste as physical destruction caused solely by the Harrying; McClain also warns that an absence of recorded villagers does not prove a settlement was empty. These interpretations do not establish a harmless conquest. The sources consulted here do not verify a national land-transfer percentage or a death total.
note: This case follows the conquest and landholding changes from 1066 to the 1086 survey. McClain’s evidence from later churches and commemoration extends into the twelfth century; those developments are not dated to this interval. The Lewis citation covers the publisher summary, not the full chapter. The inherited event record names Marcus Meer at the same URL, but the publisher identifies C. P. Lewis. The original record is preserved; the public citation uses the actual byline.
placeGloss: England; northern landholding examples from Yorkshire, including Richmond, Pontefract, Upper Hopton and Huddersfield. Odiham is in Hampshire. Evesham and Beverley identify the accounts discussed by Lewis, not a reconstructed refugee route.
geometryExplanation: The consulted sources identify places and regional patterns but do not supply an authenticated movement route or a bounded displacement footprint for this combined conquest and landholding event. No coordinates or route are proposed. The Domesday waste distribution is not treated as a map of destruction or depopulation.

name: Expulsion of the Moriscos from Spain
displaced: Morisco communities in Spain, descended from Muslims subjected to forced conversion; the policy risked expelling sincere Christians as well
settlers: Philip III and his ministers, regional authorities and military forces directing expulsion; royal and private ships carrying deportees
evidence: Míkel de Epalza’s chapter on conflict and expulsion, including its summaries of regional decrees and exceptions, and Már Jónsson’s published article abstract
story:
Between 1609 and 1614, the Spanish monarchy expelled Morisco communities through a sequence of regional orders. Forced conversion in the preceding century had made them legally Christian, without producing a uniform religious identity. Philip III’s government sought their removal; its intended general expulsion did not mean that every Morisco left Spain.

The operation began in Valencia. The viceroy published the order on 22 September 1609, after preparations to assemble soldiers and ships. Epalza describes embarkations from ports along the Valencian coast, attacks on departing people, and armed resistance in inland mountain communities that was bloodily suppressed. He connects that resistance with news of mistreatment suffered by deportees arriving through Oran. The government’s security arguments treated Moriscos as a potential internal enemy; that rationale does not establish the loyalty or conduct of every person expelled.

The provisions varied by region. Epalza contrasts the sale of goods in Valencia, sometimes at depressed prices, with partial confiscation for the royal treasury prescribed for Andalusia. The Andalusian provisions required parents to leave children under seven behind unless the family went to Christian lands. Epalza links that rule to departures directed toward France, while some ships instead changed course for Morocco. The Aragonese order allowed children under four to remain if their parents agreed. These were different rules, and the Valencian provisions were only partly fulfilled.

The orders extended to the Castiles and Extremadura in July 1610 and to Murcia in October, with a temporary exception for the Ricote valley. Epalza reports departures across the Pyrenees and through Mediterranean and Andalusian ports. In Granada, some people stayed under legal exceptions or with the help of established Christian neighbors. His account also records young children taken from departing Morisco families and retained in Valencia.

Most operations occurred in 1609–1610, with further removals continuing through 1614. Jónsson’s abstract estimates 300,000 expelled and says that a majority settled in North Africa. Epalza distinguishes roughly 275,000 documented expulsions, attributed to Lapeyre and Bernard Vincent, from an estimate of more than 300,000 affected when clandestine departures and deaths during the hardships of exile are included. These are attributed estimates with different counting bases. People who remained and people who later returned prevent the expulsion from being described as complete demographic disappearance.
contested: Epalza presents a historical synthesis and explicitly leaves the relative weight of political and religious motives partly unresolved. The decrees and the studies he cites were not independently consulted here. Jónsson’s full article was not accessed; its abstract’s broad description of Morisco religious adherence is not treated as a finding about every individual. Valencia’s violence, property arrangements and child retention are not generalized to all regions. Epalza’s mention of people remaining or returning under Philip IV is later aftermath, not a new date within the 1609–1614 event.
note: This case concerns forced removal under a common royal policy carried out through regional orders. The inherited family and complete eight-trait profile are unchanged. Their ordinal values are not percentages: they do not establish that all Moriscos left, that nobody returned, or a measured number of replacement settlers. Earlier forced conversions and the dispersal after the Alpujarras war are background rather than additional phases of this event.
placeGloss: The affected communities lived in several Spanish kingdoms. Valencia, Andalusia, the Castiles, Extremadura, Aragon, Catalonia and Murcia had distinct departure arrangements. France and North Africa appear as routes or destinations, not a single destination shared by every deportee.
geometryExplanation: The chapter names ports, overland passages and regional destinations, but the reviewed evidence does not supply verified historical coordinates, departure-area boundaries or a complete set of routes for the whole expulsion. No case point, polygon or route is proposed. A generic Spanish or North African point would collapse different movements; the map remains background context.

name: Okinawan land seizure and displacement for United States military bases
displaced: Okinawan residents whose home sites and farmland were taken for U.S. bases, including people prevented from returning after internment.
settlers: U.S. military occupation authorities, troops and base administrators taking land for military installations.
evidence: Okinawa Prefecture’s official retrospective history describes land seizure during internment, settlement around bases by residents unable to return home, and further postwar removals enforced by armed troops. Its chronology ends U.S. administration in 1972; it does not provide a census of displaced residents.
story:
The Battle of Okinawa devastated the island in 1945. Base construction brought a further loss of homes and land. In its account of Futenma Air Station’s construction, Okinawa Prefecture describes U.S. forces confining residents in internment camps and taking their land for bases. The account says that people whose land had been seized could not return to their hometowns and had to settle around the bases.

The prefectural history also describes expansion after the war. Under a panel headed 1955, it reports that U.S. troops drove residents out, demolished houses and destroyed farmland to construct additional bases. It connects the military’s demand for new installations to changes in the international situation, including the Korean War. The history distinguishes these coercive acquisitions from the destruction caused by the fighting in 1945.

Okinawa remained under U.S. administration until its reversion to Japan in 1972. The prefectural account records a National Diet resolution at reversion calling for future reduction and reorganization of the bases. That administrative change did not itself mean that all seized land was returned or all displaced residents went home.
contested: This is an official prefectural account written amid continuing disagreement over the bases. It presents the prefecture’s position on land seizure and the burden of military facilities. The historical panels describe forced removal and blocked return, but supply no comprehensive count of displaced people, no parcel-by-parcel acquisition record and no complete return record. Their account of land seizure does not make every person displaced by the 1945 battle a victim of base clearance.
note: The 1945–1972 interval follows base acquisition under U.S. administration to reversion. The 1955 heading introduces a broader account of postwar expansion; it is not a date for every removal. Later agreements, protests and present-day base statistics in the brochure fall outside this event. Modern concentration figures are not measurements of the land taken or the population displaced during 1945–1972.
placeGloss: Okinawa, with Futenma Air Station named in the 1945 construction panel. The account also describes residents settling around bases, without specifying their individual routes or a complete set of destination communities.
geometryExplanation: The history identifies Okinawa and names Futenma, but does not supply a verified historical acquisition boundary or relocation route for the combined 1945–1972 event. Contemporary facility maps would not establish that historical footprint. No marker, boundary or route is proposed.

name: Peruvian slave raids across Polynesia
displaced: Polynesian islanders, including people from Rapa Nui, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, Tuvalu and Tonga, recruited by differing means and carried away for labour in Peru
settlers: Merchants, shipowners, captains and recruiters operating from Peru, with Peruvian recruiting licences; employers buying their labour in Peru
evidence: H. E. Maude’s reconstruction from scattered archival and island accounts, read in the ANU digitization of Slavers in Paradise, and the United Nations’ 1987 historical outline of Tokelau
story:
Ships operating from Peru carried islanders across the Pacific for agricultural labour and domestic service in 1862–1863. The trade used recruiting licences and the language of contracts, while captains also obtained people through deception and armed kidnapping. Maude’s account follows the sequence from the first licence in April 1862 through attempts to repatriate survivors and a Franco-Peruvian settlement in June 1864.

Initial recruitment was not uniform. At Tongareva, also known as Penrhyn, coconut-crop failure and hopes of earning money for churches encouraged people to leave. Maude distinguishes willing recruitment from misleading promises about work, destination or duration, and from outright capture. On the first Adelante voyage, recruits were allowed to move about the ship. On many later voyages captives were confined below deck to prevent escape. Agreement to embark did not mean that people retained control over their labour or return.

The raids struck Tokelau’s three atolls particularly severely. In Maude’s account of Atafu, islanders went aboard to barter for clothing; the crew trapped them in the hold and forced their chief below. Armed parties also removed people from Fakaofo. Maude estimates 253 taken from the Tokelau atolls, including women and children, while the United Nations’ historical outline gives about 140. The accounts are not reconciled here. Maude also describes dysentery reaching Fakaofo before the raiders and spreading among captives aboard the ships: deaths in that sequence cannot all be counted as people removed from Tokelau.

In Peru, buyers took some islanders into domestic service in Lima and Callao and others to coastal estates. Maude describes confinement, inadequate food, beatings, illness and high mortality, despite contractual promises. His account of a French-led inspection of twelve haciendas in two valleys records gravely ill people and employers resisting their release. This is evidence of bondage in practice, with conditions and individual experiences varying.

Repatriation brought further deaths and displacement. Maude records smallpox aboard the Diamant and the Barbara Gomez, and survivors landed on islands other than their own. Sixteen people from the latter ship were put ashore on Rapa; nine survived there, and an epidemic, probably dysentery, killed many Rapans. Other intended returnees were abandoned on Cocos Island and a small surviving group was taken back to Peru. Removal, arrival in Peru, embarkation for repatriation, landing somewhere in Polynesia and return to a home island are different outcomes. The surviving island communities faced bereavement and losses of working adults; these accounts do not establish their cultural disappearance.
contested: Maude warns that he sometimes omits words such as probably from his narrative and that reconstructed ship routes and some ship-level counts are uncertain. His recruitment tables distinguish voluntary engagement, misrepresentation, kidnapping and cases without evidence; their totals include Micronesian Gilbertese as well as Polynesians. Their aggregate removal, death and survival figures therefore cannot be treated as one purely Polynesian cohort. The UN’s later periodic raids through about 1883 and its combined raid-and-disease population decline lie beyond this case’s 1862–1864 window. Neither the UN’s about 140 nor Maude’s 253 Tokelau estimate is silently substituted for the other.
note: This case follows an outward labour-removal campaign and its immediate consequences. The inherited family and complete eight-trait profile are preserved as ordinal analytical values, not population percentages. In particular, the imported-unfree-labour value of zero must not be read as denying enslavement or forced labour in Peru, and the low durability value does not erase bereavement or lasting community losses. Maude’s underlying archival documents and the UN outline’s underlying historical sources were not independently read.
placeGloss: The source zone spans several island groups; Callao was a principal arrival port in Peru. Rapa, Rapa Nui (Easter Island), and Tongareva (Penrhyn) are distinct places. Landings during attempted repatriation do not by themselves show return to a person’s homeland.
geometryExplanation: Maude supplies schematic maps and reconstructed itineraries but explicitly qualifies route details. The bounded reading does not establish verified coordinates, complete voyage tracks or a single historical removal footprint for this campaign. No marker, route, polygon or sourced-reference registration is proposed; the world map remains background context.

name: Nishapur: massacre and removal of craftspeople
displaced: Residents of Nishapur, including men, women and children killed during the capture and its aftermath
Craftspeople selected for forced removal to Turkestan; Juvaini reports 400
settlers: Tolui’s Mongol army and the household of Toghachar; the read accounts identify conquerors, not an incoming resident population
evidence: Juvaini’s account, in J. A. Boyle’s translation, describes the April 1221 capture, massacre and selection of craftspeople for deportation. Peter Jackson places this account in the campaign’s chronology and questions the enormous medieval casualty figures.
story:
Mongol forces captured Nishapur in April 1221 after an earlier submission and renewed resistance. The city had supplied provisions to passing Mongol armies in 1220. Later that year an arrow killed Toghachar, a son-in-law of Chinggis Khan, during fighting outside its walls. When Tolui’s army approached the following spring, a request for protection in exchange for tribute failed.

Juvaini describes fighting on the walls and continued resistance inside the city, followed by the expulsion of surviving men and women onto the plain. His account connects the destruction and killing to vengeance for Toghachar, whose widow entered with her escort. It reports that 400 people were selected for their craftsmanship and taken to Turkestan. This was forced removal from Nishapur, alongside the killing of residents and destruction of their homes.

Jackson treats the removal of skilled people as an additional form of depopulation after conquest. The accounts establish a massacre and selective deportation, but do not provide a reliable count of everyone killed or displaced.
contested: The figure of 400 craftspeople is Juvaini’s report, repeated by Jackson, not an independently confirmed census. Jackson rejects the enormous reported death toll for Nishapur. Juvaini’s language of comprehensive destruction does not establish a measured survival rate or permanent disappearance of the city. His separate reference to 400 Taziks left behind to search for survivors describes another group, not the deported craftspeople.
note: The event is the April 1221 capture and its immediate aftermath; the encounters of 1220 are background. Juvaini says that some deportees’ descendants remained in Turkestan in his own time. This is a medieval report, not evidence tracing their later descendants, working conditions or return. The material read does not identify an incoming settler community at Nishapur. Outgoing artisan removal is distinct from importing workers into the city.
placeGloss: Nishapur is the conquered city; Turkestan is the broad destination named for the selected craftspeople. The cited passage does not identify a receiving town.
geometryExplanation: The retained accounts describe movement from the city onto the plain and onward to Turkestan, but provide no verified coordinates, receiving settlement, route or territorial footprint for this event. Geometry remains unknown.

name: Nicaraguan refugee flight during the anti-Somoza insurrection
displaced: Nicaraguans who fled following the September 1978 events and received refugee assistance before the July 1979 change of government, mainly in Costa Rica and Honduras
settlers: Anastasio Somoza Debayle’s government and the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) in the conflict; Nicaraguan refugees, asylum governments and UNHCR in flight, assistance and return
evidence: UNHCR’s 1980 report on its 1979 assistance operations and its later historical account of the July 1979 transition; the exact-day cutoff has a separate source-access qualification
story:
Nicaraguans fled their country following the events of September 1978. UNHCR reports that about 100,000 Nicaraguans, mainly in Costa Rica and Honduras, were the focus of its refugee assistance during the first half of 1979. This is an assistance caseload for that period, not a count of every person displaced or harmed in Nicaragua.

The flight occurred during the conflict against Anastasio Somoza Debayle’s government. UNHCR’s later history describes opposition among political parties, students, labor unions, sections of the middle class and the Roman Catholic church, alongside advances by the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN). These groups do not identify the politics of every refugee. The account dates Somoza’s departure and Sandinista control to July 1979.

The change of government enabled many of the earlier refugees to return. UNHCR’s 1980 report says that the great majority of the Nicaraguan refugees it had assisted repatriated voluntarily during the latter part of 1979. Its account also records some 17,000 remaining, mainly in Costa Rica. That report-period remainder is not a count taken on the day of the political transition, and it should not be added to the earlier assistance figure.

UNHCR reports supporting both refugees abroad and people returning to Nicaragua, including food, medical supplies and agricultural equipment for returnees. Large-scale return did not establish that every person recovered a home, land or livelihood. At the same time, other Nicaraguans departed after the change of government. The earlier flight and return form this case; the new departures belong to a different cohort.
contested: UNHCR dates the transition only to July 1979. This record uses 19 July 1979 as its cutoff, following an IACHR chronology that has not been rechecked against its original text. That date does not establish the last departure or the date of every return. The accounts used here do not enumerate every origin community, individual reason for flight, property loss or return history.
note: This case follows the refugee cohort that left after the September 1978 events before the July 1979 transition. Post-change exiles, Contra-war displacement and the later Miskito relocation remain outside it. Return was substantial but incomplete; the accounts do not establish that everyone recovered a home, land or livelihood.
placeGloss: Nicaragua is the source country of the flight; Costa Rica and Honduras were the principal countries named in the early-1979 assistance account. The report describes returnee assistance mainly in northern agricultural provinces of Nicaragua, without identifying a complete set of departure or return communities.
geometryExplanation: The exact departure communities, crossing points and return settlements of this cohort are not established in the sources used here. The chapter map depicts 1980s refugee flows, rather than the journeys of this 1978–1979 cohort.

name: First Liberian civil-war displacement, December 1989–1997
displaced: Liberian civilians forced from their homes, including people displaced repeatedly within Liberia and refugees in neighbouring countries
settlers: The National Patriotic Front of Liberia (NPFL), forces loyal to President Samuel Doe and later armed factions; the regional ECOMOG force intervened in the conflict
evidence: UNHCR’s retrospective account of war and displacement in West Africa, with Human Rights Watch used to distinguish the first war’s end from the later LURD conflict
story:
War began in Liberia in December 1989 between the National Patriotic Front of Liberia (NPFL) and forces loyal to President Samuel Doe. Armed factions multiplied as the conflict continued. UNHCR describes civilian massacres, mutilations, widespread destruction of property and the recruitment of child soldiers. Civilians fled within Liberia and across its borders.

In 1990, the Economic Community of West African States sent its military observer force, ECOMOG, into Liberia. It gained control of Monrovia while much of the country remained in rebel hands. The capital offered no lasting refuge from the fighting: repeated struggles for control displaced people who had sought shelter there. When Liberians first crossed into Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire, local residents opened their homes to them, and relatively few refugees initially lived in camps.

UNHCR’s account reports more than 1.7 million people uprooted over the war, approximately 40 per cent of whom fled to neighbouring countries; almost all the remainder were internally displaced. These are broad estimates of displacement, not a person-by-person record of departures and returns. Refugees are part of the uprooted population, and repeated flight does not necessarily mean another person was displaced.

In April 1996, renewed fighting in Monrovia sent more than 350,000 civilians fleeing, according to UNHCR. They included people already displaced in the city. Some escaped by sea on the Bulk Challenge and the Zolotista, only to be refused entry at ports along the West African coast. Ghana eventually allowed the Bulk Challenge to land after reports of serious illness aboard. The Zolotista returned to Monrovia after three weeks at sea. Escape from the city did not ensure a secure place to stay.

A peace agreement after the 1996 violence held, and an internationally supervised election in 1997 brought NPFL leader Charles Taylor to the presidency. That political transition closes this first-war case; it does not establish that everyone could return home or recover property. Human Rights Watch’s later report distinguishes the war ending with the 1997 elections from the LURD incursion beginning in July 2000. The later conflict and its displaced populations belong to a separate event.
contested: The population figures describe different categories and observation periods. The inherited record cites about 700,000 refugees through UNHCR’s 1999 return-operation report, whose body was not reread here. That refugee estimate and the chapter’s more than 1.7 million uprooted are not inherently contradictory: refugees are a subset of all displaced people. They are not reconciled here into a precise internally displaced total. The chapter’s 1994 map gives dated stocks; these cannot be added to repeated Monrovia flight or to later refugee and returnee counts. Its regional figures also include Sierra Leone and other conflicts. Neither a unique displaced-person total nor an exact final day of displacement is established.
note: This case concerns civilians driven from their homes, without a demonstrated replacement-settlement program. Child-soldier recruitment is documented; recruiting people during the war is distinct from bringing a separate population from elsewhere for unfree labour. The 1997 transition does not establish complete return or property recovery. The original reports cited for detailed return and reintegration operations have not been rechecked.
placeGloss: Monrovia is Liberia’s capital. Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire were important neighbouring asylum countries; the ship episode also reaches Ghana. These places identify the account’s setting, not a complete itinerary for Liberian refugees.
geometryExplanation: The UNHCR map shows country-level movements and population estimates for 1994. It does not establish the exact communities affected or the land and sea routes taken across the 1989–1997 war.

name: Mutsu: frontier reorganization and fortified settlement
displaced: Emishi-classified communities and other prior residents of the Mutsu frontier, affected by expanding court administration and settlement; the number physically removed is not established
settlers: Immigrants placed in the affected frontier area by the Japanese court, alongside officials and soldiers; the sources consulted do not count these groups
evidence: Kimio Kumagai’s study links immigrant placement, new counties and fortified offices to the reorganization around the 720 uprising. Taga’s monument dates its foundation to 724. Karl F. Friday describes the wider stockade settlement system and the sparse records of campaigns in 720 and 724.
story:
The Japanese court reorganized the Mutsu frontier during the years between the 720 uprising and Taga’s recorded foundation in 724. Kumagai describes the establishment of new counties and the placement of immigrants in the area affected by the uprising. The government also suspended taxation, stationed a provisional military force, and annexed Iwaki and Iwashiro into Mutsu.

Taga combined provincial administration with military command. Kumagai reports that archaeological research connects its construction with five other fortified government offices. He cites Hirakawa’s proposal that work on Taga began soon after the 720 uprising and was completed in 724. Kumagai suggests that the uprising may have prompted its foundation.

This reorganization formed part of a wider frontier system that joined settlement to government control. Friday describes households transplanted into Emishi territory around stockades, protected by troops. Those outposts were centers of administration as well as defense. His account describes that broader system; it does not supply a count of settlers arriving during 720–724. The same frontier was a site of armed resistance: Friday records punitive campaigns following the killing of provincial officials in 720 and 724, while stressing how little detail survives.
contested: The 720–724 dates mark an institutional sequence, not a measured period of continuous migration. The proposed construction start and the uprising’s causal role remain interpretations. The passages consulted give neither a settler census nor a measured number of prior residents killed, expelled or deprived of land. Administrative expansion and immigrant placement should not be read as proof that all prior inhabitants were removed.
note: Emishi was a political classification for people outside the court’s rule, rather than a securely defined single ethnic population. Ryohei Takehiro describes changing legal treatment and possibilities of incorporation across the eighth century; his broader account does not date every change to this event. The separately recorded transfer out of Mutsu in 725 and the later campaigns of 774–811 fall outside this case.
placeGloss: Mutsu is the frontier province; Taga is the administrative and military center. Iwaki and Iwashiro are the provinces Kumagai describes as annexed into Mutsu.
geometryExplanation: The consulted passages identify Taga and a wider area of frontier reorganization, but do not establish a verified footprint, settlement coordinates or movement route for this event. Geometry remains unknown.

name: Guatemalan civil-war displacement and refuge in Mexico
displaced: Indigenous communities and other Guatemalan civilians displaced within Guatemala or seeking refuge in Mexico; the documented account concentrates on displacement from 1981 onward
settlers: Guatemalan armed forces and guerrilla organizations in the conflict; Mexican authorities, refugees, UNHCR and aid organizations in asylum, relocation and integration
evidence: UNHCR’s retrospective history documents the 1981 campaign, refuge in Mexico and the 1996 peace agreement; earlier chronology and domestic militarized resettlement remain incompletely sourced here
story:
In late 1981, Guatemala’s military began an 18-month counterinsurgency campaign that targeted guerrillas and Indigenous communities it regarded as bases of rebel support. UNHCR reports that tens of thousands of civilians, mostly Indigenous people, were killed or disappeared. At the height of the violence, an estimated one million people were internally displaced as a result of the campaign. The military’s view of these communities does not establish the allegiance of every resident.

Many Guatemalans also crossed into Mexico. According to UNHCR, more than 200,000 entered between 1981 and 1982. Mexico initially deported thousands, then established a registration process after international protests and allowed 46,000 registered refugees to remain. Many others were unregistered, including people who joined existing migrant workforces, reached Mexico City or arrived after registration closed. They lived with the threat of deportation.

Registered refugees lived in more than 50 camps in remote parts of Chiapas, where conditions were poor. From 1984, the Mexican government moved refugees to settlements in Campeche and Quintana Roo; eventually some 18,000 moved. The government cited Guatemalan military attacks across the border on refugee sites. UNHCR also describes the Chiapas governor’s opposition to the refugees and the Mexican government’s interest in development on the Yucatán peninsula.

Some 25,000 registered refugees resisted that relocation and remained in Chiapas. Low wages and restricted access to land and services made life difficult. In 1987, some left the camps and some returned to Guatemala. UNHCR says security and living conditions in Chiapas subsequently improved somewhat.

The Mexican government, UNHCR and nongovernmental organizations supplied refugees in Campeche and Quintana Roo with land, shelter, food aid and social services. UNHCR describes those settlements as successful in achieving self-sufficiency and local integration. Most refugees who moved there remained permanently, and Mexico eventually granted them citizenship. These settlements in Mexico were different from the militarized resettlement within Guatemala mentioned in the original record; the chapter passages used here do not establish that domestic program.

Guatemala reached a formal peace agreement in 1996. UNHCR notes that many refugees had returned before the peace agreements in Guatemala and El Salvador. Return and integration abroad were different outcomes: neither establishes that every displaced Guatemalan recovered a home, land or livelihood.
contested: This record uses the broader 1960–1996 civil-war interval. The cited chapter focuses on the 1980s: its passages establish neither the 1960 onset nor every earlier phase, and this account concentrates on displacement from 1981 onward. The original source listed for the record, UNHCR’s Global Appeal 1999 regional overview, has not been consulted in full. The chapter does not establish the record’s specific claim of militarized model-village resettlement within Guatemala. Its wider Central American totals combine several wars and are not Guatemala-only estimates. Peak internal displacement, border arrivals, registrations and later relocations measure different populations and periods; they cannot be added into a unique displaced-person total.
note: The 1996 peace agreement marks a political boundary, not the last displacement or a date when every person returned. Some refugees returned earlier; others built lasting lives in Mexico. Their different outcomes do not prove universal property recovery.
placeGloss: Chiapas borders Guatemala. Campeche and Quintana Roo are on Mexico’s Yucatán peninsula; the settlements described here were places of refuge and integration in Mexico.
geometryExplanation: The account names countries and Mexican states but does not establish the exact communities, border crossings or routes for this displaced population. The chapter’s regional map does not provide a verified footprint for the whole 1960–1996 case.

name: Mozambique: civil war and mass displacement
dates: 1977–1992 (record period; UNHCR dates the war’s onset to 1976)

periods.yearLabel: 1977–1992 (record period; UNHCR dates the war’s onset to 1976)

displaced: Mozambican civilians who fled their homes within the country or sought refuge in neighboring states; UNHCR reports about 1.7 million refugees by 1992
settlers: FRELIMO government forces and RENAMO insurgents were the armed actors driving displacement; the account does not identify an incoming population replacing those who fled
evidence: UNHCR’s retrospective account describes violence, widespread flight and conditions in neighboring Malawi. It dates the war from 1976 to 1992, while this record retains the period 1977–1992. Its population figures are rounded estimates.
story:
Mozambican civilians fled a war between the FRELIMO government and RENAMO insurgents. UNHCR describes RENAMO’s systematic killing, maiming, rape and pillage as means of controlling people in its areas of operation. Flight increased as its territorial control expanded. Government forces also adopted increasingly brutal measures. The account identifies the white-minority governments of Rhodesia and South Africa as RENAMO’s founders and supporters.

By the refugee crisis’s peak in 1992, UNHCR reports about 1.7 million Mozambicans in neighboring countries and at least twice as many displaced within Mozambique. In several districts of Tete province, as many as 90 percent of inhabitants had fled. Malawi hosted the largest share of the refugees: as many as 1.1 million at the height of the exodus. These people were part of the refugee total, not an additional group.

Many early arrivals in Malawi settled alongside local people, and some obtained land to farm. Others depended on aid. Malawi initially used its existing clinics and services to help refugees, then sought UNHCR assistance in 1986. In 1987, as arrivals grew, the government asked UNHCR to establish camps and directed all new refugees to move into them. It also barred local people from providing refugees with agricultural land. Eventually, more than two-thirds of the refugees in Malawi lived in camps.

Refugees continued to earn income through activities such as making pots, raising animals and trading part of their rations for other necessities. Aid helped sustain both refugees and local services, but transport and storage problems interrupted food supplies. By 1992, prolonged displacement had strained relations with host communities. UNHCR’s account records the war ending that year; it does not establish how completely people recovered their homes or land afterward.
contested: The record’s 1977 starting year differs from UNHCR’s 1976 onset. UNHCR separately reports about 1.7 million refugees, at least twice as many internally displaced people, and about 5.7 million people uprooted overall. These rounded figures are retained as reported, without forcing them into a single arithmetic total. The 90 percent figure applies to several Tete districts, not Mozambique as a whole.
note: Malawi’s refugee population is a subset of cross-border displacement, and its changing land and camp policies are host-country conditions. They do not show a population replacing the refugees in Mozambique. This account covers wartime flight through 1992. The original reference to a later return programme has not been verified from its source body, so no scale of postwar return or property restoration is asserted here.
placeGloss: Mozambique is the country of origin; Malawi, South Africa, Swaziland (now Eswatini), Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe are the host countries named by UNHCR. Tete is the province containing the several districts discussed in the account.
geometryExplanation: The source names host countries and severely depopulated districts but provides no verified route, settlement coordinates or event footprint for this case. Geometry remains unknown.

name: Civilian internment at Douglas and Knockaloe
displaced: Civilian men classified as enemy aliens and confined at Douglas and Knockaloe. Camp residents had different religious, social and economic backgrounds.
settlers: British wartime authorities, island camp administrators and guards; civilian property owners whose premises were requisitioned.
evidence: Manx National Heritage’s catalogue describes the Douglas camp records and supplies a historical account of internment. The original journals and registers have not been inspected for this account.
story:
British authorities requisitioned Cunningham’s Holiday Camp in Douglas for civilian internment after the outbreak of the First World War. The first civilian detainees arrived on the island by September 1914. A place used for holidays became a detention camp.

Douglas’s internees ranged from poor men to wealthy and highly educated residents. The camp developed separate ordinary, paid privilege and Jewish sections. The privilege section offered additional facilities to those who could afford them; the Jewish section provided kosher food and facilities for religious observance. These differences existed within compulsory confinement.

Manx National Heritage reports that approximately 2,600 men were at Douglas by late October 1914, temporarily rising to 3,300 after transfers from other camps. Its account links overcrowding, boredom and complaints about food to a November riot in which five internees were shot and killed. It also reports that an inquest justified the guards’ actions. That is the catalogue’s account of the inquest, not an independent endorsement of its judgment.

The much larger Knockaloe camp on the island’s west coast had four sub-camps within a barbed-wire compound. According to the catalogue, it housed more than 20,000 men by the end of the war. The camps developed workshops, art, theatrical groups and a school; internees could keep their own clothes and personal belongings. These activities show forms of life within detention, rather than freedom to leave it.

After the November 1918 armistice, the Douglas camp closed: the catalogue states that all its internees had been released by 1919 and that Cunningham’s resumed holiday operations for the summer season. That statement concerns Douglas. It does not establish each Knockaloe sub-camp’s exact closure date or each person’s release and later destination.
contested: The population figures are snapshots at different camps and dates, not numbers to add into a unique total. The catalogue also describes an enclosure listing 24 deaths using the term “prisoners of war.” The underlying list has not been examined, so that figure is not used here as a civilian or island-wide death total.
note: This account concerns civilian detention during the First World War. Compulsory residence in the camps did not make the detainees a colonizing settler community. The documented return to holiday use concerns Cunningham’s at Douglas; individual destinations after release remain unresolved.
placeGloss: Douglas’s camp occupied Cunningham’s former holiday premises at Victoria Road. Knockaloe was on the island’s west coast.
geometryExplanation: Town and nearby historical-site orientation points only; camp boundaries, individual buildings and transport routes are not represented.

name: Civilian internment on the Isle of Man during the Second World War
displaced: Civilians classified under wartime enemy-nationality rules, including German, Austrian and Italian men and women and refugees from Nazi persecution. Children accompanying their mothers had a different formal status from internees.
settlers: The British government, camp authorities and guards, and tribunals that considered release; boarding-house owners and other island residents affected by requisition and camp boundaries.
evidence: Manx National Heritage’s teaching resource describes the May 1940 arrest decision, camp locations, differing periods of detention and life at Rushen. It is an institutional educational account, not a complete internee register.
story:
In May 1940, fear of invasion and sabotage led the British government to order the arrest of many foreign-born civilians. People whose nationality or documents brought them under these measures were sent to detention camps, including camps on the Isle of Man. Some had already fled Nazi persecution to seek safety in Britain. Their nationality did not establish that they supported the regimes from which they had escaped.

Male camps occupied former boarding houses in Douglas, Ramsey, Onchan and Peel. Manx National Heritage reports that owners were given one week’s notice to leave before barbed wire went up and internees arrived. Women were sent to Rushen, comprising enclosed areas around Port Erin and Port St Mary; a married camp was later established at Port St Mary. The requisitioning of property and restriction of movement affected the surrounding community as well as those detained.

The teaching resource records the arrival of 3,025 women with 300 children in May 1940. It reports that more than 5,800 women and children had passed through the women’s or married camp areas by the end of the war. Children under sixteen could remain with their mothers but were not formally interned. Those figures describe different categories and periods, rather than a single island-wide internee total.

Some local people also found their homes within the fenced areas and had to show documents to guards when leaving the town. Within Rushen, a Service Exchange allowed women to exchange skills such as sewing, hairdressing, language teaching and legal advice for tokens that could buy goods in the camp.

Detention did not last five years for everyone. Manx National Heritage describes many internees, especially refugees from Nazi persecution, obtaining tribunal release after a few months. Some subsequently undertook war work. Its teaching example of Martha Probst’s registration card records internment in July 1940, release in December 1941 and a return to London. The displayed card is identified as a reproduction; it illustrates an individual sequence, not the experience of every detainee.
contested: The 1940–1945 interval identifies this wartime system; it is not a shared term of imprisonment. Exact opening and closure dates for every camp, a complete population crosswalk and individual release histories remain unresolved. The source’s broad description of nationality and age rules is not treated as proof that every eligible person was arrested.
note: Refugees from Nazi persecution were among the civilians detained. Their earlier flight did not make them colonizing settlers. Children under sixteen accompanying their mothers were not formally interned, and tribunal releases mean the wartime interval cannot be assigned to every person as a five-year detention.
placeGloss: Male camps were in Douglas, Ramsey, Onchan and Peel. Rushen included fenced areas of Port Erin and Port St Mary; the teaching resource reproduces a plan of Port Erin showing barbed wire.

targets.name: Port St Mary — Rushen town locator

geometryExplanation: Town and nearby historical-site orientation points only; camp boundaries, individual buildings and transport routes are not represented.

name: Salvadoran war displacement and refuge in Honduras
displaced: Salvadoran civilians uprooted by war and repression; the cited account follows refugees in Honduras, including people at La Virtud, Mesa Grande and Colomoncagua.
settlers: Salvadoran military and paramilitary forces, FMLN insurgents in the wider war, and Honduran authorities and armed forces; UNHCR and relief organizations involved in protection, assistance and contested relocation.
evidence: UNHCR’s retrospective history describes Salvadoran political repression and war, flight to Honduras, forced return at the border and a contested camp relocation. Its detailed Honduras account supports a particular part of the wider displacement, rather than a complete census of people displaced within El Salvador or abroad.
story:
Political repression and killings accompanied opposition organizing in El Salvador during the 1970s. In the following decade the government fought the FMLN insurgency. UNHCR’s account dates the first Salvadoran refugee arrivals in Honduras to 1980 and describes settlement in border communities, especially La Virtud. Honduran authorities treated the refugees as suspected guerrilla collaborators; this suspicion did not establish that all the displaced civilians were combatants.

In May 1980, Honduran troops turned back hundreds fleeing attack by the Salvadoran military. UNHCR reports that many of those forced back were subsequently killed. Intensifying fighting drove further flight, and by early 1981 the Salvadoran refugee population in Honduras had reached about 30,000. This was a dated population in one host country, not the number displaced throughout the war.

In October 1981, Honduras announced that refugees at La Virtud would be moved farther from the border to Mesa Grande. The stated aim was protection, which UNHCR supported. Some NGOs and other observers believed the purpose was to clear the border for military operations and prevent assistance to guerrillas. Refugees and most NGOs at La Virtud opposed the move. After Salvadoran soldiers and paramilitaries entered La Virtud and abducted refugees on 16 November 1981, Honduras proceeded immediately, although Mesa Grande was not ready. UNHCR assisted despite its concerns and the refugees’ resistance.

Within five months, UNHCR says, 7,500 refugees had been relocated, while more than 5,000 others returned to El Salvador rather than move to Mesa Grande. Many promised amenities did not materialize and conditions worsened. Closed-camp rules barred outside employment and restricted farming to camp land. Refugees nevertheless developed vegetable gardens, fish ponds, animal raising and workshops making clothes, shoes and hammocks. Their work and organization coexisted with restrictions on movement.

Colomoncagua had a different outcome. In 1983, Honduran authorities told its Salvadoran refugees to relocate or return to El Salvador. UNHCR supported relocation but opposed forced repatriation; NGOs backed refugee resistance. The authorities withdrew the demand and the refugees were not forced to leave, although insecurity and internal disputes persisted. El Salvador’s formal peace agreement came in 1992. UNHCR notes that many refugees returned before the peace agreements, without establishing that everyone returned or recovered their former homes and property.
contested: This record uses 1979–1992 for the wider displacement. The cited history describes repression in the 1970s and refugee arrivals from 1980; it does not independently establish 1979 as the first year of this movement. The detailed evidence here concerns refuge in Honduras and does not verify every cause, location or duration of internal displacement in El Salvador. The original 1999 regional overview has not been checked against its full text. Refugee stocks, relocated groups and people returning instead of relocating are different categories and are not added into a total.
note: These were displaced civilians, including people who resisted relocation or chose return under constrained conditions. Refuge in another country did not itself make them colonizing settlers. The 1992 agreement marks a political boundary, not a verified last departure or universal restoration of homes and property.
placeGloss: La Virtud was a Honduran border community where Salvadorans sought refuge. Mesa Grande was the more distant site to which a documented group was relocated after November 1981. Colomoncagua was another camp near the Salvadoran border; its 1983 relocation threat was withdrawn. The chapter does not identify every refugee’s home community or travel path.
geometryExplanation: Qualified town/locality anchors show the documented La Virtud-to-Mesa Grande relocation following the 16 November 1981 incursion. The connecting line is schematic, not a traced travel path or all Salvadoran displacement during1979–1992. Exact camp boundaries and individual home communities remain unresolved.
mapLabel: La Virtud → Mesa Grande · one documented relocation

name: Merv: capture, captivity and repeated destruction
displaced: Residents of Merv driven out of the city; selected artisans and children taken into captivity, and survivors exposed to renewed attacks.
settlers: Tolui’s Mongol army and later Mongol commanders and detachments; officials installed after the capture.
evidence: Juvaini describes the forced evacuation, selection of captives and repeated killing at Merv. Peter Jackson’s critical comparison supports caution about the chronicle’s enormous death totals. Neither source supplies a reliable population count or a complete history of the captives.
story:
In Juvaini’s account, Tolui arrived at Merv on 25 February 1221. After inspecting the defenses and fighting at the gates, his army surrounded the town. Its governor sought terms and was reassured by promises. The Mongols then drove the inhabitants onto the plain, a process the chronicle says took four days and nights, and separated women from men.

Juvaini says the Mongols selected 400 artisans and an unspecified number of girls and boys for captivity and ordered the remaining population killed. This is an attributed account of selection, not a surviving register of 400 named people. The narrative also describes destruction of the outworks and citadel and the burning of part of a mosque.

The destruction was not a single episode after which nobody remained. Juvaini describes people emerging from hiding, others returning, and renewed attacks. He also records the appointment of officials after the first capture and later attempts to restore walls, cultivation and the dam. These efforts did not prevent further killings and destruction.

A later passage names a destination for one group. Barmas, the Mongol official at Merv, took artisans and others out of the city to proceed to Bokhara. Around a revolt dated 7 November 1221, he departed with those accompanying him. Juvaini says Barmas died in Bokhara and the people from Merv remained there. The passage does not establish that these were the same 400 artisans and children selected at the first capture.

Subsequent Mongol forces again attacked inhabitants and people who had come back. Juvaini’s closing account includes destroyed crops and scattered survivors. It supports severe depopulation and repeated coerced removal, while leaving the final number of survivors and the later lives of the captives uncertain.
contested: The record uses 1221–1222 for the sequence. The cited chapter dates the first arrival and a later revolt within 1221, but does not establish an exact final departure or killing date in 1222. Its million-person death claims cannot serve as a reliable total: Jackson points to the tension between a reported 1.3 million dead and later arrivals and survivors. There is also a numerical discrepancy in the later massacre account: Boyle’s translation says a hundred thousand, while Jackson’s discussion says 10,000. No total or inferred proportion is adopted.
note: Captivity, flight, killing and surviving residence were different outcomes. The later Bokhara passage establishes a particular connection, not the destination of every captive or the permanent disappearance of everyone from Merv. It does not establish how all the selected artisans were subsequently employed.
placeGloss: Merv was the city attacked. Juvaini names Bokhara, now commonly spelled Bukhara, as the destination where a later group from Merv remained. The locations and journeys of all the people selected at the first capture are not established.
geometryExplanation: Heritage-site reference points orient Merv’s historic urban complex and Bukhara’s historic centre. The connection represents the later group reported to have accompanied Barmas to Bukhara, not the first 400 artisans and children or everyone displaced from Merv. It is schematic, not a traced journey or an exact capture, departure or arrival location. The full event retains its 1221–1222 range; the exact final 1222 date remains unresolved.
mapLabel: Merv → Bukhara · one later reported movement

name: Cambodian refugees forced back at Preah Vihear
displaced: Cambodian refugees rounded up in Thai border camps and forced into Cambodia at Preah Vihear.
settlers: Thai soldiers carrying out the roundup and forced return; the ICRC and UNHCR appear in the protection response, not as settlers.
evidence: UNHCR’s retrospective history describes a specific forced return in June 1979. It reports the scale of the roundup and an uncertain death toll, and criticizes the organization’s own failure to protest.
story:
In June 1979, Thai soldiers rounded up Cambodian refugees in border camps and forced them down the steep mountainside at Preah Vihear into Cambodia. UNHCR’s retrospective account puts the group at more than 42,000 people. It reports that at least several hundred, and possibly several thousand, were killed in the minefields below.

One day after the pushbacks began, the representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross publicly appealed for them to stop. He was ordered to leave Thailand. UNHCR’s history says that the organization feared an adverse Thai reaction and effectively kept silent. It describes the operation as refoulement, or forced return, and acknowledges its failure to protest.

The operation moved refugees back across the border into Cambodia. Their earlier flight out of the country was a separate movement; this account concerns the June roundup and forced return.
contested: The number forced back and the uncertain fatality range come from one institutional retrospective, not an independently checked person-by-person count. The chapter does not establish each refugee’s earlier route, the fate of every survivor or how many later fled again. Its underlying witnesses have not been separately checked here.
note: The June operation is distinct from Thailand’s October 1979 opening to further Cambodian arrivals and the later holding centres. Regional refugee and resettlement totals do not measure this forced-return group and are not added to it.
placeGloss: The source places the roundup in Thai border camps and the forced descent at Preah Vihear into Cambodia, with minefields below. It does not name the individual origin camps or identify each person’s home community.
geometryExplanation: The named mountainside and direction of movement are documented, but the exact descent, origin-camp locations and minefield boundary have not been established. A temple location would not by itself locate the forced descent. No precise point or route is shown.
geographicContext: In a contemporary report reproduced in the Congressional Record on 15 June 1979, Henry Kamm described buses moving northeast along the Thai side of the border from the Aranyaprathet area toward the Preah Vihear border landscape. These markers show a town and a temple for orientation; they do not locate an origin camp, assembly point, crossing or forced descent. The report does not establish that everyone in the later UNHCR total came from one camp or followed one route.
mapLabel: Preah Vihear · exact 1979 crossing/descent location not established

name: Hmong asylum seekers pushed back to Laos
displaced: Several hundred Hmong reported pushed back from Thailand to Laos in 1986.
settlers: Thai authorities in the border pushback and screening system; UNHCR had an observation and appeal role in screening. The chapter does not identify the units carrying out the reported pushbacks.
evidence: UNHCR’s retrospective history records border reports of several hundred Hmong pushed back to Laos in 1986. It supplies no exact count or individual account of those returns.
story:
In 1986, several hundred Hmong were reported pushed back from Thailand to Laos. UNHCR’s retrospective history attributes this account to reports from the border. The passage identifies a forced return across the border but does not follow the families to their destinations in Laos.

Thailand had announced a border screening process for Laotian arrivals in July 1985. Immigration officials conducted interviews, which UNHCR legal officers could observe. People recognized as refugees were sent to camps; UNHCR could appeal rejected applications before detention pending return. The chapter reports that hardly any of the Laotians interviewed by the end of 1986 were Hmong. The reported Hmong pushbacks therefore cannot be counted as the full screened population or treated as a documented set of rejected applications.

The chapter says Thailand’s position toward the Hmong eased somewhat by early 1988. That later change does not establish what happened to the people pushed back in 1986.
contested: The scale is a reported magnitude, not a verified census or a numerical range. The underlying border reports were not separately consulted. The passage gives no exact crossing, individual destination, death toll or account of these families’ livelihoods after return. Limited documentation does not establish low harm or zero deaths.
note: This case concerns the 1986 forced return to Laos. Earlier outward flight is a separate movement and must not be added as another set of unique people. The chapter’s later figures for screened applicants, voluntary repatriation and rejected asylum seekers describe other periods and cannot establish this group’s size or treatment.
placeGloss: The reported movement was from Thailand back into Laos. The source does not locate the crossings or the families’ destinations. Ban Vinai and Na Pho are described as camps for admitted refugees, not established departure points for this pushback group.
geometryExplanation: Country labels provide regional orientation on the atlas’s land map. The source documents forced return from Thailand into Laos, but does not establish the exact crossings or destinations. No camp, crossing point or event route is plotted.
mapLabel: Thailand to Laos · exact 1986 crossing unknown

name: Old Urgench: destruction and captive removal
displaced: Residents of Gurganj, or old Urgench, including artisans, children and young women taken captive, and men selected for execution in Juvaini’s account.
settlers: Mongol forces sent by Chinggis Khan under Chaghadai and Ögedei; the sources do not establish the composition of the later city’s resident population.
evidence: Juvaini’s chronicle describes the capture and separation of the inhabitants. Peter Jackson examines the conflicting accounts and unreliable totals; his account of artisan removal draws on Juvaini, rather than an independent census.
story:
Mongol forces besieged Gurganj, the Khwarazmian capital also called old Urgench, in 1221. Juvaini describes resistance in its streets and lanes, the destruction of houses, and the capture of the city quarter by quarter. The conquerors drove the inhabitants into the open.

In his account, artisans and craftsmen were separated from the rest, children and young women were enslaved and taken captive, and the remaining men were assigned to soldiers for execution. He later states that the artisans were divided up and sent east. The account establishes a distinction between killing and captive removal, but does not identify the artisans’ receiving towns or their route.

Jackson reports that Ibn al-Athir, writing before 630 AH / 1232–1233 CE, had heard of a new city built by the conquerors near the old capital. This records nearby rebuilding after destruction; it does not establish who populated the new city or whether the captives returned.
contested: The chroniclers’ totals cannot support a reliable count of those killed or removed. Juvaini gives enormous figures for artisans and executions, yet declines to repeat another death total because he disbelieves it. Accounts also differ over flooding and the extent of survival. Jackson’s statement that the entire population perished sits uneasily with the artisans, children and young women taken captive in Juvaini’s narrative. Neither complete annihilation nor a numerical population loss is established here.
note: The interval “1221–before 1232 CE” combines the conquest with the later report of nearby rebuilding. Its endpoint is a source-based bound: Jackson places Ibn al-Athir’s writing before 630 AH / 1232–1233 CE. It is not an exact foundation date or evidence that killing and deportation continued until 1232.
placeGloss: Gurganj or old Urgench is identified in Boyle’s translation with Kunya-Urgench. It is distinct from the modern Uzbek city of Urgench. Juvaini’s “countries of the East” does not identify individual receiving settlements.
geometryExplanation: Old Urgench is named in the sources, but the precise places where people were assembled and removed are not established. The eastern destinations and routes of the captive artisans remain unspecified.
geographicContext: The square marks the southern section of the UNESCO archaeological site at Kunya-Urgench, for regional orientation. It does not locate the 1221 city boundary, an assembly or execution place, or a point of departure. The artisans’ eastern destinations and route remain unknown; no journey is drawn.
mapLabel: Old Urgench · removal locations and eastern destinations unknown

name: Compulsory Ujamaa villagization in Tanzania
displaced: Rural Tanzanian households compelled to move into concentrated villages; detailed evidence here concerns Mtwara in the southeast.
settlers: The Tanzanian government and TANU party; in Mtwara, TANU Youth League and People’s Militia members carried out forced resettlement.
evidence: Lal’s study documents compulsory movement in Mtwara during 1973–1975. A World Bank sector report describes the national directive and village residence through the end of 1976. Neither source supplies a verified count of people forced to move for this case.
story:
In September 1973, Tanzania’s ruling party directed rural people to live in villages by 1976. The national drive followed years of Ujamaa policy that had promoted voluntary settlement while also involving growing pressure and some local forced removals. Villages were intended to bring people closer to schools, health services and agricultural support, and to encourage cooperation.

In Mtwara, southeastern Tanzania, the compulsory phase changed both dispersed settlement and smaller villages already formed under Ujamaa. Priya Lal describes TANU Youth League and People’s Militia members forcibly moving people who had initially refused to relocate, along with residents of small villages, into larger settlements during 1973–1975. Earlier village registration had sometimes renamed existing settlements without requiring anyone to move.

Lal’s later interviews record different experiences of the changes. Many forcibly relocated elders described losing property and access to permanent farms. Some remembered impoverishment and destruction; others criticized the coercion while continuing to value village cooperation. Promised services and practical assistance also varied. These accounts describe local experiences, not a uniform outcome for every Tanzanian village.

The World Bank’s retrospective report describes the forced relocation following the 1973 directive and reports village residence at the end of 1976. That national deadline and reporting point frame this case’s closing year; they do not establish when the last compulsory move occurred.
contested: The sources establish coercion but do not provide a verified forced-mover total or a death toll for this event. National totals of people living in registered villages include a different population from those compelled to relocate. Lal’s detailed evidence comes from three Mtwara villages and retrospective interviews, and cannot establish how every locality experienced the campaign.
note: This case concerns state-directed resettlement within Tanzania. Its inclusion rests on forced removal and loss of access to homes and farms; the narrative does not establish an incoming foreign settler population. Earlier voluntary moves and existing settlements registered as villages are not counted as forced displacement. Unknown death and displacement totals do not mean zero harm. The comparison profile groups this case under conquest and incorporation; the evidence presented here establishes internal forced resettlement, not military conquest.
placeGloss: The campaign had a national policy frame. Mtwara in southeastern mainland Tanzania supplies the detailed local evidence used here. A regional label indicates that evidence focus, not a single removal site or the full distribution of forced moves.
geometryExplanation: Mainland Tanzania and Mtwara provide geographic context. The sources do not establish matched journeys for the affected households, so no route or village endpoint is supplied.

name: Merina expansion, military colonies and coerced labour
displaced: People subjected to Merina conquest, enslavement and compulsory labour, including Betsileo and Betsimisaraka communities. Merina subjects also owed compulsory service; large parts of Sakalava country remained outside effective Merina rule.
settlers: The Merina monarchy, army, officials and allied elites, including soldiers established in military colonies.
evidence: Gwyn Campbell’s economic history and study of unfree labour describe land seizure, military colonies, enslavement and compulsory service. Both works are by the same historian; they do not provide independent counts of people killed or displaced.
story:
From the 1790s, the Merina monarchy expanded from Imerina in Madagascar’s central highlands. Its armies sought control of people, land, cattle and trade. Under Radama I, conquest included the establishment of soldier colonies on farmland in northern Betsileo and around Lake Alaotra. Campbell describes destruction and famine in Ankay, where campaigns targeted a region on the route to the east coast.

The British alliance of 1820 provided military assistance in return for ending slave exports. It did not abolish slavery within the expanding empire. Campaigns supplied enslaved captives, while the court also relied on fanompoana: compulsory, unpaid military and civilian service imposed on Merina and non-Merina subjects. Soldiers, skilled workers and other labourers faced different demands. Enslaved people imported from East Africa formed a distinct part of the labour population, rather than another count of those captured in Madagascar.

Campbell describes Radama’s early-1820s order for armies in non-Merina regions to kill males aged ten and over and enslave women and children. That order does not establish how many were killed. His account also identifies groups of Antaimoro and Antaifasy people forcibly resettled on east-coast plantations during the first half of the nineteenth century. This specific relocation is one part of the wider history, not a route shared by everyone affected.

Merina power remained uneven. Central and eastern regions were more firmly controlled, while much of the south and west remained independent or contested. Campbell describes flight from slavery and compulsory labour, as well as resistance to the imperial court. The intensity of military service changed: campaigns against other Malagasy peoples largely subsided from 1853 to 1880, before service became more severe during the 1880s and early 1890s.

In 1895, French forces captured Antananarivo as imperial troops deserted. This closes the case’s account of the Merina imperial project. It does not mark the end of coercion in Madagascar, nor make the whole preceding century one uninterrupted campaign.
contested: The sources document military settlement and forced removal, but do not establish islandwide settler replacement or uniform Merina control. Campbell challenges earlier accounts that treated Madagascar as a unified kingdom and sharply contrasted Radama’s policies with those of Ranavalona I. Those earlier works and the primary reports he cites were not independently read here. Regional reports of devastation, army losses and slave-population figures cannot supply a verified death or displacement total for this entire event.
note: The date range c. 1790–1895 covers a changing imperial project, including conquest, military settlement, enslavement and compulsory labour. The reported plantation transfers belong to the first half of the nineteenth century. Slave imports, captured people and repeated labour service are different populations or measures and are not added together. Unknown totals do not mean zero harm.
placeGloss: Imerina lies in the central highlands. Northern Betsileo and the Lake Alaotra area are named in Campbell’s account of soldier colonies. The regional names provide orientation; they do not identify every colony, place of captivity or plantation receiving displaced people.
geometryExplanation: Madagascar provides geographic context for the full period. The sources used here do not establish precise colony sites or matched removal routes. No point, route or shaded area is supplied as a map of Merina conquest.

name: Peru internal armed conflict displacement
displaced: Civilians uprooted within Peru, many from rural Indigenous and Quechua-speaking communities in the Andes and central forest.
settlers: Shining Path (PCP-SL), Peruvian security forces, and—in some Amazonian localities—the MRTA; abusive self-defense groups also caused displacement.
evidence: Peru’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission describes internal displacement caused by attacks, threats, fear and disrupted livelihoods. It estimated approximately half a million people displaced during 1980–2000, while warning that the available migration data did not give a precise count.
story:
Violence drove civilians from homes and farmland across Peru during the internal armed conflict of 1980–2000. Shining Path attacks, killings and threats made communities unsafe; abuses by state forces also prompted flight. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission identifies the MRTA as a cause of displacement in some Amazonian localities and notes that self-defense groups also drove people away when they committed abuses. These actors did not operate everywhere in the same way.

Some people left after an attack or direct threat, and some were ordered to move by security forces. Others fled because prolonged insecurity and the loss of livelihoods made remaining untenable. The commission’s account includes both these forms of coercion. It does not describe every displaced family as having been transported or assigned a destination. The commission also reports that, in the central forest, some Asháninka and Nomatsiguenga people were abducted or forcibly concentrated in Shining Path camps and made to provide agricultural labor or military support. This was a distinct form of forced movement within the wider displacement crisis.

Many of those uprooted came from rural Indigenous communities and spoke Quechua. Movement often occurred in stages: from a community to a nearby town, then to a provincial or larger city. Lima, Huamanga, Huancayo and Ica became major places of refuge. Others remained within their home department or sought shelter in rural communities, including in the central forest. Some families moved repeatedly as violence followed them.

Leaving could mean losing access to land, housing and belongings. In cities, displaced people faced poverty, insecure work and ethnic or linguistic discrimination. Many kept ties to their home communities. Some returned, with an important period of returns in 1994–1996; others settled for the longer term in cities or moved again. Return did not necessarily restore their property or former livelihoods.

The commission estimated approximately half a million internally displaced people over 1980–2000. That figure is an approximation, not a precise census. Its discussion uses migration comparisons and an uncertain adjustment for people who moved for economic or other reasons. The end of the reporting period in 2000 did not mean that displacement and its consequences had ended.
contested: The estimate is affected by incomplete data and difficulty separating conflict displacement from other migration. Different tables cover different periods and populations; their totals cannot be added together, and repeated moves and returns are not additional people.
