Refugees from nearby villages told the investigators that some had seen their villages burning, while others had heard of the destruction after leaving. The report’s main account describes the systematic burning of empty Muslim and Greek quarters during the withdrawal.

The same report distinguishes the Greek or Patriarchist branch. Although pressure and promises shaped that movement, the commission judged it on the whole voluntary. Those arrivals, including people taken to Kukush, are not included in this Muslim expulsion case. Nor are the earlier violence of 1912, the separate Bulgarian flight from Kukush, or later onward migration.

The investigators saw Muslim refugees camped near Salonica with uncertain prospects for shelter and land. That wider refugee population is not a count of people expelled from Strumnitsa. The report records uprooting and loss, but does not establish this bounded group’s full death toll, complete receiving roster or eventual resettlement.
contested: The report distinguishes what investigators observed from testimony and interpretation. Its appendix and main narrative disagree on the withdrawal date; no exact final day or universal itinerary is adopted.
note: Muslim compulsion is kept separate from the Greek/Patriarchist movement and the broader Salonica refugee population. Death and displacement totals remain unassessed; this does not mean no harm occurred.
placeGloss: Strumnitsa and the Salonica area provide textual orientation only.
geometryExplanation: No town footprint, village boundary, route or refugee-camp coordinate is adopted.

name: Mongol retaliatory destruction of Bamiyan
displaced: Residents of the besieged fortified city of Bamiyan
settlers: Chinggis Khan and Mongol forces carrying out the siege and retaliation; no incoming settler population is established for this event.
evidence: Juvaini narrates the retaliatory killing and prohibition of habitation; Jackson corroborates the episode and reports the town’s later ruined condition.
story:
During the Mongol siege of Bamiyan, a projectile from the town killed Chinggis Khan’s favoured grandson, a son of Chaghatai. Juvaini describes resistance by the inhabitants and fighting with arrows and siege engines. His account dates the capture and retaliation to 618 in the Islamic calendar, corresponding to 1221–1222.

After the town fell, Juvaini says that Chinggis Khan ordered every living creature killed, no prisoners taken and no future habitation permitted. This was an account of deliberate destruction and killing, not a policy of taking the inhabitants elsewhere as captives. The sweeping wording belongs to the chronicler: it does not establish how many people died or the fate of every person in the surrounding valley.

Historian Peter Jackson places Bamiyan among the cities subjected to especially severe retaliation after the death of an imperial prince or commander. He identifies the grandson as Möetügen, corroborates the capture and retaliatory order, and reports that the town was still in ruins in Hamd-Allah Mustawfi’s day. This later report concerns the ruined town; it does not establish uninterrupted depopulation of the entire Bamiyan valley or conditions there today.
contested: The sources support severe retaliatory destruction, but their universal wording is not a census. Exact population, casualty totals, the fate of residents beyond the fortified city and its precise footprint remain unresolved.
note: This case concerns the besieged fortified city, not every settlement in the wider Bamiyan valley. No death count, displacement count or population share is established here. The comparison profile is preserved; the source reading does not independently verify its numerical scores.
placeGloss: Bamiyan in present-day Afghanistan; the affected fortified-city site is not mapped here.
geometryExplanation: The broad region provides orientation. The sources used here do not establish a mapped city boundary, affected valley-wide area or movement route.

name: Deportation of German-origin residents from Estonia
displaced: People of German origin removed from Estonia in the 15 August 1945 action
settlers: Soviet authorities carrying out the deportation; no incoming settler cohort is established for this case
evidence: The Estonian Commission’s conclusions identify the date, affected group, reported minimum and broad destination, but not individual receiving locations.
story:
On 15 August 1945, Soviet authorities rounded up people of German origin in Estonia and deported them to remote places in the Soviet interior. The Estonian International Commission for the Investigation of Crimes Against Humanity reports that at least 439 people, of all ages, were removed in this action.

The Commission describes a population with deep roots in Estonia. Some had stayed despite Nazi orders to leave for Germany in 1939–1940 and 1941; others had been taken to Germany and subsequently returned. It says that, in almost all cases, the deportees and their ancestors had lived in Estonia for generations or centuries, held Estonian citizenship and had intermarried with ethnic Estonians.

The Commission characterizes the deportation as collective punishment based on national origin. It states that the deportees’ wartime conduct was not investigated. That is the Commission’s finding, rather than a claim that individual case files have been independently examined here.

This case concerns that August 1945 action alone. The German-resident deportation from Lithuania, Estonia’s March 1949 deportations and the April 1951 removal of Jehovah’s Witnesses and their families are separate events. Their receiving locations and return histories cannot fill the gaps in this cohort’s story.
contested: The cited conclusion does not identify the operation order, full implementing chain, transport route, property-disposition rule or duration of exile for this cohort.
note: Labor status unknown: the cited source does not establish work assignments or labor conditions for this German-origin cohort. The profile’s imported-labor category does not mean that free conditions have been established. The reported minimum of 439 is not a separately validated impact measure; death and displacement totals remain unassessed here.
placeGloss: Estonia and the Soviet interior provide textual orientation only; precise receiving locations are not established.
geometryExplanation: No route, settlement coordinate, deportation boundary or historical footprint is adopted.

name: Deportation of German residents from Lithuania
displaced: German residents of Lithuania deported in the 1945 nationality-based action
settlers: Soviet authorities directing and carrying out the deportation; no incoming settler cohort is established for this case
evidence: The Lithuanian International Commission identifies a distinct 1945 German-resident deportation and reports its broad destinations and affected count.
story:
In 1945, Soviet authorities deported German residents of Lithuania to Siberia and Kazakhstan under general Soviet directives targeting Germans. Lithuania’s International Commission on the crimes of the Nazi and Soviet occupation regimes identifies this as a nationality-based deportation, distinct from the deportations associated with resistance to Soviet rule.

The Commission reports that 1,048 people were deported in this German-resident branch. It states that they were not included in the lists of Lithuanian deportees. That distinction matters: counts and experiences reported for the wider Lithuanian deportations cannot simply be added to, or assigned to, this group.

Forced removal from Lithuania is established, but the conclusions do not identify this group’s exact transport dates, routes, individual receiving settlements or duration of exile. The same document describes property seizure, compulsory labor and severe mortality among other deportees. It does not establish which of those specific conditions applied to the German-resident group described separately in conclusion 2.

This case therefore follows the 1945 removal from Lithuania to the broad receiving regions named by the Commission. The separate German-origin deportation from Estonia, resistance-family and later kulak campaigns, and subsequent transfers within the Soviet interior are outside this event.
contested: The Commission’s conclusions give limited detail about this particular group. Adjacent accounts of other deportations do not supply its property rules, work assignments, mortality or return history. The reported 1,048 is retained as an attributed source statement; no death total or population share is established.
note: Labor status unknown. The report documents compulsory labor for other deportees but does not establish work duties for this German-resident group. This is not evidence that the group was exempt from work. The existing profile is retained; its labor classification should not be read as proof of voluntary conditions.
placeGloss: Lithuania to Siberia and Kazakhstan; the source names broad receiving regions, not a single destination.
geometryExplanation: No departure locality, receiving settlement, transport route or territorial footprint is plotted. The map provides broad regional orientation only.

name: Obstruction of Jewish return to Cisr-i Mustafa Paşa
displaced: Jewish households whose return to Cisr-i Mustafa Paşa was obstructed or whose renewed departure followed local exclusion
settlers: Local actors obstructing Jewish return; no distinct incoming settler cohort is established for this case
evidence: Ginio’s scholarly account distinguishes contemporary newspaper reports and communal correspondence from his interpretation of local exclusion.
story:
In the spring of 1913, Jewish families began trying to return to Cisr-i Mustafa Paşa, now Svilengrad, after fleeing during the previous year’s war. Historian Eyal Ginio reconstructs these attempts from contemporary Jewish newspapers and communal correspondence. Early reports described some families recovering homes or finding rented accommodation, with Bulgarian authorities promising protection.

Return nevertheless faced local obstruction. Reports cited by Ginio described fires at Jewish homes and communal buildings, hostility toward returning families, and looted houses and shops. A report in La Luz described families remaining in Edirne after news that communal property had been burned. Another contemporary account said that Bulgarian authorities investigated the fires but did not identify the perpetrators. Ginio interprets control of abandoned property as a probable motive; that is an inference, not a confession by named attackers.

Central policy and local conduct did not simply coincide. Ginio describes Bulgarian political and military leaders accepting the right of the Jewish residents to return and taking or promising protective measures. Those measures did not overcome the reported local hostility or restore the material conditions needed to live in the town. This case therefore concerns local exclusion rather than treating the central protective orders as deportation policy.

Reports later in 1913 described renewed departures and reliance on Jewish communal assistance. A March 1914 newspaper account described refugees in Edirne facing hunger and lacking the money needed to travel back and pursue property claims. The account documents severe hardship, but supplies no verified death toll for this bounded episode. The surviving accounts do not establish one final day of displacement or a complete roster of households whose return was defeated.
contested: Individual perpetrators are not identified in the cited account. Different reports describe different family groups and stages of displacement; their numbers do not form a single event denominator.
note: Initial anticipatory flight in 1912, state-managed population exchanges, separate pressure in Uzun Köprü and later voluntary dispersal are excluded. Death and displacement totals remain unassessed; missing totals do not erase the reported arson, dispossession and hardship.
placeGloss: Cisr-i Mustafa Paşa, now Svilengrad, and Edirne are textual orientation only.
geometryExplanation: No household location, town footprint, route or receiving site is plotted.

name: Soviet deportation of Koreans from the Far East
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Soviet Koreans collectively removed from the Far East in the 1937 operation
settlers: The Soviet government and NKVD directing compulsory removal and resettlement; the arriving deportees are not thereby identified as voluntary colonizers
evidence: Pohl documents the two 1937 orders, implemented removals to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and severe deprivation after arrival.
story:
In 1937, the Soviet government ordered the removal of Koreans from the Far East to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. J. Otto Pohl describes a campaign driven by official suspicion that ethnic Koreans might assist Japanese intelligence. These were state allegations against a population, not findings of individual guilt.

Pohl identifies an order of 21 August targeting Koreans in the Far East’s border districts, followed on 28 September by an order covering the remaining Korean population east of Lake Baikal. He reports that the NKVD had transported 171,781 Koreans to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan by 25 October, and records a final removal of 700 on 1 November. These are Pohl’s operation figures at different dates, not a new combined total or a count of deaths.

Removal was followed by deprivation in the receiving regions. Pohl describes local authorities unprepared for the arrivals, inadequate shelter, and families living in dugouts or temporary huts. Many deportees could not find work; letters to the government complained of unemployment and impending starvation. Pohl distinguishes their classification as administrative exiles from the special-settler category, while emphasizing that the distinction did not ensure adequate food or housing.

Pohl reports deaths from disease, malnutrition and exposure. Citing Michael Rywkin, he gives an estimate of 40,000 deaths, or 23.2 percent, during 1937–1938. This attributed estimate concerns the wider aftermath in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, not deaths on the trains alone or a verified death total for this atlas event’s 1937 window. Rywkin’s underlying study has not been independently checked here.

Pohl also interprets the deportation as supplying cheap labor to the receiving republics. That interpretation sits alongside his evidence of unemployment and disrupted livelihoods; it does not establish one uniform work arrangement for every deportee. This case covers the 1937 Korean removal operation and completion of its initial transports. Accompanying Chinese removals, later births, and subsequent deportations of other populations are excluded.
contested: The reported removal figures and the attributed 1937–1938 mortality estimate have different dates and meanings. No combined removal total, transport death count, affected-community share or structured impact estimate is adopted. The underlying administrative records and Rywkin study were not independently read.
note: The profile is retained from the existing dataset. Its zero for imported unfree labor does not mean that removal was voluntary or that the deportees escaped exploitation. Pohl discusses cheap labor as an outcome but also documents unemployment; the passages read do not establish a uniform labor arrangement or its scale. Settler implantation remains marked as insufficient evidence.
placeGloss: The Soviet Far East, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are broad locations named in the source, not plotted departure or receiving settlements.
geometryExplanation: The precise departure places, receiving settlements and transport paths are not established for mapping here. No route, endpoint or territorial footprint is plotted.

name: Killing and displacement at Boulgar-Keui and Pichman-Keui
displaced: Bulgarian residents of Boulgar-Keui and Pichman-Keui, including survivors displaced during the July 1913 offensive
settlers: Ottoman military authorities and troops; some testimony alleges Greek participation in particular acts, without establishing a distinct incoming settler cohort
evidence: The Carnegie Commission combines mediated refugee depositions, a survivor interview and documentary material; its conclusions remain attributed.
story:
During the Ottoman offensive in eastern Thrace in July 1913, Bulgarian residents of Boulgar-Keui and neighboring Pichman-Keui suffered killing, sexual violence, plunder and displacement. The Carnegie Commission’s 1914 report describes the two villages together, while giving more detailed testimony for Boulgar-Keui. Its account combines refugee depositions transmitted by relief workers, an interview with a male survivor in Constantinople, and Greek official documents reproduced or discussed in the report.

For Boulgar-Keui, the report describes soldiers taking property before an order summoned the men of the village. The survivor account says that the assembled men were shot. Refugee women reported searches for men, killings at homes and sexual violence. Some testimony also alleged Greek participation in particular acts, including binding men and assaults. These are attributed participant accounts; they do not establish an identical actor pattern in every village. Testimony from Pichman-Keui includes sexual violence against a named elderly woman.

The Commission interpreted the combined evidence as showing a systematic military purpose to destroy the Bulgarian population. That is the Commission’s conclusion, rather than a separately authenticated extermination order. Its wider discussion reproduces Greek reports about other localities; those neighboring episodes are not added to this two-village case.

Survivors became refugees. The Commission reports women from the villages being questioned in Haskovo and Varna. It also describes a broader group of displaced Bulgarians eventually sent to Bulgaria after being mistaken for Greeks, and identifies women from Boulgar-Keui among those later seen at Varna. That broader movement is not a complete itinerary or count for either village. The account preserves severe violence and loss without providing one reconciled total of those killed, displaced or able to return.
contested: The sources give differently scoped house, family, victim and survivor figures. They also use a July sequence including old-style dates; no single harmonized day or casualty total is adopted.
note: This case excludes other eastern-Thrace villages, the Cisr-i Mustafa Paşa episode, Western-Thrace militia removals and later population exchanges. Death and displacement totals remain unassessed; that uncertainty does not negate the reported killings, sexual violence and loss of homes.
placeGloss: The historical village names are textual orientation only; no modern-location match is adopted.
geometryExplanation: No village footprint, survivor destination, route or point is plotted.

name: Soviet deportation of Meskhetian Turks and other Muslim communities from Georgia
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Meskhetian Turks, Kurds, Khemshils and other Muslim communities removed from southern Georgia in November 1944
settlers: The Soviet government, NKVD and NKGB directing compulsory removal and resettlement; the arriving deportees are not thereby identified as voluntary colonizers
evidence: Pohl describes the bounded November 1944 operation and distinguishes recorded transit deaths from deprivation and mortality after arrival.
story:
Between 15 and 26 November 1944, Soviet security agencies removed Meskhetian Turks, Kurds, Khemshils and other Muslim communities from Georgia’s border region to special settlements in Central Asia. Historian J. Otto Pohl links Stalin’s order to preparations for a possible war with Turkey and official fears that these communities might assist Turkish intelligence. Those suspicions were a rationale for collective removal, not demonstrated individual guilt.

Pohl reports that the NKVD and NKGB deported 94,955 people in this operation to Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kirghizia, now Kyrgyzstan. That figure covers the several communities named in his account; it is not a count of Meskhetian Turks alone. The geographic names identify broad departure and receiving regions, not a verified itinerary or a single settlement.

The journey itself cost lives. Pohl states that the NKVD recorded 457 deaths in transit among this contingent, and cautions that the actual number was probably much higher. The recorded figure is therefore an attributed administrative count with an explicit undercount warning, not a complete death toll.

Deprivation continued after arrival. Pohl describes inadequate housing, food and medicine, overcrowding, and outbreaks of disease. He cites a report dated 15 January 1945 in which the NKVD chief of Uzbekistan said that 8,000 deportees from Georgia in that republic lacked sufficient food, clothing and shoes. This is a later report about a receiving-republic subgroup, not an additional deportation total.

For the longer aftermath, Pohl reports that the NKVD–MVD recorded 19,047 deaths among Meskhetian Turks, Kurds and Khemshils in special settlements during 1945–1950. This multi-community figure concerns years after the 1944 removal operation; it is neither a Turks-only total nor a transport death count. In his article published in 2000, Pohl also wrote that most of these exiles were still unable to return to their homes in Georgia. That is a dated observation, not a claim that present-day return conditions have been verified here.
contested: The reported removal, transit-death, January 1945 deprivation and 1945–1950 mortality figures have different scopes. None is adopted as a structured impact estimate for this 1944 event, and they are not added together or narrowed to Meskhetian Turks alone. The underlying records were not independently checked.
note: The existing profile is retained. Its zero for imported unfree labor does not make the deportation voluntary or erase the deprivation described here. Special-settlement status in the passages read does not establish this cohort’s particular work obligations or the scale of unfree labor; no new labor score is inferred.
placeGloss: Southern Georgia and the receiving republics of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kirghizia (now Kyrgyzstan) are broad textual orientation.
geometryExplanation: No departure locality, receiving settlement, transport route or territorial footprint is plotted. The account supports regional orientation only.

name: Deportation of the Balkars and authorization to return
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Balkars removed from Kabardino-Balkaria in the March 1944 operation and living under the subsequent exile regime
settlers: Soviet authorities directing deportation and later restoration; no distinct voluntary incoming settler cohort is established here
evidence: Pohl and Helsinki Watch supply differently scoped operation, population, mortality and restoration evidence; their shared underlying authorities are not independent corroboration.
story:
In March 1944, Soviet authorities removed the Balkars from their North Caucasian homeland to special settlements in Kazakhstan and Kirghizia, now Kyrgyzstan. Historian J. Otto Pohl dates the NKVD operation to 8–9 March and reports 37,713 Balkars exiled. Helsinki Watch describes settlements surrounded on 8 March, residents driven by truck to railheads, and transport in cattle cars. Its estimate of 42,666 refers to the Balkar population at the time; it is not substituted for Pohl’s operation count.

The journey was lethal. Pohl reports that close to 3,500 Balkars died en route. Helsinki Watch, citing Vera Tolz, gives 3,494 presumed transit deaths. These remain attributed source reports, not a newly reconciled death toll. Helsinki Watch also describes non-Balkar women married to Balkar men being offered a choice between breaking their marital ties and remaining at home or sharing their husbands’ and children’s exile. Collective punishment disrupted families as well as removing people from their homes.

Pohl describes crowded trains, disease and severe shortages of food, medicine and shelter among the deported North Caucasian peoples. His later housing and mortality figures combine several nationalities; they cannot be assigned to Balkars alone. Helsinki Watch connects the removal with suppression of Balkar autonomy and describes the restrictions of the special-settlement system. Neither the hardship nor the absence of a separately verified total should be mistaken for a complete account of each family’s experience.

Policy changed after Khrushchev’s 1956 speech condemning the deportations. Helsinki Watch reports that the Balkars were exempted from special-settlement regulations, followed by a decree of 9 January 1957 reorganizing the Kabardinian republic as the Kabardino-Balkar republic. The 1957 boundary here marks this restoration and opening for return, not a claim that everyone had returned by then.

Return did not restore everything that had been lost. Helsinki Watch, drawing on its 1991 interview with Balkar historian Khanafiy Khutuev, describes returnees finding pillaged and damaged homes and farms. The report describes substantial return over time, but its later population and return estimates are not a measure of completed return in 1957. Permission to return, actual return and recovery of homes and autonomy were distinct outcomes.
contested: 37,713 deportees and an estimated population of 42,666 are different source scopes. The reported transit-death figures are not averaged, added or converted into a new percentage. Aggregate North Caucasian deaths and later census populations are not Balkar event totals.
note: Karachays and other deported nationalities are excluded from this case’s cohort. The profile is retained, including insufficient evidence for legal/property machinery, durability and separation from homeland. Imported-labor applicability is not established by these passages; exile and deprivation do not by themselves settle work obligations. Structured death and displacement totals remain unassessed.
placeGloss: Kabardino-Balkaria, Kazakhstan and Kirghizia (now Kyrgyzstan) are regional textual orientation only.
geometryExplanation: No household route, transport stop, receiving settlement or territorial footprint is plotted.

name: Operation Ring: expulsion from Armenian villages
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Armenian civilian communities within the bounded Shahumyan/Geranboi and Chaikent/Getashen Operation Ring referent
settlers: Azerbaijani SSR OMON and USSR forces as described by the Court and Human Rights Watch; no distinct incoming settler cohort is established here
evidence: The Sargsyan judgment provides an attributed April–May 1991 background account; Human Rights Watch names Operation Ring and distinguishes expulsions from later returns and the 1992 counteroffensive.
story:
In April and May 1991, USSR internal forces and Azerbaijani SSR special-purpose militia units, known as OMON, carried out an operation in Armenian villages with the stated purpose of checking passports and disarming local Armenian militants. This dating and terminology come from the historical background in the European Court of Human Rights’ Sargsyan judgment. That account reports that government forces used the stated purpose as a pretext to expel Armenian residents from villages in the Shahumyan region, with arrests and violence against civilians.

Human Rights Watch describes Operation Ring more broadly as taking place in the spring and summer of 1991, naming Azerbaijani OMON accompanied by Soviet Army troops. Its account records the authorities’ passport and weapons explanations alongside reported violent removals. These descriptions identify each source’s account; they do not establish a newly verified single command structure or expand this case beyond the bounded April–May phase.

The judgment describes people forced from their homes toward Nagorno-Karabakh or Armenia. Human Rights Watch separately identifies forced displacement from Geranboi, also known as Shaumyan, and from Chaikent/Getashen. These places locate affected communities in the sources, rather than defining a complete village roster or a route followed by every household. Arrest, violence and loss of access to home remain the central harms described here; no complete death or displacement total is established.

Human Rights Watch notes that some displaced people returned in late 1991 and early 1992. Those returns are aftermath context, not evidence that all residents returned or recovered their property. The later June 1992 counteroffensive and the Sargsyan applicant’s own displacement in 1992 belong outside this case. Earlier pogroms, later district offensives and subsequent onward movements are also excluded.
contested: The Court refers to various sources for the expulsions; its background account is not independent project verification of every participant or order. Human Rights Watch’s broader spring–summer wording is not used to invent one precise ending day for the narrower phase. Source village counts and general war refugee stocks are not event totals.
note: The Court’s historical background and Human Rights Watch’s reporting have distinct scopes. The 1991 removal episode is not the applicant’s 1992 flight or the subject of every later legal finding. The existing profile is retained, including its partial and insufficient-evidence displays; the passages read do not establish a uniform work regime, property transfer or permanent ban on return.
placeGloss: Shahumyan/Geranboi and Chaikent/Getashen are source names for affected areas and communities, not plotted event endpoints.
geometryExplanation: No village point, household destination, transport route or territorial footprint is plotted. Regional orientation does not imply that every displaced family followed one path.

name: Post-liberation expulsion and residency pressure against Palestinians in Kuwait
displaced: Palestinians still present in Kuwait after 26 February 1991 who were expelled or pressured to depart, including long-term residents and affected families
settlers: Restored Kuwaiti authorities, security forces, government employers and residency authorities; no distinct incoming settler population is established by this account
evidence: A contemporary Middle East Watch report connects direct deportation and coercive pressure while distinguishing changes during 1991. Its witnesses and cited materials remain mediated through the report.
story:
After the Kuwaiti government returned from exile on 26 February 1991, Palestinians still living in Kuwait faced arrests, expulsions and pressure to leave. Middle East Watch’s account describes a campaign against alleged collaborators with the Iraqi occupation that affected long-term residents. Its report places responsibility for much of the abuse on official security forces and armed groups working closely with them; accusations against whole communities did not establish individual guilt.

The pressure included physical violence. Middle East Watch reports killings, torture, deaths in custody and disappearances after liberation, with Palestinians among those affected. Its account describes summary expulsions beginning in March and regular large-scale deportations from June. Families could be caught in the roundups. The report describes people being deported even after they had been cleared of accusations or acquitted, and says that most deportees had no practical opportunity to challenge their removal. These are the report’s findings, not a complete record of each Palestinian resident’s experience.

Government employment and residence rules reinforced the pressure. According to the report, the authorities terminated foreign and Bedoon government employees’ contracts retroactively to the start of the Iraqi occupation. Palestinian employees were among those losing jobs and unpaid wages; severance payments were held until departure arrangements were completed. The report connects job loss with administrative deportability under the Foreign Residents Act, including provisions concerning financial support and the termination of foreign government employees’ jobs. Loss of employment could therefore undermine both a household’s livelihood and its ability to remain.

Foreign residents were also required to re-register for residence permits. The deadline was extended to 31 December 1991; the report warned that people who had not secured employment risked summary deportation afterward unless the period was extended again. Some detention conditions and procedures improved later in the year, but the report says expulsions and pressure to leave continued. This case’s 1991 endpoint bounds the documented sequence, not the end of every exclusion or consequence.

This account concerns Palestinians present after liberation who were expelled or pressured to depart. Palestinians who had already left during the occupation and war form a separate cohort. The government’s subsequent refusal to readmit most of those earlier leavers is not counted here as another departure. The report combines several nationalities in many of its figures and does not supply a complete, nonduplicative roster of Palestinian expulsions, family departures and departures under pressure.
contested: The approximately 180,000 Palestinians who left during occupation and war are excluded. Mixed Palestinian, Bedoon, Iraqi and other resident figures, detention stocks and before-and-after population estimates cannot be added or subtracted into a Palestinian operation total. Direct removal and pressured departure are distinct forms of coercion, but the report does not link them for every person.
note: The complete existing profile is retained. Legal and property machinery, durability, separation from homeland and imported-labor applicability remain insufficiently established in that profile; elimination over incorporation retains its evidence range. Describing documented residency and employment measures does not certify every inherited score. Structured death and displacement totals remain unassessed. The separate report Nowhere to Go was not read for this account.
placeGloss: Kuwait is regional textual orientation only; no complete departure-destination pattern is established.
geometryExplanation: No individual departure route, border crossing, detention-site marker or territorial footprint is plotted.

name: Post-surrender violence and dispossession of Biharis in Bangladesh
displaced: Bihari and other Urdu-speaking non-Bengali residents targeted after the Pakistani surrender; later transfers and refugee returns are distinct movements.
settlers: People involved in anti-Bihari retaliation and property seizure; later Bangladesh and Pakistan authorities shaped citizenship and transfer options. No complete perpetrator roster or distinct incoming settler population is established.
evidence: UNHCR’s 2000 retrospective describes post-surrender killings and property seizure, then a prolonged camp and citizenship aftermath. It does not provide a complete victim total, movement sequence or common endpoint.
story:
After the Pakistani army surrendered in mid-December 1971, Biharis in the newly independent Bangladesh faced retaliatory violence. UNHCR’s retrospective explains that the community was perceived as aligned with Pakistan and that many Biharis had joined Pakistani militias or collaborated with the army. That account does not establish the conduct of every individual. UNHCR reports that many Biharis were killed and much of their property was seized. Collective suspicion exposed people to violence and loss of their homes and possessions.

The consequences extended beyond the initial attacks. UNHCR describes problems acquiring citizenship under Bangladesh’s 1972 provisions concerning allegiance to a foreign state. It also notes that many Biharis were accepted in practice. Its account of 1999 nevertheless records more than 200,000 Biharis living in 66 camps with poor facilities. This later camp population is not a count of those initially attacked or displaced, and the passage does not establish that everyone was forcibly transported into a camp or held under one detention order.

Transfers to Pakistan were a later response to the changed political situation. The August 1973 New Delhi Agreement covered several populations, including non-Bengalis in Bangladesh who opted for repatriation to Pakistan. UNHCR describes restrictive admission by Pakistan, a further agreement in April 1974 and additional transfers in later years. Those movements are kept separate from the initiating violence and dispossession; their totals cannot be added together as the number of victims of this event.

Writing in 2000, UNHCR described unresolved citizenship and a refugee-like existence for many Biharis, while noting indications that some preferred Bangladeshi nationality. These are observations from that publication’s period, not a claim about everyone’s legal status today. The source establishes neither a single end to the dispossession nor a common date when affected families recovered secure homes and citizenship. The event therefore begins after the 1971 surrender and leaves its endpoint unresolved.
contested: The read UNHCR passages do not identify a complete perpetrator roster, a single central order, every route into camp residence, or complete killing and property-loss totals. Later camp stocks and transfer figures have different dates and populations. The ICJ report named in the frozen source record has not been read and is not used to fill these gaps.
note: The preceding Pakistani-army displacement, Bengali and Hindu refugee returns from India, and subsequent agreed transfers are excluded from the initiating unit. Death and displacement totals remain unassessed; that uncertainty does not negate the documented killings and property seizure. The profile’s uncertain traits remain visible. The timeline position marks the 1971 start, not a resolved end in that year.
placeGloss: Bangladesh is the setting; Pakistan and India appear in the distinct return and transfer context. No individual itinerary is mapped.
geometryExplanation: No verified event-specific origins, receiving camps, routes or territorial footprint are plotted.

name: Anti-Greek pogrom in Istanbul
displaced: Greek residents of Istanbul targeted by violence and destruction; later departures are reported without a complete roster
settlers: Organized rioters and looters; police nonintervention or encouragement is reported, with government involvement in the bombing pretext attributed to a later court finding; no distinct incoming settler cohort established
evidence: Helsinki Watch’s retrospective report combines contemporary consular observations, reported figures and an account of a later court finding.
story:
On 6–7 September 1955, organized anti-Greek violence struck Istanbul’s Greek residents and communal institutions. Helsinki Watch’s account describes the looting and destruction of homes, businesses, churches, schools, monasteries and cemeteries. It quotes the American Consul-General reporting that he saw shops looted while police stood aside or encouraged the mob. A subsequent consular dispatch reproduced in the report’s notes described widespread wrecking, looting and desecration, with some buildings damaged by fire. These observations are presented through Helsinki Watch’s later report, not a complete record of every attacker or police officer.

The destruction involved bodily harm as well as property loss. Helsinki Watch reports more than 4,000 Greek shops sacked and more than 2,000 homes vandalized and robbed, along with extensive damage to religious and educational institutions. The report contrasts the Turkish government’s initial account of three people killed and thirty injured with subsequent reports of fifteen deaths. It also records competing monetary-loss estimates. These are attributed reports, not a reconciled casualty list or property inventory; the exact scale is not established here.

The violence was presented as a response to a bombing at the Turkish consulate in Thessaloniki that also damaged the nearby birthplace of Kemal Atatürk. According to Helsinki Watch, a Turkish court six years later found that Prime Minister Adnan Menderes and other government figures had ordered that bombing to incite and justify anti-Greek violence. This account of a later court finding does not establish an independently verified order for every act committed during the pogrom.

Helsinki Watch says that some thousands of Greeks left Istanbul after the riots, while explicitly noting that exact numbers had never been established. The destruction of homes, livelihoods and communal places therefore had a departure aftermath, but the account does not give a complete roster, a common destination or a date when every departure ended. This case is bounded to the Istanbul pogrom of 6–7 September 1955. The separate 1964 expulsion and asset-control program and the histories of Imbros and Tenedos are excluded.
contested: Casualty, damage, monetary-loss and departure figures are reported or approximate. Different reports are not added into a single total. The passage does not establish a complete command chain, attacker roster or departure itinerary.
note: The complete existing profile is retained: government direction and elimination over incorporation show evidence ranges; durability and separation from homeland remain insufficiently established; imported unfree labor remains structurally not applicable. These indicators are not death or displacement counts. Structured impact remains unassessed.
placeGloss: Istanbul provides textual orientation only; no attacked-site inventory or departure destination is mapped.
geometryExplanation: No historical footprint, route, origin point or destination point is adopted.

name: Deportation of the Karachays and the difficult return from exile
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Karachays deported from the Karachay Autonomous Oblast in November 1943 and living through exile and the subsequent return process
settlers: Soviet authorities directing deportation, exile and rehabilitation; the Karachay deportee cohort, with no separate voluntary incoming settler population established here
evidence: Pohl’s historical article and Helsinki Watch’s report distinguish the operation, earlier population, exile and later return testimony. Their underlying sources may overlap.
story:
On 6 November 1943, the NKVD deported the Karachays from the Karachay Autonomous Oblast to special settlements in Kazakhstan, Kirghizia—now Kyrgyzstan—and other eastern areas of the Soviet Union. Historian J. Otto Pohl reports 68,939 deportees. Helsinki Watch describes the November arrests and removal without warning, drawing on earlier historical accounts. The removal also abolished the Karachay autonomous territory; the report says that part of it was transferred to Georgia.

Helsinki Watch, quoting Robert Conquest, describes families assembled outdoors before being taken to railheads. Pohl describes the deported North Caucasian peoples crowded into cattle cars, with disease and deaths during the journeys. Helsinki Watch’s Karachay section characterizes the deportation as exceptionally harsh and reports heavy losses through its cited authorities. These accounts establish serious harm without supplying a separately verified Karachay death toll. Pohl’s transit-death figures for Balkars or all North Caucasian deportees are not figures for this case.

Exile continued the disruption. Pohl specifically notes reports of severe food shortages among Karachays soon after their arrival in Kazakhstan in November 1943. His broader discussion describes inadequate housing, food and medicine among several deported North Caucasian peoples. Those combined figures cannot be assigned to Karachays alone. Helsinki Watch gives 75,737 as the Karachay population in the 1939 census; that earlier population is distinct from Pohl’s 68,939 operation deportees.

Policy changed after Khrushchev’s 1956 speech condemning the deportations. Helsinki Watch reports a decree of 24 November 1956 restoring national autonomy to the peoples concerned, but describes the Karachays’ incorporation into a Karachay-Cherkess autonomous region rather than restoration of their former separate region. Permission to return opened a path home. Neither that permission nor the report’s statement that most returned soon afterward establishes a date when return was complete.

Return did not automatically restore homes or compensate losses. Helsinki Watch’s published 1991 interview with Karachay spokesman Kazbek Iskhakovich Chomaev describes initial restrictions on building homes and a lack of compensation provisions. He said returnees received little assistance and that some went back to their places of exile. This is an attributed account from 1991, not a statement about conditions today. The case begins in 1943; its closing year remains unresolved.
contested: 68,939 operation deportees and 75,737 people in the 1939 census are different counts. Aggregate North Caucasian mortality, Balkar losses and later census populations cannot establish Karachay deaths or a return rate. The closing year remains unknown.
note: Balkars and other deported nationalities are excluded from this case’s cohort. The full profile is retained: legal and property machinery has partial evidence, while lethal coercion, durability and separation from homeland have insufficient evidence for a solid point. Those limits do not erase the reported deaths and deprivation. The imported-labor zero does not mean that exile was voluntary or that no coerced work occurred; the passages read do not establish detailed Karachay work assignments. Structured death and displacement totals remain unassessed. The 1943 timeline position marks the start, not a completed return.
placeGloss: The Karachay homeland, Kazakhstan and Kirghizia (now Kyrgyzstan) are regional textual context only.
geometryExplanation: No individual route, railhead, receiving settlement or territorial footprint is plotted.

name: Expulsion of Greek citizens from Istanbul and restrictions on their assets
displaced: Greek citizens living in Istanbul who were expelled or denied residence renewal; Turkish citizens of Greek descent who departed under pressure are a distinct associated group
settlers: Turkish government and authorities directing expulsion, residence permits and asset restrictions; no distinct incoming settler cohort is established here
evidence: Helsinki Watch’s retrospective report distinguishes the 1964 state program, citizenship groups and reported property restrictions; its underlying decrees and press accounts were not independently read.
story:
On 16 March 1964, the Turkish government began expelling Greeks who held Greek citizenship. Helsinki Watch places the action in a period of heightened tension over Cyprus and describes the government’s stated security justification. The people affected included Greeks born in Turkey, some of whom had never been to Greece. Citizenship determined the legal target of the expulsion program; it did not establish that each person posed a threat.

The removals allowed little time to prepare. Helsinki Watch reports that over a thousand people were promptly expelled, most on only a few hours’ notice, with permission to take just $22 and one suitcase of clothes. It reports another 5,000 expelled shortly afterward. After September, the government stopped renewing Greek citizens’ residence permits, and the report describes a further 10,000 to 11,000 expulsions. These are reported figures for different stages, not a newly verified total; the report’s footnote also cites a different estimate of 9,000.

The pressure reached beyond those legally expelled. Helsinki Watch cites an October 1964 newspaper report that 30,000 Turkish citizens of Greek descent had also left permanently. Those departures are a distinct reported group, not another count of Greek citizens served with expulsion orders. The report describes continued departures in later years by people fearful for their lives and property; that later history is context, rather than an extension of this case’s initiating 1964 program.

Property controls made departure more damaging. According to Helsinki Watch, Greeks affected by the measures could not sell their homes or other property or withdraw money from their bank accounts. Its footnote identifies Ministerial Decree No. 6/3807/1964 as ordering seizure of Greek citizens’ real property and bank accounts, and Decree No. 3706/1964 as prohibiting their acquisition of real property. These descriptions establish the reported policy machinery, not the disposition of every person’s assets.

The consequences outlasted the year of expulsion. Helsinki Watch reports that the ban on selling property was lifted in 1989, followed by complicated court proceedings, many still pending when the report appeared in 1992. That later change does not move the event’s endpoint to 1989 or establish complete restitution. The 1955 pogrom and the separate history of Imbros and Tenedos are outside this case.
contested: The reported expulsion and departure figures are not a person-level roster and are not added together. Different citizenship groups, households and reporting periods may overlap. The report does not establish each asset outcome or a complete death toll for this program.
note: The full profile is preserved, including the evidence range for elimination over incorporation, insufficient evidence for durability and separation from homeland, and the structural imported-labor status. The source account does not newly certify those scores. Structured death and displacement totals remain unassessed. The 1964 boundary covers the initiating expulsion and asset measures; the 1989 change is aftermath, not complete restitution or a current legal-status claim.
placeGloss: Istanbul and Greece are geographic context; no individual departure itinerary is mapped.
geometryExplanation: No route, border crossing, receiving settlement or territorial footprint is plotted.

name: Drainage and forced displacement of Iraq's Marsh Arabs
displaced: Marsh Arab communities of southeastern Iraq whose subsistence and homes were undermined by government policies
settlers: Iraqi government authorities responsible for repression and water diversion; no distinct incoming settler population established by the cited passage
evidence: Human Rights Watch’s pre-invasion account describes water diversion, destruction of subsistence and forced displacement; its population estimate cites an underlying study not independently read here.
story:
In the early 1990s, the Iraqi government diverted water from the southeastern marshlands near the Tigris and Euphrates through dams and canals. Human Rights Watch’s pre-invasion account describes this as repression of the Marsh Arabs. The government presented displacement from the marshes as a way to provide better living conditions. HRW instead reports that the policies deprived people of food, destroyed their agricultural traditions and forced them from their homes.

HRW connects this assault on the marshes to the 1991 revolt and to the government’s hostility toward people it regarded as opponents. The report also describes the believed presence of army deserters and political opponents in the marshes, alongside earlier drainage and oil-development plans. These are the report’s explanations of the policy’s background; they do not establish that every resident was an insurgent or that a proposed oil project was completed. The documented harm was the destruction of conditions needed to live in the marshes and the displacement that followed.

The report states that at least 100,000 displaced Marsh Arabs were among approximately 300,000 displaced people in southern Iraq. This is a reported population already displaced at the time of the account, not a count of new removals during a single operation. The wider southern estimate includes other people and cannot be added to the Marsh Arab figure. HRW cites an October 2002 study for this passage; that underlying study has not been independently read here. This account is limited to conditions reported before the 2003 invasion and does not establish when displacement or return was complete.
contested: The source reports a displaced population rather than a complete event roster. It does not establish a common destination, an exact event total, individual attack chronology or the completion of return. Northern Iraq’s Arabization and property-transfer measures belong to separate cases.
note: The frozen 1991–2003 event bounds and complete eight-trait profile are retained. The source account stops before the 2003 invasion; the ending year does not establish completed displacement or return. The reported population stock is not a new quantitative impact estimate.
placeGloss: The southeastern Iraqi marshlands near the Tigris and Euphrates provide textual orientation only.
geometryExplanation: No historical drainage footprint, departure route, origin point or destination point is adopted.

name: Palestinian flight from Kuwait during Iraqi occupation and Gulf War conditions, 1990–1991
displaced: Palestinian residents of Kuwait who left during Iraqi occupation and Gulf War conditions; the report does not provide a complete person-level or legal-status roster
settlers: Iraqi occupation and Gulf War conditions drove the movement described here; the restored Kuwaiti government enters the account only through later non-readmission and absentee-property measures. No distinct incoming settler cohort is established.
evidence: Middle East Watch distinguishes the occupation/war leavers from later post-liberation measures and reports their approximate number, abandoned homes and property, predominant destination, and blocked return.
story:
During the Iraqi occupation of Kuwait and the Gulf War, a large part of Kuwait’s Palestinian community left the country. Middle East Watch reports that around 180,000 Palestinians departed to avoid the hardships of occupation and war. In many cases, they left homes and property accumulated over decades. Most reportedly went to Jordan, while some had no country in which they were entitled to reside.

The report does not divide this population into people fleeing occupation, active warfare or both, and it does not provide a person-level roster or complete set of routes and destinations. The reported figure therefore remains an attributed approximation in the narrative. It is not used here as a structured displacement total.

After Kuwait was liberated, the restored Kuwaiti government refused to readmit almost all of the people in this reported cohort. Middle East Watch also describes a July 1991 measure affecting property left in rented homes. These were later consequences for people who had already left; they are not counted as another movement.

This case is limited to the occupation- and war-era flight. A separate case covers Palestinians who were still in Kuwait after liberation and were then expelled or pressured to depart. The source does not provide a complete crosswalk between those populations, so their counts cannot be combined and exact person-level disjointness remains unresolved.
contested: The source does not supply a person roster, exact legal-status breakdown, causal allocation between occupation and war, complete route or destination set, month-by-month departure series, or person-level crosswalk with the post-liberation sibling. The reported movement count is approximate and must not be added to the sibling’s figures.
note: The complete frozen eight-trait profile is retained without recoding. Around 180,000 remains an attributed narrative figure rather than structured impact. Later non-readmission is return foreclosure for the same reported cohort, not a second departure. Exact disjointness from the post-liberation sibling remains unresolved.
placeGloss: Kuwait and Jordan provide textual orientation only; the source says most went to Jordan but does not give a complete destination set.
geometryExplanation: No exact origins within Kuwait, routes, border crossings, receiving settlements or complete destination geometry are adopted.

name: Soviet deportation and confinement of Volga Germans
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Volga Germans forcibly removed from the Volga region; broader Soviet-German deportation and labor-army populations remain separately described
settlers: Soviet government and NKVD authorities directing deportation, special settlement and compulsory labor; the sources do not establish a bounded incoming replacement-settler cohort
evidence: Pohl and Helsinki Watch document the 1941 Volga operation, special-settlement confinement, forced-labor transfers and the limited 1955 change in status. Broader and overlapping Soviet-German figures remain distinct and attributed.
story:
After Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, Soviet leaders treated German ethnicity as a collective security threat. Pohl traces a sequence of leadership decisions, an NKVD operational order and the 28 August decree directing removal from the Volga region. Helsinki Watch reports that the decree accused the population collectively and that a September decree transferred the territory of the Volga German republic to the Saratov and Stalingrad provinces. The evidence does not establish individual disloyalty; Helsinki Watch also notes Soviet Germans who had fought against Nazi Germany.

Pohl reports that between 3 and 20 September 1941 the NKVD forcibly deported more than half a million Soviet Germans from the Volga region to special settlements in Kazakhstan, Siberia, the Urals and Central Asia. This is an attributed operation-scale statement, not a verified roster. His later figures of 799,459 Soviet Germans in special settlements by 1 January 1942 and 1,209,430 by 1946 cover broader Soviet-German populations and later stages. They are not Volga-only totals and are not added to the Volga operation figure.

Removal was followed by confinement and compulsory labor. Pohl describes primitive special-settlement housing and reports that nearly 400,000 Soviet Germans were mobilized into labor battalions and colonies during the war. Helsinki Watch likewise reports forced-labor drafting and a postwar decree that treated assigned settlements as permanent and punished unauthorized departure. The labor-army figure covers a broader and overlapping Soviet-German population. It therefore remains separate from deportation and special-settlement figures.

The conditions were lethal, but the retained evidence does not support a single structured death total for this case. Pohl states that Soviet-German statistics for deportation, special settlements and the labor army are incomplete and contradictory for 1941–1944. His cited excess-mortality range and postwar administrative table have different scopes and periods. They remain attributed evidence of severe harm rather than a death, displacement, community-share or world-share indicator.

The special-settlement regime outlasted the war. Helsinki Watch reports that a 13 December 1955 decree freed Germans from MVD surveillance but withheld confiscated property and did not permit return to the places from which they had been deported. The endpoint therefore marks a change in surveillance status, not restitution, completed return or restoration of Volga German autonomy. Later measures in 1964 and 1974 form aftermath: the collective accusation was voided and return was eventually allowed, while the autonomous republic remained unrestored and practical barriers continued.

The full statistical profile is retained without recertification. The sources directly document forced labor as a receiving condition and transfer stage, while the frozen F8 imported-unfree-labor value remains zero. That tension is visible here and is not resolved by this authoring packet. Any F8 reconciliation or recoding requires separate Astra High review.
contested: The retained sources do not provide a person-level crosswalk across deportation, special settlement and labor-army stages. Volga-operation figures cannot be added to broader Soviet-German stocks. Mortality evidence for 1941–1944 is incomplete and contradictory, and the identity and scale of people later occupying the former autonomous republic are not established here.
note: The frozen 1941–1955 bounds and complete eight-trait profile are preserved. The 1955 endpoint marks release from MVD surveillance without property restitution, authorized return or restored autonomy. Forced labor is documented in the narrative while frozen F8=0 remains unchanged and visibly qualified pending any separate Astra High reconciliation. Structured impact remains unassessed.
placeGloss: The Volga region, Kazakhstan, Siberia, the Urals and Central Asia are textual orientation only; broader destination references do not define a complete route or settlement roster.
geometryExplanation: No origin point, deportation route, receiving settlement or territorial footprint is plotted.

name: Anfal campaign against Iraqi Kurds
displaced: Kurdish rural communities and Assyrian and other minorities captured or forcibly relocated during the eight Anfal operations; the source does not establish a complete person-level roster
settlers: The Iraqi Ba'athist state, army and security services carried out the campaign. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
evidence: The retained Human Rights Watch report defines eight 1988 Anfal operations, documents their state command structure and describes settlement destruction, detention, disappearance, killing and forced relocation.
story:
Human Rights Watch describes Anfal as eight Iraqi military operations against Kurdish rural areas from 23 February through 6 September 1988. The first began with the assault on Sergalou-Bergalou; later operations moved through other designated areas, and the Final Anfal targeted Badinan before the government announced an amnesty on 6 September.

The operations sat inside a wider command period. Ali Hassan al-Majid held special powers over northern Iraq from 29 March 1987 through 23 April 1989. The report identifies regular army corps, security and military-intelligence agencies, the Ba'ath Party, the Popular Army and pro-government Kurdish militia as parts of the state structure used to carry out the campaign and process captured civilians.

The report describes attacks on settlements, chemical attacks, destruction and looting, followed by capture, transport, detention and separation of villagers. Many detainees disappeared or were executed; other survivors were forcibly relocated and forbidden to return to their villages. The stages followed a broadly recurring pattern, but the evidence does not establish one universal sequence for every household or person.

The report gives separate estimates for disappearances, destroyed villages, detainees, displaced villagers, deaths in particular chemical attacks, deaths during Anfal and deaths after detention or forced displacement. These quantities describe different populations, places, outcomes and periods. They are not added here, and the evidence does not establish a deduplicated total for the event.

Halabja is part of the report's broader account of genocide against Iraqi Kurds, but the report expressly says that the city was not technically part of Anfal. Its deaths are excluded from the Anfal figures. The longer Arabization of Kirkuk and Khanaqin is also kept separate, as are earlier and later campaigns outside the eight operations.
contested: The 1987–1989 special-powers frame is wider than the eight operations. Halabja and its deaths are outside the technical Anfal unit, and Kirkuk Arabization remains a separate case. The report's disappearance, village, detention, displacement, attack-death and later-mortality quantities are not commensurate and cannot be combined into a deduplicated event total.
note: The complete frozen eight-trait profile is retained without recoding. Structured impact remains null. Named places and facilities provide textual context only; no geometry, route, universal household sequence, completed return or property restoration is inferred.
placeGloss: Northern Iraqi Kurdistan, named operational areas, holding facilities and relocation sites provide textual orientation only.
geometryExplanation: The source does not establish a single exact origin, destination, route, district polygon or complete spatial representation for the affected population.

name: Mogadishu public-land and settlement evictions and relocation pressure, 2012-2013
displaced: Internally displaced people and urban poor removed from Mogadishu public buildings, public land, or private property. Displaced families living in informal settlements appear only in the unproven 2013 relocation plan; no complete household roster is available
settlers: Somali government authorities reclaiming public property and private owners reclaiming property. The report generally identifies some returning refugees and diaspora members among owner-evictors but supplies no person-level flight-history crosswalk and does not establish that every owner was a returnee.
evidence: The World Bank directly documents increased authority- and owner-led urban evictions, expressly dates implemented Mogadishu public-building summary evictions to 2012, and separately describes the 2013 relocation announcement as a plan.
story:
As security and commercial activity increased in Somalia’s cities, competition over urban land intensified. The World Bank reports that authorities evicted internally displaced people from public buildings and land, while private owners removed them from private property. Those affected often received little notice and no alternative place to go.

In Mogadishu, the report expressly dates one implemented episode to 2012. The government began reclaiming public buildings, and many internally displaced people and urban poor were summarily evicted. The source does not give an implemented-removal total, identify every household, or trace where those removed went.

The report also describes a number of refugees and diaspora members returning to Somalia and evicting internally displaced people from their properties as land values and private activity rose. This is a general account of some returning owners. It does not establish that every private owner was a returnee, and it does not connect any particular evictor to a refugee history.

On 20 January 2013, the Ministry of Interior and National Security announced a plan to relocate displaced families from settlements across Mogadishu. A task force and six-step plan contemplated locations outside the city by 20 August 2013. These details show planned relocation pressure and a risk of forced movement; they do not prove that every proposed relocation occurred or establish a completed destination outcome.

This case is limited to the implemented 2012 public-building removals and directly documented Mogadishu owner-led evictions; the 2013 plan is included only as pressure and planning. Earlier movements caused by conflict, drought, flood or land loss remain separate, as do later Somalia event units. The source provides no unique-person crosswalk across those movements, so no combined total or deduplicated roster is claimed.
contested: The report provides no implemented-removal total, household roster, destination outcome, or unique-person crosswalk. The 2013 plan cannot be treated as completed movement; every private owner cannot be treated as a returnee; and no individual evictor can be assigned a refugee history.
note: The complete frozen eight-trait profile is preserved without interpretation or recoding. Structured impact is null, geometry is unknown, and there is no incoming-flight note. Earlier conflict, drought, flood and land-loss movements and later Somalia units remain separate under the frozen parent rule.
placeGloss: Mogadishu is the bounded city context. Public buildings, public land, informal settlements, private property, and contemplated locations outside the city are textual orientation only.
geometryExplanation: The source does not establish exact buildings, settlement polygons, parcel boundaries, routes, destination sites, or a complete implemented-movement geography.

name: South Sudan civil war and mass displacement
displaced: South Sudanese civilians repeatedly displaced within the country or across borders during the 2013–2018 civil-war window; no complete or deduplicated person-level roster is established
settlers: South Sudanese government and opposition forces drove displacement. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
evidence: The retained UNHCR-commissioned report directly documents the 2013 escalation, the 2015–2016 agreement sequence, abuses by government and opposition forces, repeated displacement and separately dated mortality and later displacement figures.
story:
The report traces the civil war from South Sudan's post-independence political crisis. President Salva Kiir removed Vice-President Riek Machar in July 2013; over the following months, political conflict became armed struggle between government and opposition forces and had spread across many parts of the country by the end of 2013.

The parties signed the Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan in 2015, and a transitional government followed. Machar returned as vice-president in 2016, but violence continued despite a permanent-ceasefire agreement. This case preserves the frozen 2013–2018 window; it does not claim that conflict or displacement ended in 2018.

The report describes serious violations by government and opposition forces. Civilians were killed on the basis of ethnicity or perceived political loyalty; women and girls were abducted and raped; hospitals, schools, civilian property and livelihoods were destroyed or looted; humanitarian personnel were attacked; and combatants obstructed assistance. These documented forms of conduct do not establish that every affected person experienced the same sequence.

Many internally displaced people fled more than once as fighting shifted across the country. Some civilians who reached United Nations Protection of Civilians sites still faced insecurity. The report does not provide a person-level crosswalk, a universal itinerary or a complete set of origins and destinations, so this case adopts no route or geometry.

The report separately cites a modeled estimate of 383,000 conflict-caused deaths from December 2013 through April 2018, including about 190,000 people killed. These are nested mortality measures, not two additive totals and not displacement counts. The report also gives later 2021–2022 IDP and refugee stocks; those figures postdate the frozen window and remain aftermath context. None of these quantities is adopted as structured impact or as a deduplicated event-wide total.
contested: The frozen event ends in 2018, but the source describes continuing violence and later displacement. The 383,000 conflict-caused death estimate includes about 190,000 killed and is not added to it; neither is a displacement count. Later 2021–2022 IDP/refugee stocks remain aftermath context and are not combined with each other or with the frozen event.
note: The complete frozen eight-trait profile is retained without recoding, including F6 coverage 0.9038663149. Structured impact remains null, geometry remains unknown and no incoming-flight note is added.
placeGloss: South Sudan and neighboring asylum countries provide textual orientation only; named countries do not constitute a complete route set.
geometryExplanation: The report describes nationwide, repeated internal and cross-border movement without a person-level crosswalk or complete origin, destination and route set.

name: Late-April 1994 Karabakh Armenian front-line displacement
region: Russia, the Caucasus, and Central Asia
displaced: Azerbaijani civilians making a first departure from the named front-line tract because of the late-April 1994 offensive; the reported approximately 50,000 flow overlaps earlier displacement and is not a complete person or household roster
settlers: Karabakh Armenian forces conducted the offensive, with support from Republic of Armenia forces as reported by Human Rights Watch. No incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
evidence: The retained Human Rights Watch report directly identifies the late-April 1994 front, advancing forces and resulting refugee flow, and expressly warns that the reported displaced group included people who had fled earlier offensives.
story:
Human Rights Watch reports that heavy fighting near Agdam and Mardakert in mid-April 1994 developed into a Karabakh Armenian offensive by the beginning of May. The report says Karabakh Armenian forces, with support from forces of the Republic of Armenia, advanced north along the Agdam-Barda road and into Terter and Geranboi.

The report says this fighting created approximately 50,000 Azerbaijani displaced persons. It immediately warns that some of those people had fled earlier offensives. The figure is therefore an overlapping, nonunique report of the refugee flow, not a household count, a roster of first departures, or a structured impact total.

Human Rights Watch also records later interviews with people displaced by the April-May offensive who reported indiscriminate fire and hostage-taking. The report says still-burning villages were visible from the interview location. This evidence supports coercive flight and limited property-damage context, but it does not establish what happened in every village or supply a property-damage denominator.

This case is limited to a first departure from the named front-line tract caused by the late-April 1994 offensive. People already displaced from the same home during the 1993 surrounding-district offensives and people making onward movements are excluded. The source provides no unique-person crosswalk, complete settlement or household roster, exact destinations, return history, or durability finding for this episode.

The 1993 offensives, Operation Ring in 1991, the 1992 Azerbaijani counteroffensive in Mardakert and Geranboi, the Lachin displacement, Kirovabad, Baku and Sumgait violence, and the parent reciprocal-expulsions totals remain separate event units. Their estimates are not combined with the late-April 1994 report.
contested: The approximately 50,000 estimate is overlapping and nonunique. The report supplies no complete settlement or household roster, day-level chronology, unique first-departure crosswalk, exact destinations, return history, property-damage denominator, governing-law change, or bounded livelihood evidence for this episode.
note: The complete frozen eight-trait profile is retained without recoding or interpretation, including insufficient-evidence and structural-not-applicable statuses. Structured impact remains null, geometry remains unknown, and no incoming-flight note is added.
placeGloss: The Agdam-Barda road and the Terter and Geranboi fronts provide textual orientation only.
geometryExplanation: The report names a front and direction of advance but does not establish a complete origin set, destination set, route, or polygon for the displaced population.

name: Somalia state-collapse and inter- and intra-clan conflict displacement, 1991-1995
displaced: Somali civilians internally displaced during the 1991–1995 state-collapse and inter-/intra-clan conflict wave; no complete or deduplicated person-level roster is established
settlers: Armed clan factions and militias drove conflict and displacement. No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
evidence: The retained World Bank report directly labels the 1991–1995 wave, reports the 1992 peak stock, and describes conflict, threat, clan targeting and land-loss mechanisms with explicit mixed-cause and count limits.
story:
The World Bank report separates a 1991–1995 state-collapse and inter- and intra-clan conflict wave from earlier and later phases. It reports approximately two million people internally displaced at the 1992 height and says drought and famine compounded the wave. Movements whose documented immediate trigger is drought or famine remain outside this conflict unit, with conflict retained only as a secondary factor. The two-million figure is a peak stock, not an additive flow or a unique-person event total.

Conflict and threatened violence drove displacement, while forcible land acquisition could remove assets and livelihoods and prompt departure. Clan alignment could provide protection or expose people to abuse. The report gives examples of ex-regime-aligned Darod fleeing south toward the Juba Valley and Kismayo and minority groups losing assets after targeting by dominant clans; these examples do not establish one universal route or experience.

The report also describes early-civil-war appropriation of plantations, real estate and river-valley farming land by militarily stronger clans. Agricultural and minority groups could be displaced and lose access to livelihoods. This supports a land-loss mechanism but does not provide a parcel list, household denominator, complete perpetrator roster or event-wide property outcome.

Somali displacement mixed direct conflict, threat, land loss, drought, famine and other movements, sometimes across more than one episode. Later December-2013 IDP and regional refugee stocks, returnees and repeated-movement cautions are separate context. They are not combined with the 1992 peak, and no refugee, IDP or repeated movement count is adopted as structured impact.

The report separately labels late-1980s displacement and the 1995–2000, 2000–2005, 2005–2009, 2009–2011 and 2011–2014 phases. Because the 1991–1995 and 1995–2000 roster labels overlap at 1995 without a month/day division, this case preserves the frozen outer boundary without assigning every 1995 movement. The Mogadishu 2005–2009 conflict, the contemporaneous Puntland–Somaliland front, and the 2012–2013 eviction case remain distinct.
contested: Approximately two million internally displaced at the 1992 height is a peak stock, not a cumulative flow, refugee count or unique-person total. Drought and famine compounded the wave. The source’s 1991–1995 and 1995–2000 labels overlap at 1995 without a finer dividing date.
note: The complete frozen eight-trait profile is retained without recoding. Low-coverage and partial traits remain visibly uncertain; latent values are not historical findings. Structured impact remains null, geometry remains unknown and no incoming-flight note is added.
placeGloss: Mogadishu, the Juba Valley, Kismayo and river-valley areas provide textual orientation only; examples do not constitute a complete route or event footprint.
geometryExplanation: The report gives national phase labels and selected movement examples but no complete origin set, destination set, person-level crosswalk, route or polygon.

name: Second Congo War internal displacement in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, August 1998–June 2003
