name: Operation Vistula deportation and dispersal
story:
Operation Vistula was carried out under communist rule in Poland in 1947 to move a population that authorities defined as Ukrainian from the southeast to northern and western territories. The article identifies Lemkos as principal victims and describes dispersal away from their native territory.

The source reports military proposals for westward settlement in dispersal and describes rapid planning steps in April 1947. Its interpretation of causes, responsibility and Moscow’s role remains attributed to the author, who also notes unresolved Soviet archival evidence.

The article reports that restoration of public rights for displaced Ukrainians began in 1950. Later cultural measures, limited returns after 1956 and later redress remain separate from the 1947 removal and do not establish complete reversal.
displaced: People whom communist authorities defined as Ukrainian and removed from southeastern Poland, including Lemkos emphasized by the source
Cohort composition and unique-person totals remain unresolved; earlier border transfers and later returns are separate
settlers: Communist state, military and security authorities in Poland directed the removal and dispersed resettlement.
No distinct incoming settler population is established for this event unit.
evidence: Zięba’s article supports the 1947 removal direction, authority-defined affected category, Lemko emphasis, dispersed-resettlement proposals, April planning chronology and the 1950 public-rights marker. Its causal and responsibility arguments are attributed rather than adopted as uncontested findings.
contested: Exact cohort composition, unique deportee total, individual affiliation, causes, Soviet and Polish decision roles, property outcomes, detention, labor, returns, restitution and the event’s terminal meaning remain unresolved or outside this source’s direct support.
note: The frozen 1947–1950 boundary is retained. Earlier 1944–1946 transfers, other Polish-Ukrainian violence, Jaworzno detention, post-1950 return and redress, and later identity politics remain separate.
placeGloss: Southeastern Poland and northern and western receiving territories are textual geography only; no origin, destination, route, settlement point or event polygon is inferred.
geometryExplanation: The source supports district-scale removal from southeastern Poland and dispersal to northern and western territories, but it does not establish a single reliable origin point, destination point, route, settlement point, or event polygon.

name: Rwandan genocide, mass flight, and refugee return
story: Within the frozen 1994–1998 unit, the 1994 genocide and RPF victory were followed by a mainly Hutu exodus of more than two million people. UNHCR attributes that movement to renewed fighting, fear of vengeance and panic organized by the collapsing government. By late August 1994, UNHCR estimated more than two million refugees in neighboring countries; it separately reported about 1.5 million internally displaced people at the end of the year, and the figures are not combined here. Return unfolded in distinct phases: more than 200,000 refugees returned from the Goma area between July 1994 and January 1995 before that movement halted, while a Zairean camp closure forcibly returned about 15,000 people in August 1995. Camp attacks in eastern Zaire in 1996 produced renewed flight and pressure-driven movement back toward Rwanda, and Tanzanian troops separately redirected refugees across the border in December 1996. Through September 1997, UNHCR transported more than 260,000 Rwandans it reached, including about 60,000 flown to Rwanda; the airlift is nested within the transported group and neither figure is added to earlier stocks or flows.
displaced: Mainly Hutu civilians who crossed Rwanda’s borders in 1994, including refugees held under former-government and militia influence in camps
Rwandans internally displaced in 1994; this category remains separate from refugee stocks and return flows
Zairean Tutsi displaced from Masisi and earlier-1959 Tutsi refugees who moved to Rwanda in 1995–1996; these are distinct cohorts
Refugees moving west or returning to Rwanda during the 1994–1997 phases; repeated appearances across stocks and flows are unresolved
settlers: Earlier Tutsi refugees returning to Rwanda are preserved as a distinct return cohort.
The source does not establish a universal settler label, property receipt or common reintegration outcome for returnees.
evidence: UNHCR’s 31-page retrospective chapter distinguishes the 1994 exodus and dated refugee stocks, internal displacement, camp control, phased returns, forced or pressure-driven movements, disputed estimates and nested 1997 transport figures.

name: Burundi civil war and renewed mass displacement

Internal displacement took different forms: some people settled near urban centres and military positions seeking protection from rebel groups, while others, mainly Hutu, were forced by the armed forces into regroupment camps during the second half of the 1990s. All but two conflict parties signed the Arusha Peace Agreement in 2000; the report then records substantial spontaneous return in 2001, organized repatriation beginning in 2002, and elections and a power-sharing constitution in 2005. These markers do not show that every return was voluntary or final, or that all displacement ended in 2005. A 2006 estimate of 100,000 remaining IDPs is retained only as later context and is not combined with the earlier refugee and IDP measures.

name: Macías Nguema’s dictatorship and mass exile from Equatorial Guinea
extent: national dictatorship and dispersed international exile frame
story:
After Equatorial Guinea became independent in 1968, President Francisco Macías Nguema concentrated power in a single-party state. Delmas Tsafack describes decrees that weakened constitutional limits, a party youth and paramilitary apparatus, arbitrary detention, political killings and summary executions. Political opponents, intellectuals, officials and activists were among the first to flee. As the economy deteriorated, a wider group also left in search of safety and workable living conditions. The regime treated departure itself as subversion, making return dangerous.

This was not one administratively counted removal. Tsafack distinguishes people who fled during the dictatorship, students and civil servants already abroad who became unable to return safely, and children later born in exile. Cameroon and Gabon received many refugees; Nigeria and Spain were also destinations. Those country names describe a dispersed exile, not a universal route or destination for every person.

The available estimates describe different populations and moments. Tsafack cites an exile organization that put the number in Cameroon at 40,000 in 1978. He also cites an estimate of about 125,000 Equatoguineans outside the country in 1979, described as roughly one third of the population. A separate 1978 aid program reached 2,011 families, about 7,060 people. These figures are attributed stocks or program counts; they are not added into a new total.

Cameroon, international agencies and church organizations provided food, housing, schooling, work and local-integration assistance. Some refugees worked for sugar companies around Akonolinga and Mbandjock. Earlier writers and Equatoguinean exile organizations alleged that some plantation work was compulsory and abusive, but Tsafack concludes that those allegations are difficult to substantiate from the evidence he examined. That controversy remains separate from the state repression that produced the exile.

Macías was overthrown in 1979. Relations with Cameroon then eased, and the two governments coordinated the repatriation of some refugees. The source gives no total return figure and does not establish that exile, property loss or separation ended for everyone. It also does not identify an incoming population replacing those who left Equatorial Guinea.
displaced: Equatoguinean political opponents, intellectuals, officials, students and other residents driven abroad by repression and economic collapse; people already abroad and unable to return are a distinct cohort
settlers: No incoming settler population is established by the source
evidence: Tsafack's complete article supports the regime, cohort, destination and host-response distinctions; its mediated estimates remain attributed and nonadditive.
contested: The article mediates several estimates through opposition organizations and earlier writers. The 1976, 1978 and 1979 figures have different dates, locations and denominators and are not reconciled. Plantation-compulsion allegations remain disputed. No unique displacement or death total, universal route or destination, general property outcome, complete return rate or incoming settler population is established.
note: The frozen statistical profile is preserved unchanged. The article supports lethal state coercion and mass exile but does not independently recertify the profile values. Nigerian contract workers in Equatorial Guinea, Cameroonian plantation employment and the outgoing Equatoguinean exile are separate cohorts. Geometry remains unknown, structured impact remains unassessed, and this packet creates no structured flight note.

geometryExplanation: The reviewed source does not establish individual origins, border crossings, destinations, route lines, settlement points or an event polygon.

name: Civil-war displacement within and from Sierra Leone
extent: national conflict with recurrent internal and cross-border displacement
story:
Sierra Leone’s civil war ran from 1991 to 2002. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission describes a conflict in which attacks and threats repeatedly uprooted civilians, while killing, pillage and property destruction made many homes and communities unsafe. The commission identifies the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) as the principal driver in its history of the war, while also recording serious violations by the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council, government forces and allied militias. Responsibility for every episode therefore cannot be assigned to one faction.

Flight was recurrent rather than a single outward journey. People moved within Sierra Leone and across borders, especially into Guinea and Liberia. Families were separated. The commission’s chapter on children documents children becoming internally displaced or refugees elsewhere in West Africa; that child-specific evidence is not generalized into a count for the whole civilian population.

Return did not always end the danger. The commission records refugees forced back into Sierra Leone and exposed to renewed abuse, and civilians could be displaced again as control and violence shifted. This case therefore keeps departure, return and renewed displacement distinct. It does not draw one route for a nationwide, changing process.

The commission’s statement database recorded forced displacement more often than any other coded violation and separately recorded killing and property destruction. Those are counts of statements received from a non-random process, not a census or probability sample. They cannot be converted into national totals, added to refugee or internally displaced person stocks, or used as a population severity ranking. The reviewed sources establish recurrent coercive displacement and destruction, but not a universal blocked-return result, a single durable land transfer, or an incoming replacement population.
displaced: Sierra Leonean civilians repeatedly driven from homes and communities within the country and across borders, including into Guinea and Liberia
settlers: RUF as principal driver; AFRC, government forces and allied militias also committed violations; no incoming replacement population is established
evidence: The Sierra Leone Truth and Reconciliation Commission supports the 1991–2002 boundary, actor qualifications and recurrent flight; its statement database is non-random and supplies violation records rather than population totals.
contested: No exact national displacement total, additive refugee-and-IDP total, universal itinerary, complete return rate, universal blocked-return outcome, durable land-transfer result or incoming replacement population is established. Child-specific evidence is not generalized to all civilians, and statement counts are not treated as population estimates.
note: The exact frozen eight-trait profile and family are preserved unchanged. Killing, property destruction, internal displacement, cross-border refuge, return and renewed displacement remain separate outcomes. Structured impact is unassessed, geometry is unknown, and this packet creates no structured flight note.
placeGloss: Sierra Leone is the regional camera anchor. Guinea and Liberia are documented receiving-country context, not endpoints assigned to every displaced person.
geometryExplanation: The reviewed sources describe recurrent nationwide and cross-border movement but do not establish one representative origin, destination, route line, settlement point or event polygon.

name: ADF attack-driven displacement from Beni Territory and nearby Ituri villages, January–March 2021
extent: Beni Territory in North Kivu and only nearby Ituri villages directly included in the same reported episode
story:
UNHCR reported on 19 March 2021 that attacks since January, blamed on the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), had killed nearly 200 people, injured dozens and displaced an estimated 40,000 people in Beni Territory in North Kivu and nearby villages in Ituri. It said the ADF had allegedly raided 25 villages, burned dozens of houses and kidnapped more than 70 people. These are qualified attributions from the briefing, not findings that assign every incident to the group. The same source reported that the attacks were associated with retaliation against military operations, searches for food and medicine, and accusations that communities had shared information about ADF positions.

The estimated 40,000 describes the recent wave observed from January through 19 March. It is kept separate from about 100,000 people who were already displaced in Beni before that wave. It is also separate from 465 deaths attributed to ADF attacks during 2020, later provincial stocks and flows, displacement attributed to other armed groups, and later ADF activity. None of those figures is added to the 40,000 or treated as a count of unique households or people followed across time.

For people displaced during March, UNHCR named Oicha, Beni and Butembo as places of flight and said many travelled by motorbike. The source described the majority as women and children and said some men stayed behind to protect property, exposing themselves to further danger. That pattern is not generalized to every household, and the named places do not establish one route used by everyone. The briefing described severe shortages of shelter, food, water and health care after flight.

This case ends at the briefing’s observation cutoff, not at the end of ADF activity. The reviewed source establishes attack-driven departure and the burning of houses, but it does not establish return timing, title transfer, permanent vacancy, replacement settlement, governance change, labor incorporation or a durable demographic outcome. Those questions remain unknown. Later ADF operations and other Ituri displacement belong to separate periods or event units unless a future person-level review links them.
displaced: An estimated 40,000 civilians displaced during the January–19 March 2021 wave from Beni Territory and directly included nearby Ituri villages; the pre-existing Beni displacement population is excluded
settlers: Attacks were blamed on or attributed to the ADF; the source does not establish an incoming replacement population, and attribution remains qualified
evidence: The complete official UNHCR briefing body supports the observation window, qualified attribution, reported attacks, house burning, kidnapping, named March destinations and the estimated recent displacement wave.
contested: The briefing does not establish attribution for every incident, a deduplicated longitudinal count, a universal household pattern or route, return timing, title transfer, permanent vacancy, replacement settlement, governance change, labor incorporation or durable demographic outcome.
note: All 60 frozen score cells remain blank and all 60 frozen N/A cells remain U. Governance and law, labor and economy, and demography and durability remain explicit evidence gaps. Geometry is unknown, structured impact is unassessed, and this packet creates no incoming-flight note.
placeGloss: Beni Territory in North Kivu is the regional anchor. Nearby Ituri villages, Oicha, Beni and Butembo are source-named orientation only and do not create a route or event geometry.
geometryExplanation: The source names a territory, nearby villages and three places of flight but does not provide village identities, complete origins, one universal itinerary, coordinates, a route line, settlement points or an event polygon.

name: Zanzibar revolutionary property confiscation and land redistribution
extent: Published confiscation-order evidence and documented land administration across Unguja and Pemba; the dataset is incomplete and does not delimit every taking
story:
Presidential Decree No. 8 of 1964 empowered the Zanzibar state to seize immovable property in the national interest without compensation, while its text included an undue-hardship proviso. The 1965 Public Lands Decree placed land under government guardianship, and the 1966 Land Distribution Decree enabled confiscated property to be merged and distributed. The reviewed study also documents takings outside published orders and procedures that were followed unevenly, so the formal decrees do not describe every seizure.

Joireman and Verne assembled published English- and Swahili-language Gazette confiscation orders from 1964 through the latest order they recorded, in September 1987. Their explicitly incomplete dataset contains 1,565 properties: 990 recorded in the 1960s, 527 in the 1970s, and 48 in the 1980s; 1,195 were on Unguja, 363 on Pemba, and seven could not be located. The separately reported 544 properties for 1965 are included within the 1,565. These are property units, not people, households, orders, acres, departures, or a census of all confiscation.

The recorded takings included houses and land in urban and rural areas across Unguja and Pemba. Arab and Asian owners were primary targets in the records discussed, and South Asian names made up more than half of the 1970s confiscations, but the study states that confiscation was not limited to one ethnic group. Some properties were taken after owners fled; others were confiscated whether or not their owners had left, and some Asian owners were made homeless. Confiscation therefore cannot be used as a proxy for expulsion, route, exile, or a single ethnic victim population.

Redistribution is measured separately. From 1965 to 1972, more than 22,000 families received three-acre rights-of-occupancy covering about 70,000 acres. Those beneficiary and acreage measures are not counts of dispossessed owners or refugees and do not establish incoming replacement settlement. The authors found 26 revocation orders and one official cancellation between 1964 and 1987; some property was returned formally or informally, while other families continued to seek restitution decades later. September 1987 is the latest recorded published order in an incomplete dataset, not proof that confiscation or its consequences ended then. The source does not establish universal confiscation, universal permanent loss, a common route or return pattern, or one-for-one replacement.
affected: Owners of confiscated houses and land across Unguja and Pemba; Arab and Asian owners were primary targets in discussed records, but confiscation was not limited to one ethnic group
actors: Zanzibar Revolutionary Government and its land, confiscation and distribution institutions
beneficiaries: More than 22,000 families received three-acre rights-of-occupancy during 1965–1972; this is a redistribution measure and does not establish incoming replacement settlement
evidence: The complete Joireman and Verne article supports the legal instruments, incomplete published-order dataset, property-unit totals and distribution, affected-property descriptions, redistribution measures, and limited revocations through the latest recorded September 1987 order.
contested: The source does not establish a complete confiscation census, one universal ethnic victim population, universal confiscation or permanent loss, a count of unique affected people or households, departure from confiscation, route, return migration, replacement settlement, or an end to consequences in September 1987.
note: All 60 raw score cells, N/A types, nine-factor projections, family assignment, geometry, structured impact, flight composition and population-scale indicators remain independently unassessed. No field is inherited from the frozen parent.
geometryExplanation: The article provides island-level and mapped property-order evidence, but this preparation does not convert it into event geometry. No route, point set, polygon, or replacement pattern is proposed.

periods.endpointGuard: First confiscation decree to latest recorded published order in an incomplete dataset; not the end of all confiscation or consequences.

name: Expulsion, partial return, and continuing displacement of Tawergha residents
extent: Tawergha and source-documented displacement and return contexts within Libya; some flight abroad is documented, but complete destinations, routes and geometry are unknown
story:
In August 2011, Misrata-based armed groups attacked Tawergha. An OHCHR investigation reported that the town population, estimated at 42,600, was displaced to other parts of Libya or fled abroad. It documented murder, torture and cruel treatment of Tawerghans by Misrata-based armed groups and reported that the town was subsequently destroyed. OHCHR described retaliation for perceived support for the Qadhafi government and alleged abuses by some Tawerghans, while saying discrimination against dark-skinned Libyans may also have fuelled the actions. Those contextual findings do not assign wartime conduct, allegiance or a racial identity to every resident.

Return remained blocked for years. In June 2017 the Government of National Accord ratified a Misrata–Tawergha agreement allowing displaced residents to return, and the UN urged a prompt, dignified, safe and unconditional return. Permission and an agreement were not completed return. Later sources document partial returns rather than one clean reversal of the expulsion.

IOM reported 17,252 people displaced from Tawergha across more than 30 municipalities at the end of 2022, including 6,425 people in informal collective sites in eastern Libya. By mid-2023 it reported 15,000 people, or 3,000 families, returned to Tawergha, while close to 17,000 internally displaced people, or 3,400 families, remained displaced. These are dated measurements from different rounds and methods. They are not added to the 2011 estimate or treated as a complete accounting of unique people.

UN Women fieldwork in 2024 and UN reporting for 2025 describe damaged or uninhabitable homes, reconstruction costs, infrastructure and service gaps, safety concerns, unresolved property disputes, and mixed choices about return or continued residence elsewhere. A 2025 UN results report still described a smaller residual Tawergha displacement caseload with protection and service gaps. The evidence therefore supports expulsion, years of blocked return, later partial return, and residual displacement through 2025. It does not establish event-wide property seizure or title transfer, settler replacement, completed compensation, completed return, or conditions after 2025.
displaced: Residents of Tawergha displaced in 2011; later return and residual-displacement statuses are kept as dated, partially overlapping observations
settlers: Misrata-based armed groups carried out the original attack and expulsion; later governmental and local authorities appear only in agreement, return and reintegration processes; no incoming replacement population is established
evidence: Six official full bodies support the August 2011 attack and mass displacement, town destruction, years of blocked return, later partial returns, and residual displacement and barriers through the 2025 reporting period.
contested: The reviewed bodies do not establish a universal racial identity or wartime allegiance, additive person count, complete route, event-wide property seizure or title transfer, incoming settler replacement, completed compensation, completed return or durable solution, or conditions after 2025.
note: The outcome family is decided de novo as expulsion or flight without replacement. All eight factor decisions are source-bound qualitative decisions; no inherited or newly invented numeric point is displayed because the accepted packet does not provide a new 60-cell coding and projection. Impact and geometry remain unassessed. The post-2025 endpoint remains held.
placeGloss: Tawergha is the event anchor. More than 30 municipalities and some flight abroad describe dispersal, not one universal route or complete destination set.
geometryExplanation: Sources name Tawergha and dispersed locations but do not establish complete origins, destinations, one representative itinerary, coordinates, a route line, event polygon or replacement-settlement geometry.

name: First Congo War and destruction of refugee camps in eastern Zaire
extent: Eastern Zaire refugee camps and source-documented pursuit, flight and return contexts within the frozen1996–1997 unit; no complete route or destination set
story:
In 1996, AFDL forces and their Rwandan allies attacked refugee camps in eastern Zaire. This area is now part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Most refugees in the Uvira and Goma camps were unarmed civilians. Some camps also held armed groups, including former Rwandan army members and Interahamwe militia.

At Mugunga on 15 November 1996, AFDL and Rwandan forces ordered refugees to return to Rwanda. Other refugees had chosen to return. Still others fled west through Zaire. These movements followed different routes and took place under different conditions. They cannot all be classed as forced returns or voluntary returns.

The UN Mapping Report records killings of refugees and Congolese civilians. It also reports killings of local people who hid or helped refugees. Pursuing forces blocked aid in some areas. Refugees died from hunger, illness and exhaustion. In some incidents, promises of return or aid drew people to places where they were killed.

Camp attacks and later pursuit continued into 1997. Camps were burned or dismantled, and refugees moved between sites or into forests. The sources do not establish a single death toll, unique displacement total or share forced to return. Camp occupancy does not prove property ownership. Title transfers and settlement by a replacement population remain unknown.

In 2010, the Mapping Report said that some acts could support a finding of genocide if proved. It also discussed competing explanations and partly voluntary returns. This was a conditional legal assessment, not a court ruling. The case covers 1996–1997; later events are separate context.
displaced: Rwandan civilian refugees, including Hutu refugees; Burundian refugees in documented companion cohorts; Congolese civilians at documented incidents. Armed members remain a distinct group.
settlers: AFDL and Rwandan allied forces attacked and pursued refugees; other armed groups appear only at source-specific incidents. No incoming replacement population is established.
evidence: OHCHR’s 2010 Mapping Report documents alleged incidents under its reasonable-suspicion method. Attacks, killings, deprivation, flight and differentiated returns are source-located.
contested: Unique cumulative deaths, displacement and forced-return shares are unknown. No blanket combatant identity, collective guilt, universal return category, formal land title transfer or settler replacement. Genocide discussion is conditional and attributed to the 2010 report; no present-day judgment claim.
note: The frozen family and all eight traits are retained exactly for display, without new coding. Incident estimates, repeated camp stocks and returns are not added or subtracted. Note 300 contains a 1997/2009 citation-year conflict; the corresponding UNHCR body was not read. Paragraph 252 chronology remains qualified. The frozen 2009 UNHCR link is not used as contemporary event evidence.
placeGloss: Great Lakes Africa is the source-region label. Named camps and pursuit sites do not establish one complete itinerary.
geometryExplanation: The accepted source account describes multiple cohorts, camp attacks, flight and returns. It does not establish complete movement endpoints, a representative route, exact coordinates or an event footprint. No geometry is inferred from a route schematic.

name: Korean War civilian flight and permanent division
extent: Korean civilian flight, evacuation, constrained return and bounded resettlement during 1950–1953; cohorts and routes differ, and complete origins, destinations and geometry remain unknown
story:
The Korean War drove civilians from their homes in more than one wave. In summer 1950, many South Korean civilians fled south as North Korean forces advanced. In winter 1950–1951, refugees from North Korea and South Korean evacuees formed different groups.

South Korean officials first gave evacuation help to political leaders and foreigners. As fighting neared Seoul, other civilians moved farther south. Early destruction of the Han River bridges and later destruction at Waegwan killed civilians, trapped people, and blocked escape.

The winter retreat caused another wave as northern civilians fled bombing and pressure to join armed forces. South Korean civilians left before the renewed advance. Some people traveled by sea or rail, while many walked. Hŭngnam, island camps, and specific rail trips show routes for specific groups. They do not describe one route for all civilians.

Return differed by group, and some rural people in the South returned sooner. Return to Seoul stayed delayed and controlled. Refugees from the North and others who were unable to reach former homes resettled in South Korea. By August 1953, many migrants from North to South tended to settle in new areas. These areas lay near the demilitarized zone, military sites, and small or medium cities.

Relief and rebuilding did not end these differences. Camps, homes, short-term work, and aid rules changed by place, time, and agency, so their records cannot be joined into one total. The source supports flight, limits on return, and different places of residence. It does not show that all civilians stayed away for good. It also gives no general proof of title loss, one death toll, or exact routes.
displaced: Korean civilians displaced in distinct summer 1950 and winter 1950–1951 waves, including South Korean internally displaced people and evacuees and refugees who fled from North Korea
settlers: North Korean, South Korean, Chinese, United States and United Nations Command forces shaped advances, retreats and flight; South Korean and United Nations authorities also organized or restricted evacuation, transport, relief and return; no incoming replacement population is established
evidence: Kim’s 2010 synthesis separates summer internal flight, winter northern refugee and southern evacuation movements, later return controls, relocation and residence outcomes. The source is mediated and its damaged numeric tables are not used.
contested: Unique movers, cohort shares, deaths, complete routes and destinations remain unknown. The evidence does not establish universal permanent nonreturn, event-wide title loss, forced labor, incoming settler replacement or precise geometry.
note: The frozen outcome family and all eight trait values are carried forward without reinterpretation. “Permanent division” applies only to bounded cross-border separation and not to every South Korean evacuee or internally displaced person. No damaged table value is transcribed or used.
placeGloss: Seoul, Waegwan, Hŭngnam, island camps and the demilitarized-zone settlement pattern identify source-specific places. They do not form one universal route or a complete destination set.
geometryExplanation: The source describes several civilian cohorts, routes, controls and residence outcomes. It does not establish complete endpoints, exact coordinates, one representative route or an event footprint.

name: Maʻafu’s conquest and land reorganization in Lau

periods.label: Moala campaigns
periods.note: Chiefly submission, property removal and changed authority in Moala, Matuku and Totoya.

periods.label: Vanuabalavu control
periods.note: Religious war, control and establishment at Lomaloma; no inferred mass settlement in 1854.

periods.label: Land allotment and chiefdom
periods.note: Measured allotments, tax and tribute relations; formal consolidation in 1869.

story:
Maʻafu's forces began their Moala campaigns in December 1852. War and changes in faith brought chiefs under new rule. The campaigns affected Moala, Matuku, and Totoya. Spurway describes property taken to Lakeba and changes in chiefly rule. These accounts do not show that all residents left.

Religious war also changed control of Vanuabalavu. Maʻafu took control and based himself at Lomaloma in 1855. The sources do not show mass Tongan settlement there in 1854. Later land records and local accounts describe changes in rule and land control.

The later system divided land into measured plots and tied access to taxes. France describes plots for adult men who paid tax. Established Tongan residents and warriors who stayed also received plots. Pauwels describes fertile coastal plots and original owners who lost control. The accounts do not show that all land was seized or all residents expelled.

The agreement of 15 February 1869 formed the Chiefdom of Lau. It defined rule, tax, and tribute ties among the named islands. This date marks the formal chiefdom, not an end to land disputes. Many residents and chiefs remained under the changed system.

This case follows one event in three phases. Removals at Mago and Munia remain separate leads for further work. They do not supply this event's removal evidence. The number displaced, death share, and full land loss remain unknown. The map shows regional context because exact event geometry is unknown.
displaced: Residents, chiefs and original landholders of the named Lauan tracts; no generalized parent-level expulsion is established.
settlers: Maʻafu and his Tongan campaign following; established Tongan residents and warriors who stayed and received land.
note: Three phases form one parent event. Mago and Munia/Yanuyanu removals remain separate. The profile uses the accepted fixed mapping; it does not place this case in the active statistical release.
geometryExplanation: Named islands and land processes are documented. Exact source-bound event points, routes and footprints are not established in this application.

name: Almoravid deportation of Andalusi Christians to the Maghreb
extent: Named Andalusi Christian groups in an autumn 1126 removal order; Seville is best documented, with Granada and Córdoba qualified. Destinations and routes are incomplete.
story:
In autumn 1126, the Almoravid emir ordered the removal of documented Christian groups from al-Andalus. The emir had sought a jurist’s advice. The record names groups from Seville, Granada, and Córdoba. It does not show that every Christian in those cities was removed.

Families and church leaders were among those sent south. Some people from Seville went to Meknes. The sources do not give one route or one destination for all groups. They also do not give a sound mover count.

Armed men chased some people from Seville. After removal, some owners asked to sell property back home. Legal replies set rules for those sales. A church and its endowment also changed hands in one recorded case. These records do not show that all Christian property was seized.

Evidence from 1127 shows the aftermath of the order. It does not extend this case past 1126. A reported movement in 1138 is held as a separate event. Northbound flight tied to Alfonso I is also outside this case.

The sources do not give the share removed, the death share, or a return rate. They do not prove total Christian extinction or a replacement settlement. Places are kept as text because the full routes and endpoints are not known.
displaced: Documented groups of Andalusi Christians, including families and church leaders; not every Christian in each named city.
settlers: No incoming replacement population is established for this bounded case.
evidence: Specialist studies reconstruct the emiral order, armed enforcement, post-removal sale requests and legal procedures, and a specific church and endowment change from legal and narrative records.
contested: The exact mover count, removed share, death share, return rate, route set, destination set, custody, duration, blanket confiscation, total extinction, and replacement settlement are not established.
note: The case ends in 1126. Evidence from 1127 is aftermath. A reported 1138 movement remains a separate hold. Juristic advice is distinct from the emir’s order. The cited studies share some underlying legal traditions and are not counted as independent witnesses.
placeGloss: Europe / North Africa is a broad source-region label. Named places remain text context and do not create coordinates, a route, or a single destination.
geometryExplanation: Accepted sources name source communities and some destinations, but coverage is unequal and no complete or representative route is established. No map primitive is proposed.

name: Soviet collectivization, sedentarization, and the Kazakh famine
story:
In 1929–1930, Soviet authorities planned to settle Kazakh herders in large settlements. The plans aimed to free land for grain and expand collective farms. Much construction failed, and settlement sites stood empty. A further large settlement scheme in 1931 did not move beyond planning.

The famine was most severe in 1931–1933. Historian Niccolò Pianciola links its start to grain seizures and disruption from collectivization. In his 2018 account, violent forced settlement was not the usual cause. He argues that famine instead left people dependent on the state and led to partial settlement.

People fled before 1931, and flight grew during the famine. Some returned; others were forced back. A July 1932 letter described official pressure forcing people back from near Biysk, despite starvation. Receiving areas also saw violence and denied refugees shelter or food.

People who returned still faced shortages and violence. In Lapsinsk, Kurdaj and Chilinsk districts, officials ordered former nomads off collective farms. They sent them to uninhabited areas without seed or equipment.

A March 1933 letter reported that state farms received the best land. Commission records also described limits on taking animals to pasture. They recorded abandoned mountain pastures and loss of the former herding economy. These local accounts do not show the fate of every household or plot.

In March 1933, official policy called large European-style settlements a mistake. Conditions improved after that year's harvest, but recovery was limited. In December 1934, the state raised limits on privately owned livestock. Returns continued after 1934. That year does not mark the end of all famine effects or a completed return.

These accounts distinguish failed plans, forced returns, local expulsions and loss of pasture. They do not give one total for people forced to move. Deaths, flight, livestock loss and settlement totals measure different things.
displaced: Kazakh herders and returnees described in this account
settlers: Soviet state and local officials
evidence: Pianciola’s studies from 2004 and 2018
geometryExplanation: The sources do not establish a route, point or boundary for this display.

name: Slavery, indenture and colonial residence in the Mascarenes and Seychelles
extent: Selected enslaved transfers and residence in Bourbon/Réunion and Seychelles, and Mauritius indenture, estate residence and later worker landholding. The full island-period cohort is not measured.
story:
Colonial settlements in these islands drew on slave transport and contract labour. This case spans 1638 to about 1920. The sources describe selected groups and periods within that frame.

In 1718, the Courrier de Bourbon brought enslaved Malagasy people to Bourbon for coffee plantations. Bourbon is now Réunion. A ship record for 1807 lists enslaved people brought from Tamatave. Some ships stopped or transferred captives between islands. A landing does not always show where each person later lived.

The Seychelles museum describes a 1770 voyage from Île de France to Sainte Anne. Île de France is now Mauritius. Its list names seven Africans as enslaved. The account does not state the status of five Indians or a woman named Marie. It describes a move to Mahé in 1771 and another arrival with slaves in 1778. It does not show each person's later fate or task.

In Mauritius, indentured labour began in 1834 and continued into the 1910s. The article describes medical checks, contracts, quarantine and placement on sugar estates. Contracts differed from slavery, but the authors describe harsh work and colonial control. This does not prove forced recruitment or transport for every worker.

Some former workers finished contracts and bought small plots. From about 1875, large estates were divided and sold. By the late 1870s, some returnees recruited relatives in Bihar. Other workers renewed contracts. The sources do not show these paths for every worker.

Slave voyage totals, arrivals and resident populations measure different things. They cannot give one number for people forced to move across all islands. Disease records also do not give a death toll for this whole case. The share affected, later fates and complete routes remain unknown.
displaced: Enslaved Malagasy and African groups in specific island arrivals; Indian indentured workers in Mauritius, with differing recruitment, contract and residence histories. Not every traveller is shown to have been forced to depart.
settlers: Colonial authorities, traders and plantation owners shaped settlement and labour systems. Enslaved arrivals, contracted workers, former-worker landholders and returnee recruiters are distinct, possibly overlapping roles.
evidence: Reviewed French regional scholarship, an official Seychelles museum account and a full Mauritius historical article support selected transfers and residence outcomes. Allen’s official chapter summary supplies broad context only.
contested: The total forced to move, share affected, death share, complete routes, individual capture histories, later fates and exact endpoint remain unknown. No Indigenous replacement or universal forced indenture is inferred.
note: The frozen family and eight trait values remain unchanged. Their labels do not mean that every arrival was forced, every worker stayed away for good, or a prior Indigenous population was replaced. Slave transport and indentured recruitment are kept distinct. Disease figures are not a death toll for this case.
placeGloss: Bourbon is now Réunion; Île de France is now Mauritius. Source places and port calls remain text. They do not establish one route for all groups. Two selected links are shown: 1770 Île de France to Sainte Anne; 1807 Tamatave to Bourbon. They are place references, not ship tracks. The 1718 departure port remains unmapped.
geometryExplanation: Two selected voyage links are shown: Île de France to Sainte Anne in 1770, and Tamatave to Bourbon in 1807. Island and town points are approximate place references. The arcs do not show ship tracks. The 1718 Bourbon arrival is known; its departure port is not mapped. Other cohorts and complete histories remain unmapped.
